## Binance Impersonation Scam UK: Spot a Fake Message

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/binance-impersonation-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake Binance emails and texts claim your account is suspended, to steal your login. Binance's own Verify tool confirms if a message is genuine.

### What a Binance impersonation message looks like

This scam is an email, text, or direct message designed to look like it's from Binance, warning of suspicious login activity, a security hold, or account suspension. An example of the style: `Unusual login detected on your Binance account. Verify your identity within 24 hours or your account will be permanently suspended.` The message links to a fake Binance login page that captures your email and password the moment you enter them, giving the scammer direct access to your real account and any cryptocurrency in it.

### Warning signs of a fake Binance message

- It creates urgency: "immediate action required", "suspicious login detected", or a countdown to suspension.
- The sender's address or the link's domain is close to, but not exactly, binance.com — small misspellings or extra words are the tell.
- It arrives via social media DM, WhatsApp, or Telegram with account-security instructions you cannot verify inside your Binance account.
- If you've set one up, the message does not include your personal anti-phishing code, or the code looks wrong.
- You're asked to click a link to "verify", "unlock", or "reactivate" your account rather than being told to log in directly.
- Someone offers to "recover" your account or funds for a fee after contacting you about a supposed problem — this is a follow-up scam.

### How the scam works step by step

A message arrives claiming a problem with your Binance account, often urgent and threatening in tone. It contains a link to a page built to look identical to Binance's real login. You enter your email and password there, believing you're logging into your genuine account — the scammer now has those credentials and can log into your real Binance account immediately. If two-factor authentication isn't enabled, they can move any cryptocurrency held there straight to a wallet they control, usually within minutes, and often route it through several wallets afterwards to make tracing harder.

### How to check a Binance message is genuine

Don't click the link. Open a browser and type `binance.com` directly, or use the official Binance app, and check your account and security notifications there — a genuine alert should be checkable inside your account, not only in a message. Use Binance Verify, Binance's own tool for checking whether a URL, email address, phone number, Telegram contact, or social account is officially linked to Binance, before acting on anything. If you've set up a personal anti-phishing code in your account settings, check that the message contains the correct code. Binance also says it will never ask you to send funds or tokens through private communications. Report anything suspicious through Binance's in-app Support chat rather than replying to the message.

### What to do if you've already entered your details

Change your Binance password immediately from a different, trusted device, and enable two-factor authentication if it isn't already on. Check your account's recent activity and withdrawal history for anything you don't recognise. If cryptocurrency has already left your account, report it to Binance Support straight away with the transaction details and wallet address — acting fast gives the best (though still limited) chance of a receiving exchange freezing funds before they move on. Change the password on any other account that shares the same email or password, starting with your email provider.

### How to report a Binance impersonation scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, including the message, sender details, and any wallet address involved. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Forward a phishing email to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`, or a text to 7726, and report the impersonation to Binance directly through in-app Support.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Binance itself safe, or should I stop using it?**

Binance is a real cryptocurrency exchange, but crypto is high risk and that does not make any message using Binance branding genuine. In the UK, Binance is not FCA-authorised, and Binance announced in October 2023 that it had stopped accepting new UK users, so check the FCA's consumer warnings before relying on it. Access your account only by typing binance.com directly or via the official app, never through a link in an email, text, or DM, and keep two-factor authentication switched on.

**How can I check whether a Binance email is genuine?**

Use Binance Verify, the platform's own tool for checking whether a URL, email address, phone number, or social account is officially linked to Binance, and check whether the email contains the correct personal anti-phishing code if you've set one up. Never rely on how official a message looks alone.

**I entered my Binance password on a fake site — what now?**

Change your password immediately from a different device and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already active. Check your recent account activity, and if any cryptocurrency has already been moved, report it to Binance Support right away with the wallet address.

**How do I report a Binance impersonation scam?**

Report to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). Forward phishing emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk`, texts to 7726, and report the impersonation to Binance directly through in-app Support.

## Bitcoin ATM Scam UK: Why a Caller Sending You to One Is a Scam

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/bitcoin-atm-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Scammers pose as your bank or HMRC and walk you to a Bitcoin ATM to 'secure' your money. No genuine official will ask you to do this.

### What the Bitcoin ATM scam looks like

This scam is a phone call, text, or email — usually claiming to be your bank's fraud team, HMRC, or a tech-support agent — that convinces you your money or device is at risk and the only fix is to withdraw cash and feed it into a Bitcoin ATM. An example of the style: `To secure your account, withdraw £3,000 and deposit it at your nearest Bitcoin machine using this QR code.` The machines themselves are physical kiosks that convert cash to cryptocurrency, but the scam is the instruction: no genuine bank, HMRC contact, or legitimate support service will ask you to use one to protect money or fix an account.

### Why the FCA treats crypto ATMs as high risk

Any business that runs a cryptoasset ATM in the UK must register with the FCA under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017 — and none of the firms registered with the FCA is approved to offer crypto ATM services. The FCA's position is blunt: any crypto ATM operating in the UK is doing so illegally, its enforcement action has shut machines down across the country, and it warns consumers not to use them at all. There is no 'legitimate' machine to look for — and never use any crypto ATM because an unexpected caller, texter, or "support" contact told you to.

### Warning signs of the scam

- An unexpected call, text, or email claims a problem with your bank account, tax affairs, or computer, and creates urgency to act immediately.
- You're told to withdraw cash and convert it to cryptocurrency at a Bitcoin ATM to "secure", "verify", or "protect" your money.
- You're given a QR code or wallet address to scan or enter at the machine, described as a "safe", "holding", or "verification" account.
- You're asked to stay on the phone throughout, or told not to mention the real reason for the payment to anyone, including staff near the machine.
- The caller can quote your name, and sometimes partial account details, but cannot be verified independently — this proves nothing, since such details are often obtained from data breaches.
- No genuine bank, HMRC officer, or tech-support agent will ever direct you to a Bitcoin ATM.

### How to check a call like this is genuine

Hang up and contact the organisation yourself, using the number on your card, a genuine bill, or their official website — never a number given to you by the caller. Genuine banks, HMRC, and legitimate tech-support services never ask you to withdraw cash and convert it to cryptocurrency at an ATM, under any circumstances; treat that instruction alone as conclusive proof of a scam, regardless of how convincing the caller sounds. Check your real account directly through your bank's app or by logging into it independently, rather than trusting anything the caller tells you about it. If you're also asked to visit a link, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### What to do if you've already used one

Stop all contact with the caller immediately — do not send anything further, even if told an extra payment will reverse the transaction. Contact your bank straight away to explain what happened; while cryptocurrency itself typically can't be recovered once sent, your bank can flag your account and watch for further fraud, and the venue or ATM operator may hold camera footage worth preserving. Report the wallet address you sent funds to, along with the phone number and any messages, to Report Fraud — this helps investigators trace and disrupt the network even when your own funds can't be recovered. Report Fraud covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland. If you live in Scotland or the crime happened there, contact Police Scotland on 101.

### How to report a Bitcoin ATM scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, with the wallet address, phone number, and machine location. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. If contact came by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; by text, forward it free to 7726.

### Frequently asked questions

**Are Bitcoin ATMs legal in the UK?**

There are no legally operating crypto ATMs in the UK: operators must be FCA-registered, no registered firm is approved to offer crypto ATM services, and the FCA says any machine operating here is doing so illegally and warns consumers not to use them. A caller telling you to use a Bitcoin ATM is enough on its own to treat the contact as a scam.

**My bank/HMRC/tech support told me to use a Bitcoin ATM to fix a problem — is that genuine?**

No. No genuine UK bank, HMRC officer, or legitimate tech-support service will ever ask you to withdraw cash and feed it into a Bitcoin ATM for any reason. This instruction is on its own enough to confirm a scam — hang up and contact the real organisation using a number you find independently.

**I've already sent money through a Bitcoin ATM to a scammer — can I get it back?**

It's very difficult, since cryptocurrency sent to a scammer's wallet typically can't be reversed. Contact your bank to flag your account, and report the wallet address and phone number to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland — this won't usually recover your funds but helps investigators build a picture of the network.

**How do I report a Bitcoin ATM scam?**

Report to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland), including the wallet address and phone number used. Forward a related email to `report@phishing.gov.uk` or a text to 7726.

## Bitcoin Scam UK: Spot a Fake Crypto Investment

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/bitcoin-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Approached about a Bitcoin 'investment opportunity' promising guaranteed returns? How to spot a Bitcoin scam, protect your wallet, and report it in the UK.

### What a Bitcoin scam looks like

A Bitcoin scam uses the promise of guaranteed or fast returns to get you to send cryptocurrency to a fraudster, hand over your wallet details, or invest through a fake platform. Contact often comes through social media, a dating app, or an unsolicited call. An example of the style is: `Our AI trading bot guarantees 20% weekly returns on Bitcoin. Deposit now and start withdrawing profits within days.`

Once a Bitcoin payment is confirmed there is no cancellation or chargeback mechanism, and only the person who received it can choose to send it back. This guide shows the warning signs, how to protect yourself, and what to do if you have already sent crypto.

### Why these scams are convincing

Bitcoin's real-world price rises fuel a fear of missing out, and slick platforms with fake trading dashboards showing rising "profits" look genuine. Scammers on dating apps or social media may build a relationship for weeks before introducing the "investment", a pattern often called relationship-investment fraud.

The fact that protects you: a promise of guaranteed or unusually high returns is a serious scam warning, and the FCA says crypto is high risk and you should be prepared to lose all the money you invest.

### Signs a Bitcoin opportunity is a scam

- It promises guaranteed, fixed, or unusually high returns.
- You are shown a dashboard with rising "profits" that you can never actually withdraw.
- You are asked to deposit more to "unlock" a withdrawal or cover a fake tax or fee.
- The contact came from an unsolicited call, message, dating app, or social media.
- You are pressured to act quickly, or told the opportunity is exclusive.
- You are asked to move crypto to a wallet or platform you cannot independently verify.
- A "recovery" service later offers to get your lost crypto back for a fee - this is a second scam sign.

### How the scam works

First, contact begins through an unsolicited approach, social media, or a dating app. Second, trust is built, sometimes over weeks. Third, you are shown a platform or app with rising profits and encouraged to deposit more. Fourth, when you try to withdraw, you are told to pay a fee or tax first, or the platform simply disappears with your crypto.

Because a confirmed Bitcoin payment cannot be undone, verifying any platform independently before you send anything is the only real protection.

### How to protect yourself

Treat a Bitcoin pitch promising guaranteed or unusually high returns as a serious scam warning. Do not send until you have independently checked the firm, the promotion and the receiving party.

- Think about the payment rail before you think about the pitch. Bitcoin itself has no chargeback or cancellation mechanism once a payment is confirmed. A card or bank provider may have a dispute or recovery process of its own, though that is not a simple recall right on an ordinary bank transfer, so sending Bitcoin is effectively the last decision you get to make.
- Do not use a crypto ATM. As checked on 26 July 2026, the FCA says there are no legally operated crypto ATMs in the UK. Check the FCA's current guidance before relying on that status because registrations and rules can change.
- Do not send Bitcoin solely because an online friend, romantic contact, broker or support agent supplied a wallet address. Independently establish who controls it and why payment is due.
- Refuse any "fee" or "tax" charged for unlocking your own profits; paying it usually just funds the next demand.
- Your private keys and recovery phrase go to nobody: not support staff, not a broker, not anyone offering to fix your account.

For the relationship-led version of this fraud, see our /guides/pig-butchering-scam-uk/ guide; /guides/crypto-investment-scams-uk-protection/ covers fake platforms, FCA registration checks and celebrity-endorsement adverts.

### If you have already sent Bitcoin

Copy the transaction IDs and the destination wallet addresses now. An on-chain record is one of the few pieces of evidence that survives a platform disappearing.

Contact the exchange or app used to make the withdrawal immediately. It may be able to stop a pending withdrawal or flag an account it controls, but a confirmed payment to a self-hosted wallet cannot be reversed by the exchange. Preserve the transaction ID, wallet address, account history and messages for the provider and investigators.

Be realistic about what follows. Much of the useful work is closing off the accounts and identity exposure around the loss — the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets those steps out in order.

### How to report a Bitcoin scam (UK)

Report it first to the provider you actually used to send the funds, and give it the transaction IDs and destination addresses. A custodial exchange or app may be able to halt a pending withdrawal or restrict an account it controls; a non-custodial wallet service may have no account to act on at all.

Tell the Financial Conduct Authority about the investment platform or the promotion behind it, using its financial promotion form for an authorised firm or its scam contact route and consumer helpline on 0800 111 6768 for a suspected unauthorised or clone firm.

Then file the loss itself through the national fraud route: `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Scam emails and texts have their own forwarding routes, set out in the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Bitcoin itself a scam?**

No, Bitcoin is a real cryptocurrency. The scam is how it is sold to you - a platform or contact promising guaranteed returns, or pressuring you to deposit more, is the fraud, not Bitcoin itself.

**A platform shows my Bitcoin 'profits' growing but won't let me withdraw - what's happening?**

This is a classic sign of a fake investment platform. The balance shown may not be real money. Being asked to pay a fee or tax to "release" it is the scam continuing, not a genuine requirement.

**Can I get my Bitcoin back once I've sent it?**

Usually not. A confirmed Bitcoin payment has no cancellation or chargeback mechanism, and only the recipient can choose to return it. Contact the provider you sent from straight away: a custodial exchange or app may be able to stop a pending withdrawal or restrict an account it controls, though it cannot reverse a confirmed payment to a self-hosted wallet. Keep the transaction IDs and be realistic about the chances of recovery.

**Someone is offering to recover my lost Bitcoin for a fee - is that genuine?**

Treat it as a second scam sign. The FCA warns that fraudsters may target victims again with offers to get money back after a fee. Do not pay any recovery fee without independent, regulated advice.

**How do I report a Bitcoin scam?**

Start with the provider you sent the funds from and give it the transaction IDs, because it may still be able to stop a pending withdrawal or restrict an account it controls. Tell the FCA about the platform or promotion, and report the loss itself to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Crypto Investment Scam UK: Spot a Fake Platform

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/crypto-investment-scams-uk-protection/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Approached about a crypto investment with celebrity endorsements or guaranteed returns? Spot a crypto investment scam and protect yourself in the UK.

### What a crypto investment scam looks like

A crypto investment scam uses a fake platform, a celebrity endorsement, or a relationship built online to convince you to deposit cryptocurrency into an account you cannot really control. An example of the style is: `As seen on TV — this AI-powered crypto platform, endorsed by [celebrity], guarantees 15% monthly returns. Limited spaces available today.`

The platform typically shows a rising balance that you can never actually withdraw. This guide shows the warning signs, how to protect yourself, and what to do if you have already invested.

### Why these scams are convincing

Fake celebrity endorsements, sometimes using manipulated images, video, or deepfakes, borrow a well-known face's credibility. Slick apps and dashboards showing steady, rising profits look like a genuine trading platform, and contact through social media or a dating app can build weeks of trust before money is mentioned.

The fact that protects you: a promise of guaranteed or unusually high returns is a serious scam warning, and the FCA warns that crypto is high risk — you should be prepared to lose all the money you put in, even where the firm is registered with it.

### Signs a crypto investment is a scam

- It uses a celebrity endorsement or news-style advert you cannot verify independently.
- It promises guaranteed, fixed, or unusually high returns.
- The dashboard shows rising profits you can never actually withdraw.
- You are asked to deposit more to "unlock" a withdrawal or pay a fake tax or fee.
- The approach came through social media, a dating app, or an unsolicited message.
- You are pressured to act quickly, or told spaces are limited.
- A "recovery" service later offers to get your lost money back for a fee.

### How the scam works

First, an advert, message, or online relationship introduces the "opportunity". Second, you are shown a platform with a convincing dashboard and encouraged to deposit. Third, the balance appears to grow, encouraging further deposits. Fourth, when you try to withdraw, you are told to pay a fee or tax first, or the platform disappears entirely.

Verifying any platform and any celebrity connection independently before you send money is the only real protection.

### How to protect yourself

Treat a platform promising guaranteed or unusually high returns as a serious scam warning, and check it before you deposit anything.

- Never invest on the strength of a celebrity endorsement without confirming it through that person's own official channels.
- Look the firm up in the FCA Firm Checker at `register.fca.org.uk` to see whether it is authorised and has permission for what it is selling you. The FCA's full Financial Services Register carries more detail, including restrictions on crypto activity that the Firm Checker may not show, so read the status, permissions, restrictions and contact details rather than treating a search result as approval of the investment.
- Checked on 26 July 2026, cryptoasset exchange providers, custodian wallet providers and crypto-ATM operators doing that business in the UK must register with the FCA under the Money Laundering Regulations. That is an anti-money-laundering registration, not approval of the product. The FCA says its new cryptoasset regime under the Financial Services and Markets Act is scheduled to start on 25 October 2027, so check the current position before relying on this.
- Absence from the register is a warning, not the whole test. Fraudsters also clone authorised firms and quote a genuine firm's real name, address and reference number, so call the firm back on the contact details shown on the register rather than any supplied to you.
- The FCA says access to the Financial Ombudsman Service or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme is unlikely for most cryptoassets, so do not treat registration as a safety net.
- Treat an investment recommendation from a new online friend or romantic contact as a serious scam warning, especially where the person directs you to a particular platform or coach.
- Refuse any payment demanded to unlock your own balance, and keep private keys and recovery phrases to yourself.

If you are unsure, our /guides/pig-butchering-scam-uk/ and /guides/bitcoin-scam-uk/ guides cover the wider crypto-investment pattern in more detail.

### If you have already invested

Stop sending money, including any "fee" or "tax" demanded to release a balance, and do not let the platform talk you into one more deposit to fix it. Export or screenshot the account history, the deposit records and the chat before your access is withdrawn — a fake platform can be switched off without notice.

Tell your bank or card issuer how the money left your account, then follow the payment, account and identity steps in the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report a crypto investment scam (UK)

Take the right route to the Financial Conduct Authority. A misleading promotion connected to an authorised firm goes through the FCA's financial promotion reporting form. A firm you suspect is unauthorised, or a clone using a real firm's details, goes through the FCA's scam and unauthorised-firm contact route, or its consumer helpline on 0800 111 6768. Say clearly which one you think it is, because a clone is a different investigation from an unregistered platform.

A financial loss also belongs in a fraud report: `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and Police Scotland on 101. Forwarding addresses for a scam email or text are listed in the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Is every crypto platform with celebrity backing a scam?**

Treat it as high risk. Verify any celebrity endorsement directly through their own official channels, not through the advert or platform itself. Fake endorsements, including deepfakes, are common in crypto scams.

**A platform shows my balance growing but I can't withdraw — what does that mean?**

This is a classic sign of a fake investment platform. The balance is often not real. Being asked to pay a fee or tax to "release" it is the scam continuing, not a genuine requirement.

**Does FCA registration mean a crypto firm is safe?**

No. Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is an anti-money-laundering check on the business, not approval of the investment, and the FCA says access to the Financial Ombudsman Service or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme is unlikely for most cryptoassets. Crypto remains high risk even with a registered firm.

**Can I get my money back from a crypto investment scam?**

Possibly, but often difficult once crypto has moved on. If you funded the purchase by card, ask your bank about a chargeback. An eligible domestic consumer payment sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable, and a 13-month outer reporting limit. Report it immediately rather than relying on that window.

**How do I report a crypto investment scam?**

Two routes matter. Report a misleading promotion from an authorised firm on the FCA's financial promotion form, and a suspected unauthorised or clone firm through its scam contact route or consumer helpline on 0800 111 6768. A financial loss goes to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk`, or to Police Scotland on 101 north of the border.

## Crypto Recovery Scam UK: A Second Scam to Avoid

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/crypto-recovery-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Told your crypto has been recovered after a scam and just needs a fee to claim? Don't pay or share wallet keys. Verify independently.

### What a crypto recovery scam looks like

This scam targets people who have already lost money to a crypto investment scam, contacting them again to say their funds have been located and can be returned for a fee. A reported FCA-impersonation pattern involves a caller claiming the FCA has recovered funds from a crypto wallet opened illegally in the victim's name, and that a payment or personal details are needed to release it.

### Why it's convincing

Having already lost money once, the promise of getting it back is understandably appealing. The caller may already know details of your original loss, either because the same group ran both scams or because your details were sold on to a separate operation.

### Signs a crypto recovery offer is a scam

- You're contacted unexpectedly by someone claiming to be the FCA, a government body, or a 'recovery specialist'.
- You're told funds or a crypto wallet have been 'recovered' and a fee or your details are needed to claim them.
- You're asked for your wallet's private key or seed phrase.
- There's pressure to act quickly to avoid missing the recovered funds.

### How the scam works step by step

First, someone who has already lost money to a crypto scam is contacted again, told their funds have been traced or recovered. Second, a fee is requested, or sensitive details like a wallet's private key or seed phrase are asked for. Third, if a fee is paid, no funds are returned; if a private key or seed phrase is shared, any remaining crypto in that wallet can be stolen directly.

### How to protect yourself

The FCA has warned that fraudsters impersonate the regulator, and has stated that it will never ask you to transfer money to it or share sensitive banking information such as account PINs and passwords.

- Never share a wallet's private key or seed phrase with anyone, whatever they claim to be helping you recover.
- Be sceptical of any unexpected contact claiming your lost crypto has been found.
- Verify contact independently using the FCA's own website, Firm Checker, or published helpline details, not details supplied by the caller.

### If you've already paid or shared details

Stop all further contact and payments immediately. If you shared a wallet's private key or seed phrase, treat it as compromised and move any remaining funds to a new wallet as soon as possible if you're still able to.

### How to report a crypto recovery scam (UK)

Report a suspected recovery scam to the FCA on 0800 111 6768. If you've lost money, also report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Would the FCA really contact me saying my crypto has been recovered?**

Treat unexpected contact along those lines as a scam. The FCA has stated that it will never ask you to transfer money to it or share banking PINs and passwords.

**Should I ever share my wallet's private key or seed phrase with a 'recovery' service?**

No. Never share this with anyone, regardless of what they claim to be helping you recover. Doing so can let someone steal any remaining funds directly.

**I've already paid a fee to a crypto recovery service. What do I do?**

Stop all further contact and payments, and report it to the FCA. Also report it to Report Fraud if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. There's no guarantee of recovering the fee, but acting quickly matters.

**Is genuine crypto recovery ever possible?**

Recovering stolen or lost cryptocurrency is very difficult in practice. Be sceptical of anyone who contacts you unexpectedly claiming they can do it for a fee.

**How do I report a crypto recovery scam?**

Report it to the FCA on 0800 111 6768, and to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland) if you've lost money.

## Cryptocurrency Payment Scam UK: Why Unexpected Crypto Demands Are a Red Flag

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/cryptocurrency-payment-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Unexpected demands to pay in cryptocurrency are a major scam warning sign. Here's why criminals ask for crypto, and what to do instead.

### Why so many different scams ask for cryptocurrency

A cryptocurrency payment demand isn't one scam — it's a payment method that turns up inside dozens of unrelated scams, because it suits criminals better than almost any other option. An example of the style: `Buy £2,000 in Bitcoin at your nearest crypto ATM and send it to this wallet address to release your account.` Direct cryptocurrency wallet transfers are generally final and cannot be reversed through a bank or card chargeback once confirmed. The receiving wallet can also move funds onward in minutes. That combination — fast, hard to reverse, and outside normal payment dispute routes — is exactly why a romance scammer, a fake HMRC caller, a bogus tech-support agent, a blackmailer, or a fake investment adviser may all land on the same request: pay in crypto.

### Warning signs the request itself is a scam

- Someone you've never met in person is asking you to pay them, or a fee, in cryptocurrency — for almost any reason.
- You're told to buy cryptocurrency at a shop, supermarket, or crypto ATM and send it to a wallet address you're given over the phone or in a message.
- The request is dressed up as something else entirely: a tax bill, a court fine, a subscription renewal, a customs charge, a dating-app partner's emergency, or an investment top-up.
- You're kept on the phone while you make the payment, or told not to tell your bank, a family member, or the shop staff what it's really for.
- You're told this is the only accepted payment method, or that paying this way is faster, safer, or more private than a normal bank transfer.
- A genuine-sounding organisation — HMRC, your bank, the police, a court, a utility company — is involved in the story, but mainstream UK tax, fine, banking, policing, and utility demands are not collected by unexpected cryptocurrency transfer.

### How the crypto-payment demand plays out

The story around the payment changes constantly, but the mechanics are consistent. First, contact is made — a call, text, email, dating app message, or social media DM — with a reason you need to pay or transfer funds urgently. Second, cryptocurrency is introduced as the payment method, often framed as a technical necessity ("our system only accepts crypto") or as protection ("crypto keeps this transaction private/safe"). Third, you're walked through buying cryptocurrency, sometimes at a physical crypto ATM, sometimes through an exchange app, with the criminal staying in contact throughout to keep you moving and stop you pausing to check the story. Fourth, you send the crypto to a wallet address they control. As soon as the transaction confirms on the blockchain, it is effectively gone — there is no bank to call, no card provider to dispute it with, and the criminal has no ongoing incentive to stay in contact.

### How to check before you send any cryptocurrency

Stop and contact the organisation the message claims to be from — using a number or website address you already know or find independently, never one given to you in the message or call. Some private businesses may accept crypto, but no genuine UK bank, HMRC contact, court, police force, or mainstream utility demand should require you to make an urgent wallet transfer. If a call or message pressures you to buy crypto quickly, treat that urgency itself as the warning sign. For anything presented as an investment, check the firm on the FCA Firm Checker (`fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker`) — crypto is high risk, and crypto investments are generally not covered by the FSCS even when a firm is registered; dealing with an unauthorised firm leaves you without Financial Ombudsman Service recourse too. For further verification steps, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### What to do if you've already sent cryptocurrency

Stop sending anything further immediately, even if you're told an additional payment will "unlock" or "reverse" what you already sent — that follow-up request is a second scam. Cryptocurrency transactions are not reversible in the way a bank transfer sometimes is, so recovery is genuinely difficult, but report it anyway: a wallet address reported quickly can still help investigators trace and disrupt the network. If you paid using a bank transfer or card to buy the crypto in the first place, contact your bank or card provider straight away and explain what happened. Be wary of anyone contacting you afterwards claiming they can recover the cryptocurrency for a fee — this is a well-documented follow-up scam, not a genuine recovery service.

### How to report a cryptocurrency payment scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland — include the wallet address, any messages, and how you were contacted. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. If the initial contact was by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if it was a text, forward it free to 7726. If an investment or firm name was involved, you can also report it to the FCA on 0800 111 6768.

### Frequently asked questions

**Why do so many different scams all ask for cryptocurrency specifically?**

Because once a direct cryptocurrency payment is confirmed, it generally cannot be reversed through a bank or card chargeback, and it can move on again within minutes. Romance scammers, fake officials, tech-support scammers and investment fraudsters are all drawn to the same feature: it is fast and effectively final.

**Is it ever normal for a genuine organisation to ask for payment in crypto?**

Some private businesses can accept cryptocurrency, but it is not normal for a UK bank, HMRC, a court, the police, a utility, or a delivery company to demand an urgent wallet transfer after unexpected contact. If a message or caller claiming to be from one of these asks you to pay this way, treat it as a scam regardless of how convincing the rest of the story sounds.

**I've already sent cryptocurrency to a scammer — can I get it back?**

It's difficult, since crypto transactions are not reversible once confirmed, but report it straight away with the receiving wallet address — to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. That information can still help investigators. Don't send anything further, and be very cautious of anyone contacting you afterwards offering to recover it for an upfront fee.

**How do I report a cryptocurrency payment scam in the UK?**

Report to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). Forward a scam email to `report@phishing.gov.uk` or a text to 7726. Include the wallet address and any messages you received.

## Fake Crypto Exchange UK: Spot a Cloned Trading Platform

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-crypto-exchange-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake exchanges copy a real platform's branding and let you deposit, even withdraw small amounts, before vanishing. Check the FCA Firm Checker first.

### What a fake crypto exchange looks like

This scam is a website or app built to closely copy a real, established cryptocurrency exchange — matching its branding, layout, and even its customer-support pages — to convince you to create an account and deposit money. An example of the style: `Your exclusive early-access account is ready — deposit now to lock in this week's bonus rate.` Some fake exchanges let you make small, genuine-looking withdrawals early on specifically to build your confidence, before the platform stops responding once you deposit a larger sum.

### Warning signs to look for

- The web address is close to, but not exactly, the real exchange's domain — check it character by character, not at a glance.
- It promises guaranteed returns or bonus rates well above anything a genuine exchange advertises.
- You found it through an unsolicited message, social media ad, or a "personal account manager" who contacted you first.
- Customer support only exists through WhatsApp or Telegram, not the ticketing system or verified channels a genuine exchange publishes.
- You're asked to send cryptocurrency directly to a personal wallet address rather than through the platform's normal deposit flow.
- Under the FCA's rules for cryptoasset promotions aimed at UK consumers, firms must show prominent risk warnings and cannot use incentives such as "refer a friend" bonuses — a platform doing neither is a red flag.

### How this scam works step by step

Contact usually starts with a social media ad, an unsolicited message, or a "trading opportunity" from someone who reaches out first. The linked site looks convincing, sometimes copied wholesale from a real exchange. You create an account, deposit funds by bank transfer, card, or by sending existing cryptocurrency, and the balance shown in your account rises accordingly — some platforms even allow a small withdrawal at this stage to build trust. A "personal account manager" then encourages a larger deposit, often citing a limited-time bonus. Once that larger sum is sent, the account freezes, support goes silent, and the site typically disappears within days.

### How to verify an exchange is genuine

Type the exchange's web address directly into your browser rather than following any link sent to you, and compare it character by character against the address you know independently. Check the FCA Firm Checker (`fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker`), the Financial Services Register (`register.fca.org.uk`), and the FCA's cryptoasset register where relevant — a UK-facing exchange handling cryptoasset business should be registered, and if it isn't listed, don't deposit. Registration is not the same as FSCS protection: the FCA warns crypto is high risk and you should be prepared to lose all the money you invest. Genuine cryptoasset promotions aimed at UK consumers are required to carry prominent risk warnings and to apply a 24-hour cooling-off period before a first-time investor can proceed — the absence of either is a red flag, not a neutral sign. For further steps, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### What to do if you've already deposited

Stop sending any further money immediately, including in response to a request for a larger deposit to "unlock" a withdrawal. If you paid by card or bank transfer, contact your bank straight away to explain what happened. If you sent cryptocurrency, note the receiving wallet address — recovery is very difficult once confirmed, but the address is still useful to investigators. If you uploaded identity documents to the platform, treat your details as compromised and watch your accounts and post for signs of identity misuse.

### How to report a fake crypto exchange in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, with the platform's web address, any messages, and transaction details. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Report a suspected unauthorised firm to the FCA on 0800 111 6768, forward a phishing email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`, and forward a text to 7726.

### Frequently asked questions

**How do I know if a crypto exchange is genuinely FCA-registered?**

Check the FCA Firm Checker (fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker), the Financial Services Register, and the FCA's cryptoasset register where relevant — search by the firm's name, not a name or link the platform itself gives you. If it is not listed for the activity it claims to carry out, do not deposit; even registration does not mean crypto holdings have normal FSCS protection.

**The platform let me withdraw a small amount — doesn't that prove it's genuine?**

No — this is a known tactic. Some fake exchanges deliberately allow a small early withdrawal specifically to build confidence before asking for a much larger deposit, at which point the account is frozen and support disappears.

**Can I get my money back if I've already deposited with a fake exchange?**

If you paid by bank transfer or card, contact your bank immediately and explain what happened. If you sent cryptocurrency, it's very difficult to recover once confirmed, though reporting the wallet address to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, still helps investigators trace the network.

**How do I report a fake crypto exchange in the UK?**

Report to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland), and to the FCA on 0800 111 6768 if it claimed to be authorised. Forward phishing emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk` and texts to 7726.

## NFT Scam UK: Wallet Drainers and Fake Mint Sites

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/nft-scam-uk/
Category: Crypto Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A common high-value NFT threat is a 'wallet drainer' site tricking you into signing away access to your wallet. Here's how to check first.

### What the modern NFT scam looks like

One common high-value NFT threat is a "wallet drainer" — a convincing fake minting page, marketplace listing, or DeFi site that asks you to connect your wallet and then sign a transaction described as an "approval", "verification", or free "claim". An example of the style: `Connect your wallet and sign to claim your free mint before the drop closes.` That approval can authorise a smart contract to move assets out of your wallet later, sometimes instantly, sometimes only when the scammer chooses to trigger it. A related variant lists one of your own genuine NFTs for sale at a token amount, using a signature you were tricked into giving, and the scammer's own linked account buys it instantly.

### Warning signs to look for

- You're asked to connect your wallet and sign something described vaguely as "approval", "verification", or a "free claim" — genuine minting rarely needs a blanket approval like this.
- The site creates urgency around a closing drop, a limited allowlist spot, or a countdown timer.
- You were contacted first — by DM, a comment under a genuine project's post, or a fake customer-support reply — rather than finding the project independently.
- The web address is close to, but not exactly, a genuine marketplace or project's domain.
- You're asked for your seed phrase or private key directly — no legitimate mint, marketplace, or wallet ever needs this.
- An account claiming to be "support" messages you first after you post a public question — genuine platform support does not DM users unprompted.

### How the wallet-drainer scam works step by step

Contact often starts through a fake customer-support reply, a DM claiming to be from a well-known project, or an ad for an exclusive drop. The linked site looks like a genuine minting page or marketplace listing. You connect your wallet, which usually reveals only your public address and is not the dangerous step by itself. You're then asked to sign a transaction — worded as an approval, a claim, or a verification — and this signature is what actually authorises the malicious contract. Depending on how it's built, your assets may be drained immediately, or the scammer may wait and drain multiple connected wallets in a single sweep later. Because the blockchain simply executes what was signed, there is no bank or platform that can reverse it.

### How to check before you connect or sign anything

Only mint or trade through a project's official, independently-found link — never one sent to you in a DM or reply, even from an account that looks right. Read what you're being asked to sign, not just click through it: a wallet prompt that says "approve" or grants ongoing spending permission over your assets is different from a simple one-off payment, and should stop you. Consider using a separate, low-value "hot" wallet for minting and trying new sites, keeping valuable assets in a wallet that never connects to anything unfamiliar. Report suspicious listings or accounts through the marketplace's own report function (for example, OpenSea's three-dot "Report" option on a listing, collection, or account). For further steps, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### What to do if you've already signed a malicious approval

Use a wallet-permission checker (available through most major wallet providers' own help pages) to review and revoke any approvals you don't recognise — this stops a drainer using the same permission again, though it can't undo a transfer that's already happened. Move any remaining assets to a new wallet with a fresh seed phrase as soon as possible, since the compromised wallet's permissions may still be exploitable. Do not respond to anyone contacting you afterwards offering to recover your NFTs or funds for an upfront fee — this is a well-documented follow-up scam.

### How to report an NFT scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, including the site address and any wallet addresses involved. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Report the listing, collection, or account on the marketplace itself, and forward a phishing email to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is connecting my wallet to a site dangerous by itself?**

Connecting alone typically only shares your public wallet address and isn't the dangerous step. The risk comes from signing a transaction — often worded as an "approval" or "claim" — which is what actually grants a contract permission to move your assets.

**How do I know if a mint or NFT drop is genuine?**

Only use a link you found independently through the project's own established channels, never one sent to you first in a DM or reply. Read any wallet signature request carefully — a blanket "approval" for ongoing access is a red flag a one-off payment isn't.

**I signed something and my NFTs/crypto are gone — what do I do?**

Use your wallet provider's permission checker to revoke any approvals you don't recognise, then move any remaining assets to a brand new wallet with a fresh seed phrase. Report the receiving wallet address to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, though recovery is very difficult once assets have moved.

**How do I report a fake NFT site or listing?**

Report the listing or account directly through the marketplace (for example, OpenSea's "Report" option), and report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Amazon Scam Emails: How to Spot a Fake Amazon Email (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/amazon-order-scam-email-checklist/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Got an Amazon email about an order problem, refund, or 'account locked'? How to tell a genuine Amazon email from a phishing scam — and check safely.

### What a fake Amazon email looks like

An Amazon email scam is a phishing message that imitates Amazon so you click a link and hand over your login, card details, or a one-time code. An example of the style is an email from a display name like `Amazon` with a subject such as `Your order has been placed - action required` or `Your account has been locked`, and a button such as `Verify your account`.

The pretext changes - a high-value order you did not place, a refund waiting, a failed payment, or a Prime renewal - but the goal is the same: rush you onto a fake Amazon sign-in page. The link often points to a lookalike such as `amazon-account-verify.example`.

### Why these Amazon emails fool people

Amazon's own scam-prevention material says order-issue and account-issue impersonation scams are common themes. Phishing emails can copy Amazon's logo, layout, and language, and the visible sender name can be set to something misleading. Amazon also warns that attackers create fake websites and emails that impersonate brands such as Amazon.

None of that means the email is genuine. The safe rule is to avoid entering passwords, payment details, or one-time codes on a page reached from an email. Check the order, refund, or account issue by opening the Amazon app or typing `amazon.co.uk` into your browser yourself.

### Signs an Amazon email is phishing

- It starts with a generic greeting such as `Dear Customer`, especially when the rest of the email asks you to act urgently.
- The sender address is not a genuine Amazon domain, or the link points to an unfamiliar site.
- It pushes you to verify, reactivate, cancel, or confirm your account through a button or link.
- It asks for your password, full card number, bank details, or a one-time code on a page reached from the email.
- It asks for payment by gift card, bank transfer, crypto, or another method outside Amazon checkout.
- It includes an unexpected attachment or invoice.
- It claims there is an order you cannot find when you sign in directly.
- Spelling or layout errors can be clues, but a polished email can still be phishing.

### How the Amazon email scam works

First, an email lands that looks like an Amazon alert about an order, refund, account lock, or payment problem. Second, it pushes you to click a button to fix or verify something. Third, the link opens a fake Amazon sign-in page. Fourth, anything you type - email, password, card details, or a one-time code - is captured by the criminals.

Those details can be used to take over the account, place orders, attempt card fraud, or target you again. Checking inside your real Amazon account, rather than through the email, breaks the chain before you enter details.

### How to check if an Amazon email is genuine

Do not click links or open attachments in the email.

- Open the Amazon app or type `amazon.co.uk` into your browser yourself.
- Check `Your Orders`, account alerts, payment settings, and in-account messages.
- If the email mentions an order, payment problem, refund, or account lock, confirm it only after signing in directly.

If you cannot verify the message after signing in directly, treat it as suspicious. Hovering over links can provide clues, but links and sender names can be disguised, so do not rely on that alone. If you are unsure whether a linked site is a copycat, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### If you clicked or shared details

If you entered your Amazon password, sign in through the Amazon app or by typing `amazon.co.uk` yourself, change the password, turn on two-step verification, and review orders, payment methods, addresses, and account settings for anything you do not recognise. Change the same password anywhere else you reused it.

If you entered card details, contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to stop the card if needed, and ask about disputing the transaction. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

### How to report a fake Amazon email (UK)

Forward suspicious emails to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. The NCSC can investigate and take down phishing sites. You can also report suspicious Amazon communications to Amazon at `reportascam@amazon.com`; Amazon says sending the suspicious communication as an attachment is the best way for it to track the report.

If the same scam reached you by text, forward that text to 7726. If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Amazon send emails with links?**

Genuine Amazon emails can contain links, so a link alone is not proof of a scam. The safer rule is not to use an email link to sign in, enter payment details, or provide a one-time code. Go to Amazon yourself through the app or by typing `amazon.co.uk`.

**How can I tell who really sent an Amazon email?**

The visible sender name can be misleading. Check the full sender address and link destinations for clues, but the stronger test is to sign in directly and check your orders and account messages there.

**I clicked the link and entered my Amazon details - what now?**

Sign in through the Amazon app or by typing `amazon.co.uk`, change your password, turn on two-step verification, and review orders, saved cards, addresses, and account settings. If you entered card details, contact your bank using the number on your card.

**Can I get my money back after an Amazon email scam?**

Possibly. If you paid by card, ask your bank about disputing the transaction or chargeback. If you sent a UK bank transfer on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory APP fraud reimbursement rules may apply to Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers, subject to limits and exclusions.

**How do I report a fake Amazon email?**

Forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk` and report suspicious Amazon communications to `reportascam@amazon.com`. If you lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## CEO Fraud Email Scam UK: Spot a Fake Boss Request

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/ceo-fraud-email-scam-uk/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-19

A message appears to come from a senior colleague and requests an urgent payment or sensitive data. Verify it through a separate trusted channel.

### What CEO fraud looks like

CEO fraud is a form of business email compromise. A criminal sends an email tailored to the organisation, impersonates a senior executive or another regular contact, and asks an employee to make an urgent payment, buy gift cards or disclose valuable information. The message may include an invoice or changed bank details that look genuine.

### Why it can be convincing

The request combines authority, urgency and sometimes secrecy. Normal email filters may struggle with a low-volume, tailored message. A familiar display name or an address that looks correct is therefore not proof that the request is genuine.

### Warning signs

- The request is urgent and confidential.
- It bypasses the normal payment or data-release process.
- The supposed executive is said to be unavailable for a call.
- The payment method, payee or type of information requested is unusual.
- You are told to ignore a Confirmation of Payee warning or not involve another approver.

These are indicators, not a test: a tailored impersonation message may contain no obvious spelling or address error.

### How to verify the request

Contact the named person through another method, such as a known phone number or in person. Do not rely on contact details in the message. Follow the organisation's approval process regardless of seniority. The NCSC advises robust verification for changed payment instructions, new suppliers and unusually high transactions, and suggests requiring two or more people where losses could be significant.

### Organisational controls

Use multi-factor authentication on email and financial systems, limit payment authority to those who need it, maintain a separate verification process for important requests, and configure email-domain anti-spoofing protections. Train staff to report an unusual request without fear of delaying a genuine transaction.

### If money or data has already been sent

Contact the sending bank immediately through an official channel and ask whether the payment can be stopped or recalled. Tell the organisation's IT or security contact so they can check the relevant accounts, mailbox rules and sign-ins. Preserve the original message and audit trail.

### Reporting in the UK

Forward a suspicious email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If money was sent, data was disclosed or an account was compromised, report the crime to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101. Supplier impersonation and changed bank details are covered separately at /guides/invoice-fraud-uk-businesses/.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can a convincing internal-looking email still be fraudulent?**

Yes. A tailored impersonation can look familiar, which is why independent verification matters more than the displayed sender.

**What is the strongest practical control?**

A consistently enforced out-of-band verification and approval process for unusual payments and sensitive-data requests.

## Companies House Email Scam UK: How to Check and Report a Message

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/companies-house-email-scam-uk/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake Companies House emails use urgent verification, filing or payment claims. Learn how to check a message safely and report phishing in the UK.

### What the scam looks like

Criminals send emails that imitate Companies House notices and use copied wording, logos, reference numbers or information from the public company register. Current examples published by Companies House include fake identity-verification requests, WebFiling notices, email-verification messages, complaint notifications and requests to open an attachment or supply an authentication code.

The aim may be to steal a password or company authentication code, collect identity or payment details, install malware through a link or attachment, or induce a payment. Companies House also warns about misleading register-payment requests from organisations that are not connected with it.

Urgency, branding or correct company information does not establish authenticity. Much company data is public and can be used to personalise a scam.

### Warning signs

- Pressure to act immediately, make a payment, open an attachment or disclose an authentication code.
- A sender domain that is not a genuine `.gov.uk` address, or a display name that hides an unrelated address.
- A link whose actual destination is different from the expected GOV.UK or Companies House address.
- A request for a password, bank details, authentication code or sensitive officer information.
- False or confusing wording, spelling errors or inconsistent formatting.
- An unexpected invoice to maintain a company on a private “register” that suggests government affiliation.

These are indicators, not a complete authentication system. Email sender addresses can be spoofed, and a message ending in `.gov.uk` should still be checked if the request or link is unexpected.

### What genuine Companies House email can look like

Companies House says its real emails come from an address ending in `.gov.uk`—not exclusively `@companieshouse.gov.uk`. For example, its published notice of 17 March 2026 about the WebFiling security issue said those emails would come from `companies.house@notifications.service.gov.uk`. That is a documented example of one genuine Companies House sender for that specific communication — not a permanent universal address, and not authentication on its own, because sender details can be spoofed.

Genuine Companies House services can also send emails containing links. Its Follow service sends alerts linking to a company's filing history, and its guidance gives `ewf.companieshouse.gov.uk` as an example of a genuine password-reset address. Companies House and the Intellectual Property Office also stated in 2026 that invoices are usually posted but can be sent by email.

Therefore, “it contains a link”, “it asks for payment” or “it does not come from `@companieshouse.gov.uk`” cannot each be used as an automatic verdict. Verify independently.

Companies House says it will never ask for your company authentication code. It also says it will not call to ask for passwords, bank details, authentication codes, or details of directors or company officers.

### How to verify a message safely

1. Do not reply, open an attachment or use a link while you are checking.
2. Expand and inspect the complete sender address. Genuine Companies House email should end in `.gov.uk`, but remember that the visible From address is not conclusive by itself.
3. Hover over a link without opening it and inspect the destination. Genuine services use GOV.UK and Companies House `.gov.uk` addresses. Be alert to deceptive endings such as an unrelated domain placed after familiar words.
4. Open a new browser tab and start at the GOV.UK Companies House service: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/companies-house. Check the public company record, filing history and official guidance relevant to the request.
5. Contact Companies House using details obtained from GOV.UK. Its published enquiry number is `0303 1234 500`.

Not every genuine matter will necessarily be reproduced as a private alert in an online account, so the absence of an account notification is not definitive. Confirm the specific filing, deadline, invoice or identity-verification request through the official service or by contacting Companies House.

### If you clicked, disclosed information or paid

- If you entered a password, change it through the real service and anywhere else it was reused. Secure the associated email account and enable two-step verification where supported.
- If you disclosed a company authentication code, contact Companies House immediately. The code authorises online filings and should be protected like a signature or bank PIN.
- Review the company's filing history and details for unauthorised changes. Consider Companies House's Follow alerts and relevant account-protection services.
- If you entered card or bank details, contact the provider immediately through its official app, website or phone number. Follow its advice about cards, account security and disputed transactions.
- If you sent a UK bank transfer to a fraudster, ask the bank about APP-scam reimbursement. The rules cover many eligible Faster Payments and CHAPS scam payments, subject to scope, caps and exceptions.
- Preserve the email, headers, URL, screenshots and transaction details for your provider and investigators. Do not open a suspect attachment just to collect evidence.

Do not assume that a bank requires a police crime reference number before it can act. Contact the bank first and follow its instructions; report the fraud separately through Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

### How to report it

- Forward a suspicious Companies House email to `phishing@companieshouse.gov.uk`, then delete it as Companies House advises.
- You can also forward a suspicious email to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk` and submit a suspect URL through the NCSC scam website reporting service at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website.
- If money or information was stolen, use Report Fraud at https://www.reportfraud.police.uk/ or call `0300 123 2040` in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report fraud to Police Scotland on `101`.
- Mark the message as phishing with your email provider.
- For consumer advice, use the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do all genuine Companies House emails end in `@companieshouse.gov.uk`?**

No. Companies House says genuine messages end in `.gov.uk`. It has documented legitimate use of `companies.house@notifications.service.gov.uk`.

**Does a link prove the email is fake?**

No. Some genuine services send links. Do not use an unexpected link; navigate independently to GOV.UK and verify its destination and purpose.

**Will Companies House ask for my authentication code?**

Companies House says it will never ask you to disclose the code. Treat any such request as suspicious and report it.

**Can stolen credentials let someone change company information?**

A company authentication code authorises online filings, so disclosure creates a serious risk. A stolen password can also compromise the relevant account. Secure both, inspect filing history and contact Companies House about unauthorised activity.

**Where do I report a suspicious message?**

Send it to `phishing@companieshouse.gov.uk`; you can also forward it to `report@phishing.gov.uk`. Report actual loss through Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## DVLA Email Scam UK: Spot a Fake Tax or Fine Email

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/dvla-email-scam-uk/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Got a DVLA email about car tax, a refund, a fine, or your licence? How to spot a fake DVLA email, check safely on GOV.UK, and report it in the UK.

### What a fake DVLA email looks like

A DVLA email scam is a phishing message that pretends to come from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency so you click a link and hand over card, bank, driving-licence, or personal details. Common hooks are car tax that "failed to renew", a vehicle-tax refund, a driving-licence update, or an unpaid fine. An example of the style is: `DVLA: Your vehicle tax payment failed. Update your details within 48 hours to avoid an £80 penalty: gov-uk-vehicletax.example`.

The link opens a convincing GOV.UK-style page that captures whatever you enter. Email alone does not prove a message is fake; the red flag is an unexpected email that asks you to pay, claim a refund, or confirm details through a link.

### Why these DVLA emails fool people

They copy DVLA and GOV.UK branding and use a real-looking sender name. A money hook, such as a refund or small fee, and a threat, such as a fine or licence issue, both lower caution. A specific amount can make the message look official.

The reliable test is not the branding in the email. Go to GOV.UK yourself, search for the relevant DVLA service, and check there. Do not enter payment or personal details on a page reached from an unexpected message.

### Signs a DVLA email is a scam

- It asks you to pay or "confirm" details through a link to renew tax, claim a refund, update your licence, or clear a fine.
- The web address is a lookalike such as `gov-uk-vehicletax.example` or `dvla-renewal.example`.
- It asks for card details, bank details, or your driving-licence number through an unexpected link.
- It pressures you with a 24- or 48-hour deadline or a fine.
- It offers a refund you were not expecting.
- It uses a generic greeting, an attachment, QR code, or shortened link.
- It sends you to a page that is not a GOV.UK or GOV.UK service page you reached yourself.

### How the DVLA email scam works

First, an email claims a tax, licence, or fine problem, or offers a refund. Second, urgency pushes you to click. Third, a fake GOV.UK-style page asks for card, bank, driving-licence, or personal details. Fourth, criminals capture them for card fraud, bank fraud, or identity misuse. Fifth, they may follow up pretending to "refund" or "fix" the problem.

Going to GOV.UK yourself, rather than using the link, breaks the chain.

### How to check a DVLA email safely

Do not click links or open attachments in an unexpected DVLA email.

- Type `gov.uk` into your browser and search for the vehicle tax, driving-licence, or DVLA contact service you need.
- Check vehicle tax through the official service at `gov.uk/vehicle-tax`.
- Contact DVLA only through details published on GOV.UK.
- Never pay or enter details through a link in an unexpected email.
- If the page asks for payment or personal details, check the browser address carefully and back out if you did not reach it through GOV.UK yourself.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is a copycat of GOV.UK, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, and our /guides/dvla-vehicle-tax-text-scam/ guide covers the same scam by text.

### If you clicked or shared details

If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to secure the account or card, and ask about disputing any payment. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

### How to report a fake DVLA email (UK)

Forward suspicious DVLA emails to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`, then delete them. If the same scam reached you by SMS, forward the text to 7726.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep the sender's address, any website link, and details of anything you entered.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does DVLA send emails, or is every DVLA email a scam?**

Email alone is not proof. Treat any DVLA-branded email that asks you to pay, claim a refund, or confirm details through a link as phishing until you have checked through GOV.UK yourself.

**How can I tell a fake DVLA web address?**

Genuine DVLA online services should be reached through GOV.UK or GOV.UK service pages. A link to `gov-uk-vehicletax.example`, `dvla-renewal.example`, or another lookalike domain is a scam sign. Type `gov.uk` yourself rather than using a link in an email.

**The email says my car tax failed and I will be fined - is it real?**

Check it yourself at `gov.uk/vehicle-tax`. Do not pay through an emailed payment link with a short deadline.

**I entered my card details on a DVLA-looking site - what now?**

Contact your bank using the number on your card and ask them to secure the account or card. If you gave licence or personal details, consider Cifas Protective Registration and monitor your credit reports. Then forward the email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

**How do I report a DVLA email scam?**

Forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Email Account Takeover UK: Recover and Lock It Down

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/email-account-takeover-scam-uk/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-10

Recover a compromised email account, remove forwarding rules and reused credentials, and use a passkey or two-step verification to secure it.

### What email account takeover means

An attacker has gained access to an email account, often through phishing, a reused password, credential theft or malware. Email is particularly important because many other services use it for password resets and security alerts.

### Warning signs

- Password-reset or sign-in alerts you did not trigger.
- Messages in Sent, Deleted or Drafts that you did not create.
- Contacts receiving unexpected messages from your address.
- Recovery details, delegates, filters or forwarding rules you do not recognise.
- New devices or active sessions you cannot account for.

### Recover the account through the provider

Use the email provider’s official account-recovery page, reached independently rather than through a message. Once access is restored:

1. Review and remove unknown forwarding rules, filters, delegates and recovery addresses.
2. Change the account password if the service still uses one, and change it anywhere it was reused.
3. Sign out other sessions and remove unfamiliar devices or app passwords.
4. Review sent mail, deleted mail, security events and linked accounts.
5. Warn contacts if the attacker sent messages from the account.

NCSC specifically warns that attackers can add forwarding rules so they continue receiving copies of messages and password resets.

### Passkeys and two-step verification

NCSC recommends choosing a passkey over a password wherever one is available. Passkeys are phishing-resistant because they are bound to the legitimate service rather than being reusable secrets typed into a page. They still depend on a secure device, credential manager and recovery method.

If the service does not offer passkeys, use a strong unique password generated or stored by a password manager and enable two-step verification. “Three random words” remains an NCSC option for passwords you need to create yourself.

### Check breach exposure carefully

`haveibeenpwned.com` can tell you whether an email address appears in data from a known breach. It does not prove that the email account itself is currently compromised, and a clean result does not prove safety. Never reuse a password exposed in a breach.

### If money or other accounts may be at risk

Check shopping, social-media and financial accounts linked to the mailbox. Contact the bank immediately through a trusted number if payment details, banking access or money may be affected. Preserve security alerts and relevant messages.

### Reporting in the UK

Forward a suspicious email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If fraud or cybercrime caused a loss, report it at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Also report the compromise to the email provider.

### Frequently asked questions

**What should I check first after recovering an email account?**

Check recovery details, forwarding rules, filters, delegates, app passwords and active sessions, then secure every account that reused the same password.

**Does a passkey make an account impossible to compromise?**

No. It greatly reduces phishing and credential-reuse risk, but device security and account-recovery controls still matter.

**Does a breach result on Have I Been Pwned mean my email is hacked now?**

No. It means the address appeared in a known breach dataset. Treat exposed or reused passwords as compromised, but use the provider’s security records to assess the account itself.

## Festival Lineup Email Scam UK: Spot a Fake Presale

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/festival-lineup-email-scam-uk/
Category: Email Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Got an email about a festival lineup announcement with a presale ticket link? How to spot a fake festival email scam and buy tickets safely.

### What a festival lineup email scam looks like

A festival lineup email scam times a fake announcement or "exclusive presale" message to a real festival's lineup reveal, using a link that either takes payment for tickets that do not exist or harvests your card and login details. An example of the style is: `Lineup announced! Get exclusive early-access presale tickets before general sale: festival-presale-tickets.example`.

These scams exploit the rush that happens when a popular festival announces headliners and presale demand outstrips supply. This guide shows the warning signs, how to buy safely, and what to do if you have already responded.

### Why these scams are convincing

Genuine festival lineup announcements do generate real presale emails and urgency, so a scam timed to the same moment blends in easily. A link that looks like it goes to a well-known ticket platform, combined with a countdown or "limited allocation" message, pushes people to click before checking.

The reliable check is to go to the source yourself: visit the festival's official website or app directly, rather than clicking a link in an email, to find the genuine ticket sale details and authorised sellers.

### Signs a festival email is a scam

- It offers "exclusive" or "guaranteed" presale access through a link.
- The link goes to an unfamiliar or lookalike ticketing address, not the festival's own site or a named official partner.
- It creates urgency with a countdown or claims of very limited tickets.
- It asks for card or login details on a page that does not match the official ticket seller.
- It arrived unsolicited, not from a mailing list you knowingly signed up to.
- The email has generic branding or does not match the festival's usual official communications.

### How the scam works

First, a real lineup announcement creates genuine excitement and urgency. Second, a scam email or ad times a fake presale offer to the same moment. Third, the link leads to a fake payment or login page. Fourth, criminals capture card details or payment for tickets that never arrive.
