Reimbursement can be refused where the customer acted with gross negligence, which is a higher bar than simply failing to take reasonable care. The safest outcome is to never authorise the transfer in the first place. No bank — including Santander — will ever ask you to move your money somewhere else to protect it.

### What to do during and after the call

During the call: you do not have to stay on the line. Hang up. If you want to check whether there is a genuine account issue, call Santander yourself using the number on the back of your bank card or within the Santander app — never redial a number the caller gave you. On a landline, wait at least five minutes before calling out, as some fraudsters stay on the line after you hang up.

If you have already given details or authorised a transaction: call your bank immediately using the number on your card, and separately call 159 — the Stop Scams UK banking fraud shortline, which connects you directly to your bank's fraud team. Report the call to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. The case reference number you are given is useful when disputing any transaction with your bank.

### Frequently asked questions

**The caller ID showed Santander's real number — how can it still be a scam?**

Phone numbers can be spoofed — scammers can make any number appear on your screen, including Santander's genuine number. This is called caller ID spoofing, and it means the displayed number is not proof the call is legitimate. The only safe approach is to hang up and call Santander back using the number on your bank card or via the Santander app.

**Santander said they needed to recheck my mobile details in line with regulations. Is this real?**

No. This is a recognised scam phrase. Santander does not conduct regulatory mobile-detail rechecks by calling customers out of the blue. If there is a genuine need to update your contact details, Santander would direct you to do so by logging into your account, not by reading information to an unsolicited caller.

**I approved a transaction during the call — can I get my money back?**

Contact Santander immediately, before doing anything else. UK banks are required to reimburse victims of authorised push payment (APP) fraud in many cases under Payment Systems Regulator rules, but this is not automatic and depends on the circumstances of the transfer. An eligible claim is normally decided within five business days, extending to a maximum of 35 business days if the firm stops the clock to investigate. Also call 159 to reach the banking fraud line and report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland — the case reference helps when disputing the payment with your bank.

**How do I verify that someone calling me is really from Santander?**

You cannot reliably verify a caller's identity during an unsolicited call. The safe approach is always to hang up and call Santander back using the number on the back of your card or through the Santander mobile app. On a landline, wait a few minutes first — some fraudsters stay connected after you appear to hang up, ready to intercept your next outbound call.

**Is it safe to give my date of birth or address to someone claiming to be from Santander?**

Treat any unsolicited call as potentially fraudulent, regardless of what information the caller provides or requests. Even details that seem low-risk — date of birth, address, last four digits of your card — can be combined with other data to commit fraud or to pass security checks elsewhere. If there is a genuine issue with your account, Santander can address it when you call them back on the number from your card.

## Solar Panel Cold Caller Scam UK: Spot the Warning Signs

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/solar-panel-cold-caller-scam-uk/
Category: Phone Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Got an unsolicited call or doorstep visit offering free solar panels or a 'government grant'? How to spot a solar panel cold-calling scam in the UK.

### What a solar panel cold caller scam looks like

A solar panel cold caller scam is an unsolicited phone call or doorstep visit offering "free" solar panels, a government grant, or dramatic energy-bill savings, using high-pressure sales tactics to get you to sign up or hand over personal and financial details on the spot. An example of the style is: `You qualify for a Government-funded solar panel scheme — completely free installation, but you must confirm your details today to lock in your grant.`

Genuine solar panel decisions deserve time, comparison, and independent research; a caller who pressures you to decide immediately is a warning sign in itself. This guide shows the warning signs, how to check an offer safely, and what to do if you have already agreed to something.

### Why these approaches are convincing

Rising energy bills make the promise of free panels and big savings genuinely appealing, and references to a "government scheme" or grant sound official even when invented or exaggerated. High-pressure tactics — a survey booked immediately, or a discount only available "today" — are designed to stop you comparing offers or checking the company.

The fact that protects you: any genuine solar panel or energy-efficiency scheme can be checked independently through official government sources, and a reputable installer does not need you to decide during the first call or visit.

### Signs a solar panel offer is a scam

- You are cold-called or visited unsolicited about solar panels or a "government grant".
- You are pressured to book a survey or sign up immediately, often with a same-day discount.
- The caller cannot clearly identify the specific scheme or provide independent, checkable details.
- You are asked for bank details or a signature before receiving a written quote.
- The company has no verifiable address, accreditation, or independent reviews.
- You are told the offer or "grant" will disappear if you do not act today.

### How the scam works

First, an unsolicited call or doorstep visit offers free or heavily discounted solar panels tied to a grant or scheme. Second, high-pressure tactics push you to book a survey or sign an agreement immediately. Third, you may be signed into an unsuitable finance agreement, pay for work that is poor quality or never completed, or simply hand over personal and financial details. Finally, the company becomes difficult to contact once you have paid or signed.

Taking time to research the company and any scheme independently before agreeing to anything breaks the chain.

### How to check a solar panel offer safely

Never agree to anything during an unsolicited call or visit.

- Check any government solar or energy-efficiency scheme independently through official government sources, not through what the caller tells you.
- Get multiple written quotes from installers you find yourself, and compare them without time pressure.
- Check the company's accreditation with the issuing body, and check reviews and Companies House records independently.
- Never sign a contract or finance agreement on the spot; take it away to read and get independent advice.
- Be very wary of "free" panels tied to a scheme you cannot verify yourself.

Our /guides/solar-panel-scam-uk/ and /guides/driveway-cowboy-scam-uk/ guides cover related home-improvement scam patterns.

### If you have already signed up or paid

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report a solar panel cold-calling scam (UK)

Report a rogue trader or high-pressure sales approach through the relevant consumer advice service so it can be passed to Trading Standards. In England and Wales, Citizens Advice consumer service is the public route for reporting to Trading Standards; use the equivalent national consumer advice route in Scotland or Northern Ireland.

If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep all your evidence, including any contract, correspondence, and payment records.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is every unsolicited solar panel call or visit a scam?**

Not automatically, but pressure to decide immediately, a vague "government grant" claim, and no written quote before you sign are classic warning signs. Research any offer independently before agreeing to anything.

**Are free solar panels through a government scheme genuine?**

Check any specific scheme independently through official government sources rather than trusting what a cold caller tells you. Genuine schemes have public, verifiable eligibility criteria you can check yourself.

**Should I sign a solar panel contract during the first visit?**

No. A genuine installer does not need you to decide on the spot. Take any contract away to read, get independent advice, and compare with other quotes before signing anything.

**I've signed up and now regret it — can I cancel?**

If you agreed during a doorstep visit or phone sale, you may have a 14-day cancellation right, but exceptions can apply. If you signed a regulated finance agreement, you may also have a separate 14-day right to withdraw from the credit. Check the paperwork and get consumer advice quickly. If you paid by card, ask your bank about a chargeback.

**How do I report a solar panel cold-calling scam?**

Report it through the relevant consumer advice service so it can be passed to Trading Standards. If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## TalkTalk Scam Call UK: Spot a Fake Support Call

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/talktalk-scam-call-uk/
Category: Phone Scams · Updated: 2026-07-23

Fake TalkTalk callers claim a fault or refund and request passwords, bank details or remote access. Hang up and call TalkTalk through an official route.

### What a scam call looks like

A caller claims there is a broadband fault, security problem, bill issue or refund. They may ask for remote access to a computer, send the victim to a website, request a full password or bank details, or demand payment through a hard-to-trace service.

TalkTalk genuinely contacts customers, so the topic of a call does not authenticate it. Caller ID can be spoofed, and an account number may have been obtained elsewhere.

### TalkTalk's published “never” rules

TalkTalk says it will not:

- use the TalkTalk account number to prove the call is genuine;
- ask for the full password — it says it asks for only two digits;
- ask for bank details to process a refund; or
- ask for money through MoneyGram or Western Union.

Its current guidance also describes automated “press 1” engineer calls claiming to be TalkTalk as a scam pattern.

### Warning signs

- A request to install or open remote-access software.
- A demand for the full password or for bank details to issue a refund.
- The account number is offered as proof of identity.
- The caller insists you stay on the line while banking or making a payment.
- An automated message asks you to press 1 for an engineer.

### Check the call safely

Hang up and contact TalkTalk using the number on your bill or its current official contact page. TalkTalk currently lists 0345 172 0088 for customer service; calls to it are free from TalkTalk home phone services, while charges from other providers or mobile networks depend on the caller's plan. If a bank is mentioned, hang up and use the bank's trusted number or 159 if the bank participates.

### TalkTalk CallSafe

CallSafe costs £1 a month from 11 January 2026. It can be added or managed in My Account where compatible. TalkTalk says that after a withheld-number call, dialling 1472 lets a CallSafe user block or approve that caller. The separate 1471 caller-return service does not activate CallSafe.

CallSafe screens some unknown callers by asking them to record their name, but it does not make every call safe and compatibility requirements apply.

### If remote access or details were given

Disconnect the affected device from the internet if the caller may still have access. Contact the bank immediately where financial information or payment is involved. From a different trusted device, change relevant passwords and review accounts. TalkTalk advises having affected devices checked for viruses, spyware and adware; a factory reset should not be stated as routinely necessary without technical assessment.

### Reporting in the UK

Report related phishing emails to TalkTalk at `phishing@talktalk.co.uk` and to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If money was lost or an account or device was compromised, report the crime to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is CallSafe free?**

No. TalkTalk says the price increased to £1 a month from 11 January 2026.

**Does dialling 1471 activate CallSafe?**

No. Add or manage CallSafe through My Account where available. TalkTalk describes 1472 specifically for blocking or approving a withheld caller after that call.

## Virgin Media Scam Call UK: How to Spot a Fake Caller

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/virgin-media-scam-call-uk/
Category: Phone Scams · Updated: 2026-07-03

A 'Virgin Media' caller warns of a virus and wants remote access to your device? Hang up and verify through Virgin Media's official channels.

### What a fake Virgin Media call sounds like

A Virgin Media scam call is a criminal posing as Virgin Media support, most often claiming to have detected a virus or security problem on your connection. An example of the style is: `This is Virgin Media technical support. We've detected a virus on your network that could compromise your account. We need to install security software to fix it now.`

The "security software" offered is actually spyware or a remote-access tool. Other versions claim your account or payment details need confirming, or use fake tax or refund threats to create pressure.

### Why these calls are convincing

Caller ID is not reliable proof — numbers can be spoofed to look genuine. A claim about a virus or account problem sounds technical enough that many people don't feel able to challenge it, and the offer to "fix it now" removes the need to think it through.

Virgin Media's vishing guidance says that if you are concerned about a caller's identity, you should hang up and call Virgin Media directly on an official number. It also warns against giving sensitive or financial information over a cold call unless you are certain who you are speaking to.

### Signs a Virgin Media call is a scam

- The caller claims to have detected a virus, hacking attempt, or security issue on your connection.
- You're asked to install software so the caller can access your device remotely.
- You're asked for passwords, security answers, payment details, or full account details.
- The caller pressures you to act immediately, or says your service will be cut off unless you do.
- You're asked to make a payment or read out card details during the call.
- The call is unexpected — you didn't report a fault or contact Virgin Media first.

### How the scam works step by step

First, the caller creates concern with a claimed virus, security issue, or account problem. Second, they ask you to install remote-access software, or to provide account, password, payment, or security details as "verification". Third, once they have access or details, they can view your device, make changes, or use the information for fraud. Fourth, some versions add a payment demand, framed as a fee to fix the issue or avoid disconnection.

Refusing to install software or provide sensitive details on an unexpected call breaks the chain.

### How to check a Virgin Media call safely

Do not install any software or confirm full account details during an unexpected call.

- Hang up.
- Contact Virgin Media yourself using the number on your bill or on `virginmedia.com`, not a number given during the call.
- Remember: genuine internet providers should not ask for sensitive information on a cold call. If the caller says they are Virgin Media and you are unsure, hang up and validate using an official number.
- If anything involved your bank account or card, contact your bank directly using the number on your card, or call 159 to be connected safely.

### If you let them in or shared details

If you installed remote-access software or let the caller control your device, disconnect from the internet, uninstall the software, and run a security scan. Change important passwords — especially email and banking — from a different, trusted device.

If you shared Virgin Media login, security, or account details, contact Virgin Media to secure your account. If you shared bank or card details or made a payment, contact your bank or card provider immediately and ask about a chargeback or, for eligible UK transfers since 7 October 2024, APP fraud reimbursement.

### How to report a Virgin Media scam call (UK)

Tell Virgin Media using the number on your bill or through `virginmedia.com`. Forward a suspicious email to `phishing@virginmedia.com`, and forward a suspicious text to 7726.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Virgin Media call its customers?**

Virgin Media may contact customers in some circumstances, so caller ID alone isn't proof either way. The reliable test is what you're asked to do: do not install software, provide sensitive details, or make a payment on an unexpected call. Hang up and call back on an official number if unsure.

**A caller says there's a virus on my connection and wants to install software — is this real?**

Treat it as a scam. Hang up and contact Virgin Media yourself using the number on your bill or `virginmedia.com`. Genuine security issues don't need you to install software for a caller during an unexpected call.

**I let a caller install software on my device — what now?**

Disconnect from the internet, uninstall the software, and run a security scan. Change important passwords from a different, trusted device, and contact Virgin Media if your account details were shared.

**What's Virgin Media's phishing report email address?**

`phishing@virginmedia.com`. Type it directly, or use the reporting guidance on Virgin Media's official security pages.

**How do I report a Virgin Media scam call?**

Tell Virgin Media through the number on your bill or `virginmedia.com`. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Bumble Romance Scams UK: Spot a Fake Profile or Con

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/bumble-romance-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A Bumble match who moves fast, avoids video calls, then needs money or pushes 'crypto'? How to spot a romance scam and protect yourself — without the shame.

### Who sends the first message, and why it proves nothing

On Bumble, who opens a conversation depends on the match. In heterosexual connections, women decide how the first move is made; where an Opening Move has been set, a match can reply to it regardless of whose move it otherwise is. In same-gender and non-binary matches, either person can start. Against everyday nuisance behaviour that works well.

Fraud is built around the rule rather than stopped by it. A scam account never needs to start a conversation; it only needs to be swiped right on. So the profile is engineered to be picked — warm photographs, a plausible profession, prompts that echo whatever the target says she is looking for — and then it waits.

There may be a cognitive trap in that, and it is worth naming as a possibility rather than an established Bumble-specific finding: it can be harder to re-examine somebody you feel you chose yourself. Whether or not that applies to you, the mechanical point stands on its own. Opening the conversation tells you nothing whatsoever about who is at the other end of it.

### The 24-hour clock, and the urgency it hands a fraudster

A Bumble match expires if no one sends a message within 24 hours of matching. In ordinary use that keeps queues moving. Inside a scam it supplies urgency the fraudster never has to invent.

Watch how the deadline gets used.

- 'Send me your WhatsApp before this expires' in the earliest exchanges. The countdown becomes the pretext for leaving the one place where moderation and reporting function.
- Any framing that turns Bumble's timer into a reason you must answer tonight rather than tomorrow, or send something now rather than think about it.

The clock belongs to Bumble, not to them, and letting a match lapse costs very little. Every member gets one free Extend a day, which buys another 24 hours. Paid tiers can extend without limit, and Boost and Premium include Rematch, so a genuine connection is recoverable. A deadline is never a reason to make a decision you would otherwise take slowly.

### Two different verifications, and what each one can prove

Bumble runs two checks that are easy to confuse, and the difference changes what you can conclude.

- Photo Verification is a selfie check confirming that a member matches their profile photos. This is what Bumble Support's request feature triggers: you ask a match to verify, they receive a prompt to take a selfie, and an approved check shows on their profile.
- ID Verification is optional in the UK, launched there in March 2025, and asks for a government-issued document plus a live selfie. Bumble's privacy policy names Veriff as its ID-check provider.

The request you can send inside the app is the Photo Verification one, so do not expect it to put a match through the full ID process. It is still the most useful single message you can send to anybody who will not get on a call. You can also filter your experience towards members who have verified.

Be clear about the ceiling on both. Verification can add confidence that the person in the photographs is the person typing. Neither check proves intentions, and neither tests a single financial claim anybody makes. Because verification is voluntary, a missing badge proves very little — plenty of genuine members never bother with it. A match who declines a verification request while declaring strong feelings has answered a different question, and answered it clearly.

Behind the scenes Bumble also runs Deception Detector, the machine-learning screen it introduced in 2024. Bumble says that in testing it automatically blocked 95 per cent of the accounts it had identified as spam or scam profiles — the denominator there is accounts Bumble's systems had already flagged, not every fraudulent account on the app. No automated tool guarantees that a profile is safe.

### What UK police record as romance fraud

UK police describe dating and romance fraud as deceiving someone into a fictitious romantic relationship, often online, in order to gain their trust and exploit them financially. INTERPOL has asked organisations to stop using the 'pig butchering' nickname, which describes victims as livestock, and to use romance baiting instead — that is the term used here.

City of London Police figures published in May 2026 put UK romance-fraud losses at more than £102 million in 2025, across 10,784 reports, a 29 per cent rise on the year before. People aged 55 to 74 accounted for almost half of everything stolen. Men filed more reports overall, while women accounted for a larger share of the value lost.

Two things follow. Police guidance is explicit that romance-fraud victims are not to blame and should not feel ashamed or embarrassed, so making a report is a statement of fact rather than a confession. And the heaviest losses sit later in life, which is worth knowing if you are reading this about a parent rather than about yourself.

### Testing a Bumble match without accusing anyone

Every check below fits inside an ordinary conversation.

- Ask for a voice or video call inside Bumble rather than on another platform — Bumble provides both in the app. A refusal that survives two or three attempts is itself the finding.
- Send a Photo Verification request and watch whether the answer is agreement or a story.
- Keep talking in Bumble. If the account ever needs reporting, the messages are still sitting there for moderators to read.
- Use Share Date before you meet: it tells a trusted contact who you are seeing, where and when, and can update them in the app if the plan changes.
- Reverse-search the photographs. Uniformly polished images, no candid shots and nobody else in frame is a pattern worth noticing.
- Notice who raises money first. Police guidance puts the test simply: any request for money from someone you know only online should ring an alarm bell — and that covers vouchers, cryptocurrency and investment opportunities exactly as much as it covers cash.

### Reporting on Bumble, and what happens next

To report a profile, open it, scroll to the bottom, choose Report or Block and Report, and follow the prompts. To report one specific message in a chat, use the three-dot menu on that message. Either way, moderators act faster on specifics: the number they gave you, the platform they named, the wallet they sent.

Already unmatched? The in-app buttons have gone with the match, but the route has not — contact Bumble Support directly with the person's name, your reason for reporting and any screenshots, since the investigation depends on what you can supply. Reports are confidential, so the person will not learn who reported them. You can follow the progress of a report in the Help Hub, though do not expect to be told what moderation action was finally taken.

Take your screenshots before you block, not after.

### Money has gone: the first 24 hours

Speed matters more than anything else now, and self-blame is the thing that slows people down most.

- Telephone your bank immediately. Where a transfer left a UK account through Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024, reimbursement may be available under the current rules: the maximum is £85,000, firms may apply an excess of up to £100, and a claim must be raised within 13 months. Each claim turns on its own facts, so no outcome is promised.
- Cryptocurrency, vouchers and gift cards are far harder to unwind, which makes saving wallet addresses, transaction IDs and voucher serial numbers urgent rather than optional.
- Ask Cifas about Protective Registration if identity documents or personal details were shared.
- File with Report Fraud (`reportfraud.police.uk`, 0300 123 2040) if you are in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101.
- Tell one person you trust today. Isolation is part of the method, and it also makes every practical step harder to face alone.

Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the order to work through. For free, confidential support outside your own circle, contact Victim Support in England and Wales on 0808 168 9111, Victim Support Scotland through `victimsupport.scot`, or Victim Support NI through `victimsupportni.com`.

### Frequently asked questions

**I made the first move, so how could it be a scam?**

Scam profiles are built to be swiped right on, not to start conversations. Who sends the first message on Bumble depends on the match and on any Opening Move that has been set; it is not a check on who sits behind the profile. Having opened the chat is neutral evidence, and it may make later warnings feel easier to dismiss.

**Can I make a Bumble match prove who they are?**

Up to a point. The request you can send in the app asks a match to complete Photo Verification — a selfie check that they match their profile photos. ID Verification, which uses a government-issued document plus a live selfie, is separate and optional in the UK. Neither proves intentions or financial claims, and because both are voluntary an absent badge proves little on its own. A refusal alongside declarations of love is still informative.

**My match says reply now or we will expire. Is that a warning sign?**

On its own, no — a Bumble match expires if no one sends a message within 24 hours of matching, so the timer is a normal rule. Paired with pressure to move to WhatsApp before the countdown ends, yes. One free Extend a day, plus Rematch on Boost and Premium, means a lapsed match is not a lost one.

**Doesn't Deception Detector remove the fake profiles for me?**

Not reliably. Bumble says that in testing it automatically blocked 95 per cent of the accounts it had identified as spam or scam profiles — the denominator is accounts Bumble had already identified, not every fraudulent account. No automated tool guarantees that a profile is safe, and screening is weakest against one patient human who does nothing unusual for weeks.

**How do I report someone on Bumble after unmatching?**

The in-app buttons go with the match, so contact Bumble Support instead, giving the person's name, your reason and any screenshots or payment details you kept. You can check the report's progress in the Help Hub. Where money was lost, report to Report Fraud as well, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

## Facebook Dating Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Profiles and Protect Yourself

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/facebook-dating-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Facebook dating scams use fake profiles to build trust, then ask for money. Learn the warning signs, how to verify a profile, and how to report it.

### What is a Facebook dating scam?

A Facebook dating scam happens when a criminal creates a fake profile — often using stolen photos — and targets you through Facebook Dating or direct messages. The scammer's goal is to build an emotional connection with you over weeks or months, then ask for money. The requests usually start small (a few pounds for a meal or transport) and escalate to larger sums for supposed emergencies, medical bills, business investments, or travel costs to meet you in person. Some scammers also use the relationship to trick you into sharing personal information, which they then use for identity theft or to blackmail you. The scam is effective because it exploits loneliness and the ordinary human desire for connection — not because victims are careless. Victims often feel embarrassed to report it because they have developed genuine feelings for a person who turned out not to exist. The criminal may rely on that embarrassment to discourage reporting.

### Warning signs of a fake Facebook dating profile

No single sign proves a profile is fake. Each one below shifts the odds, and several appearing together is a strong reason to stop and verify before you send money or share personal details.

- Stolen or generic photos — the profile picture looks professionally taken or like a stock image, and a reverse image search shows the same photo used elsewhere online. Plenty of real people have flattering photos, so treat a match as a prompt to dig further rather than a verdict on its own.
- Vague or inconsistent personal details — they claim a specific profession but give evasive answers about their work, location, or family, and the story shifts each time they tell it. Inconsistency over time matters more than any single vague answer.
- Reluctance to video call — they make excuses (broken camera, poor internet, work restrictions) whenever you suggest a video call or meeting. Some genuine people are camera-shy or have real constraints, but a pattern of excuses stretching over weeks, especially alongside money requests, is a serious concern.
- Fast emotional escalation — within days or weeks they say they love you, want to marry you, or talk about a shared future, far faster than the relationship would warrant.
- Requests for money or financial information — cash for emergencies, travel, medical treatment, business opportunities, or debts. They may also ask for bank details, card numbers, or passwords. A money request is enough reason not to pay and to treat the interaction as high risk; you do not need another warning sign before stopping.
- Isolation tactics — they discourage you from telling friends or family about the relationship, or suggest the people close to you are jealous and trying to break you up.
- Requests to move off Facebook — they push early to move conversations to WhatsApp, Telegram, or email, away from Facebook's reporting and monitoring systems.
- Messaging that does not fit the conversation — replies that read as copy-pasted, answer a question you did not ask, or arrive in a rhythm suggesting several people share the account. Judge the fit between question and answer, not the standard of the English itself. Many genuine people on UK dating platforms write in a second or third language, and treating imperfect English as evidence of fraud will cost you real connections while missing the fluent scammers entirely.

### How the scam unfolds from first contact to money loss

The scam typically begins when the fake profile sends you a message or likes your photo. They will compliment you, ask personal questions, and seem genuinely interested. Over the following weeks they build rapport by messaging regularly, sharing false details about their life, and expressing affection. They may send small gifts to make the relationship feel real. Once they believe you are emotionally invested, they introduce a problem: a family emergency, a business deal needing funding, medical bills, or travel costs to visit you. They ask if you can help — often starting with a small amount to test whether you will comply. If you send money, they thank you profusely and promise to repay you, then create another emergency and ask for more. Some victims have sent thousands of pounds over months.

Two variants are worth knowing. In the first, the scammer asks you to receive money into your bank account and pass it on, claiming they cannot access UK banking. They may be trying to use you as a money mule. Do not receive or forward money for them, and contact your bank immediately if any funds have already arrived. Accounts used to move criminal funds can be frozen or closed, and knowingly continuing after you suspect where the money came from can lead to a criminal investigation or prosecution. In the second, there is no money request at all — the scammer patiently collects your full name, address, date of birth, and identity document details, which are then sold or used to open credit in your name.

### How to verify if a Facebook dating profile is genuine

If you are unsure whether someone is real, work through these checks before sending money or sharing personal information. None is conclusive alone, but together they can help you make a more informed assessment.

Ask them to video call. Use Messenger's video call feature or suggest WhatsApp video. A video call does not prove identity or intentions, and some genuine people may be reluctant, but repeated excuses over time are a warning sign — especially when they appear just as the conversation turns to meeting or money.

Reverse-image search their profile photo. Go to Google Images, click the camera icon, and upload the photo. If it appears on modelling sites, stock libraries, or other dating profiles under different names, that is strong evidence the profile is not genuine, though it does not prove who created it or how the image was obtained. A clean result is weaker evidence than a match — it means the photo is not in the indexes, not that the person is real.

Search their name and stated details — workplace, hometown, university — and see whether a consistent real person emerges. Ask specific questions about their life and note whether answers stay consistent over weeks.

Look at the shape of the account. Long posting history, tagged photos from friends, and a friends list mixing family, colleagues, and school friends are all harder to fake than a profile photo. A sparse account is common among scammers, but also among people who simply do not use Facebook much or who set up a fresh profile after a breakup — weigh it alongside everything else rather than on its own.

Be cautious with cover stories that conveniently explain why someone can never meet or video call — deployed military officer, offshore oil rig worker, surgeon on an overseas contract. These are heavily used precisely because they pre-empt the obvious question.

And if they ask for money, stop and do not pay. The request alone is enough to treat the interaction as high risk, however close you feel and however plausible the emergency sounds.

### What to do immediately if you have already sent money or shared details

Act quickly — speed materially affects whether the money comes back.

Contact your bank or payment provider straight away. Call the number on the back of your card, use your banking app, or, if your bank supports it, call 159 to be connected safely to your bank — it is the outbound route you dial that cannot be spoofed. Ask them to attempt a recall of the payment.

If you paid by bank transfer, you may be entitled to be reimbursed. Since 7 October 2024, UK payment firms have operated under mandatory reimbursement rules for authorised push payment (APP) fraud, which includes romance scams where you were deceived into authorising the payment yourself. The rules cover eligible Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers between UK accounts. Report the claim promptly and no later than 13 months after the final payment. Your bank should normally reimburse an eligible claim within five business days, up to a maximum of £85,000. Your firm may apply an excess of up to £100, and some may choose to waive it; neither the excess nor the gross-negligence exception can be applied if the firm assesses you as a vulnerable consumer. Limited exclusions apply, so cooperate with reasonable questions from your bank. You do not need to prove the scammer's identity or catch them. If your bank refuses, make a formal complaint and ask for its final response in writing; you can then take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free.

Different payment methods take different routes. If you paid by debit or credit card, contact the card issuer immediately and ask whether it can attempt a chargeback under the card-scheme rules. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act is not general scam reimbursement: it may apply only to a qualifying credit-card purchase costing more than £100 and no more than £30,000 where the supplier breached the contract or misrepresented what was being supplied. Money transfer services such as Western Union or MoneyGram should be contacted immediately to try to halt a transfer still in transit. PayPal payments you sent deliberately should be reported through PayPal's scam reporting route, not as an unauthorised transaction — an unauthorised claim means someone used your account without permission, and reporting it that way will be investigated and rejected on the facts, costing you time.

Report the scam to Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) on 0300 123 2040 or at reportfraud.police.uk. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101 instead — Report Fraud does not cover Scotland. Ask for a crime reference number and keep it; your bank or a later dispute process may ask for it.

If you shared personal information such as your name, address, date of birth, or identity document details, apply for Cifas Protective Registration. This places a flag against your name in the National Fraud Database, so lenders carry out extra checks before opening credit in your name. It is a paid service and it will slow down your own credit applications — that is the point of it. Then check your credit file with the UK credit reference agencies MoneyHelper lists: Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three main agencies, plus Crediva. Each is required to provide statutory access to your file, and checking each of them matters because lenders do not all report to the same agency.

Do not send any more money, whatever they say — including if they now claim they can release your earlier payments once you cover one final fee. That follow-up demand is a standard part of the script, not a change in the situation.

### Reporting the scam in the UK

Report the fake profile to Facebook. In Facebook Dating, open Matches or your conversations, tap through to the profile or conversation, then use Options and choose Report. For a standard Facebook profile outside Dating, use the three-dot menu on the profile and select the reporting option, choosing the fake account or scam category. Facebook will investigate and may remove the profile, though this takes time and you should not wait on it before contacting your bank.

Report the crime to Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) on 0300 123 2040 or at reportfraud.police.uk, which handles fraud reports for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland and shares intelligence with police forces. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If you received suspicious emails or links, forward them to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you received scam text messages, forward the text to 7726, free of charge. These routes are for suspicious messages only — they are not a route for reporting the romance scam itself, and they will not reach anyone who can act on a crime report.

The consumer service for your nation can help you understand your rights and next steps: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262. For free, confidential emotional support, contact Victim Support in England and Wales on 0808 168 9111, Victim Support Scotland through `victimsupport.scot`, or Victim Support NI through `victimsupportni.com`. That support is offered, independently of the police, and you do not need to have reported the crime to use it.

Keep everything as evidence: messages, screenshots of the profile before it disappears, the profile URL, payment references, and bank correspondence. Scammers delete accounts quickly once they are challenged, and evidence you did not capture is usually gone for good. The more people who report the same profile, the faster Facebook and law enforcement can connect it to other victims.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I get my money back if I sent it to a Facebook dating scammer?**

Often, yes — more often than most people expect. For eligible Faster Payments or CHAPS transfers between UK accounts made on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory reimbursement rules mean your bank should normally reimburse an eligible APP fraud claim within five business days, up to £85,000. Report promptly and no later than 13 months after the final payment. A firm may apply an excess of up to £100, but it cannot apply the excess or the gross-negligence exception if it assesses you as a vulnerable consumer. Romance scams are covered: being deceived into authorising the payment yourself is precisely what these rules address, and you do not have to identify or catch the scammer to qualify. If you paid by card, ask the issuer whether it can attempt a chargeback; Section 75 applies only to qualifying credit-card purchases involving breach of contract or misrepresentation, not to scam payments generally. Money transfer services such as Western Union should be contacted immediately in case the transfer can still be stopped. PayPal payments you sent deliberately should be reported through PayPal's scam route rather than as an unauthorised transaction. Report to your bank first and fastest, then to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. If your bank declines to reimburse you, make a formal complaint and ask for its final response in writing; you can then take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free to use.

**What should I do if the scammer is threatening me or asking me to send explicit photos?**

Do not send any images, and do not pay. Paying does not end it — it signals you will pay again.

Preserve evidence before you block: screenshot the threats, the profile, and the profile URL. Once you block, you may lose access to the conversation, and the police and the platform will both want it.

Then report the profile to Facebook using the reporting tools on the profile or conversation. If you are in immediate danger call 999. Otherwise call the police on 101 — in Scotland, 101 reaches Police Scotland directly. Threatening to share intimate images is a criminal offence in the UK, and the police can act on it.

For specialist help, the Revenge Porn Helpline on 0345 6000 459 supports adults facing intimate image abuse and can work with platforms to get content removed. StopNCII.org lets you create a digital fingerprint of an image from your own device — the image itself is never uploaded — which participating platforms including Facebook use to block it from being shared. If you are under 18, contact Childline's Report Remove service instead. For free emotional support, contact Victim Support in England and Wales on 0808 168 9111, Victim Support Scotland through `victimsupport.scot`, or Victim Support NI through `victimsupportni.com`.

Do not report this to report@phishing.gov.uk. That inbox handles suspicious emails and nothing else — no one there can act on image abuse or a threat against you.

**Is it safe to meet someone from a Facebook dating profile in person?**

Meeting someone you have only known online carries risk, particularly if you have not video called them. Use a video call and reverse-image search as preliminary checks, while remembering that neither proves identity or intentions. If you do meet, tell a trusted friend or family member where you are going, who you are meeting, and when you expect to be back, and arrange to check in with them. Meet in a public place in daylight, never at their home or a private location, and arrange your own transport there and back so you are not dependent on them to leave. If they do not match their photos, or anything else feels wrong, leave — you owe a stranger no explanation. If they ask for money before or during the meeting, do not pay and treat the situation as high risk.

**How can I tell if someone's Facebook profile is real before I start chatting?**

Look at the whole account rather than any single feature. Genuine profiles often have a history of posts and photos, tagged photos posted by other people, a friends list mixing different parts of their life, and details that stay consistent across the profile. Reverse-image search the main photo — if it turns up on modelling sites or on other dating profiles under a different name, that is strong evidence the profile is not genuine, but not proof of who created it. A friends list made up almost entirely of attractive strangers with minimal activity is a common pattern on fake accounts.

None of this is conclusive. Real people delete old posts, keep locked-down privacy settings, or start fresh profiles after a breakup, and a sparse account is not evidence of fraud on its own. Use these checks to decide how much caution to apply, not to convict someone. A video call can be a useful check, but it does not establish identity or prove the person's intentions. Any request for money is enough reason not to pay and to treat the interaction as high risk.

**What if I have already fallen in love with someone and now I am worried they might be a scammer?**

That worry is worth taking seriously, and having it does not make you foolish — these scams are run by organised criminals who are practised at this.

Ask for a video call. It can provide useful evidence, but it cannot establish identity or intentions on its own. Refusal or a fresh excuse is a strong warning sign. Ask specific questions about their life and see whether the answers hold up over time, and search their name and details online.

If they have asked for money at any point, do not pay and treat the interaction as high risk regardless of how convincing the reason was. Talk to a trusted friend or family member too — being emotionally involved makes patterns genuinely hard to see from the inside, which is why scammers work to isolate you from the people who would spot them.

If you have already sent money, read the section above on reimbursement before you assume it is gone. Recovery may still be possible, and being deceived by a practised criminal is not your fault. For free, confidential emotional support, contact Victim Support in England and Wales on 0808 168 9111, Victim Support Scotland through `victimsupport.scot`, or Victim Support NI through `victimsupportni.com`; for consumer rights, use the service for your nation — Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.

## Hinge Romance Scam UK: Warning Signs and What to Do

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/hinge-romance-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Learn the warning signs of a Hinge romance scam, what online checks can prove, how UK bank reimbursement works and where to report it.

### What is a Hinge romance scam?

Romance fraud is a deliberately fabricated relationship used to gain trust and exploit someone financially. On Hinge, a criminal may use a false or stolen identity, build contact over time and then introduce an emergency, travel cost, investment or other reason to send money.

A profile can also belong to a real person whose photos or account have been misused. The important test is the behaviour and the payment request, not whether the profile initially looks authentic.

### Warning signs

- They ask for money, vouchers, cryptocurrency, financial details or an investment.
- The request is urgent or secret, or they discourage you from discussing the relationship with friends and family.
- They quickly try to move the conversation away from Hinge. Hinge warns that people with bad intentions may do this to get away from its message filters and reporting tools.
- They repeatedly avoid meeting, a phone call or a video call. This is an indicator, not proof by itself.
- Their identity, location or personal story is inconsistent.
- A supposed emergency, journey home, business problem or investment appears only after trust has been established.

Hinge's own safety advice says to report a user who asks for money.

### How the manipulation develops

The contact may feel attentive and personal because the criminal is deliberately learning what matters to the person they are targeting. UK fraud-reporting guidance says romance fraud can continue for months or years and may isolate the victim from people who could challenge the story.

The first request may be small. Later requests can be framed as proof of commitment, a loan, an emergency or access to an investment. A second payment does not recover the first. Criminals may also return later pretending that they can recover the loss for a fee.

### Useful checks — and their limits

Run a reverse-image search to see whether profile photos appear under another identity. Ask questions, take time and speak to someone you trust before making any financial decision. Keeping the conversation in Hinge while you assess the match also preserves its reporting route.

No single online check proves that a person is genuine. A clean image search proves only that the tool found no match. Social accounts can be fabricated or compromised, and a phone or video call does not validate every claim. Never send money, vouchers, cryptocurrency or investment funds to someone you know only online.

### If you sent money

Stop further payments and contact the bank or payment provider immediately through its official app, website or the number on your card. Describe it as a scam and ask about recall and reimbursement. Preserve the profile, messages, payment details and any account or wallet identifiers before blocking and reporting the contact.

The Payment Systems Regulator says romance scams can fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement protections for qualifying UK Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers. Coverage depends on the payment, account and scheme rules, so ask the bank to assess the claim rather than assuming the loss is final. Card, cash, gift-card, international-transfer and cryptocurrency payments follow different recovery processes; contact the relevant provider urgently.

### Report the account and the fraud

Hinge says a profile or chat can be reported through the three-dot menu and that reports are confidential. If the profile is no longer visible, use Hinge's Safety and Reporting support route; its Past Matches reporting feature is not available to every user.

Report financial loss to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101. Forward a suspicious SMS text to 7726 so the mobile provider can investigate it. Forward a suspicious email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`; this reports the message to the NCSC but does not replace a fraud report.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does moving a conversation away from Hinge prove it is a scam?**

No. It is a warning sign rather than proof. Hinge says users with bad intentions often try to move conversations away quickly, so slow down and do not send money or financial information.

**Can a video call or established social account prove the match is genuine?**

No. These checks may reveal inconsistencies, but they cannot authenticate every claim or payment request. Treat any request for money, vouchers, cryptocurrency or an investment as unsafe.

**Can my bank reimburse a romance-scam transfer?**

Possibly. The mandatory APP rules can cover romance scams involving qualifying UK Faster Payments or CHAPS transfers. Contact the bank immediately and ask it to assess the claim under the current reimbursement rules; other payment methods have different protections.

**How do I report someone who has unmatched me?**

Where Hinge's Past Matches feature is available, it may show matches from the previous 30 days and provide a Report option. Because Hinge describes this as a limited test, use its Safety and Reporting support form if the feature is unavailable.

**Should I send a small amount to test whether the story is genuine?**

No. A small first payment can be used to make later requests feel easier. Do not send more money to recover an earlier payment or pay anyone who promises to recover a loss for an upfront fee.

## Military Romance Scam UK: Spot a Fake Soldier Online

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/military-romance-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Met a 'deployed soldier' online who needs money for leave, flights, or crypto? Spot a military romance scam, check safely, and report it in the UK.

### What a military romance scam looks like

A military romance scam is when a criminal builds an online relationship while posing as a soldier or service member, often claiming to be deployed overseas, then uses that bond to ask for money. They may invest weeks in messages and affection before the first request. An example of the style is: `I would fly to you tomorrow, but my leave papers are blocked unless I pay a £1,500 admin fee, and my account is frozen while I am deployed. You are the only person I can trust.`

The "deployment" conveniently explains why they can never meet and why live calls are difficult. These scams can be patient and manipulative; being targeted is not naivety. This guide shows the warning signs, how to check, and what to do if you have already sent money.

### Why these scams are convincing

Romance scammers use stolen photos, scripts, and time. A deployment story can explain no meetings, unusual hours, and poor availability. They may mirror your interests and move quickly to talk of love and a future together.

The behaviour matters more than the uniform. A person who has never met you but asks for money for leave, travel, medical care, communications, official papers, a frozen account, gift cards, or cryptocurrency is showing a major scam warning sign.

### Signs a "soldier" online is a scammer

- They say they are deployed abroad and cannot meet in person.
- They repeatedly avoid live video or voice verification, especially once money is mentioned.
- The relationship moves very quickly to love and plans for a future.
- A money request follows: leave papers, flights, a phone, medical bills, documents, or a "frozen" account.
- They ask for gift cards, bank transfer, cryptocurrency, or payment to a third party.
- Photos look like model or professional shots, and small details shift over time.
- They move the chat off the dating app to WhatsApp, email, or another private channel early on.
- Later, they introduce a "guaranteed" crypto or investment opportunity.

### How the scam works

First, contact begins on a dating app or social media with an attractive armed-forces profile. Second, they build trust and intimacy over days or weeks. Third, an "emergency" creates the first money request, framed as temporary. Fourth, payments are demanded by gift card, transfer, or crypto. Fifth, the requests continue, or the scam pivots into a fake investment where you are coached to "invest" in cryptocurrency or another product you cannot really withdraw.

That investment turn is often called a pig-butchering pattern, covered in our /guides/pig-butchering-scam-uk/ guide.

### How to check if a forces profile is genuine

Take your time, and let the behaviour - not the uniform - guide you.

- Ask for a live video or voice call before the relationship becomes financial. Be cautious if every attempt is avoided.
- Reverse-image search their photos to see if they appear under other names.
- Treat any request for money for leave, travel, medical care, communications, documents, or official fees as a scam warning sign.
- Never send money, gift cards, or cryptocurrency to someone you have not met in person.
- Be very wary if the romance turns into an investment "tip" or a platform that shows fast profits.

If you are unsure whether a linked site or platform is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, and our /guides/tinder-scam-uk/ guide covers dating-app scams more widely.

### If you have already sent money or shared details

This happens to careful, intelligent people; romance scams are designed to bypass normal checks. If you paid by card, contact your bank or card issuer using the number on your card and ask about disputing the payment or chargeback where available.

### How to report a military romance scam (UK)

Report the profile to the dating app or platform with screenshots. If the scam reached you by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if it reached you by SMS, forward the text to 7726.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Tell your bank as soon as possible if money moved. Keep all your evidence; reports help investigators link cases.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is every soldier on a dating app a scammer?**

No. The warning signs are behaviour, not the uniform: they avoid live verification, declare love quickly, and ask for money, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or investment deposits before you have met.

**A deployed soldier says he needs money for leave, flights, or a frozen account - is that real?**

Treat it as a scam warning sign. An online partner should not ask you to pay military leave, travel, medical, communications, document, or frozen-account fees by transfer, gift card, crypto, or third-party account.

**He is now suggesting a crypto investment - what is that?**

That can be a pig-butchering pattern: the romance turns into an investment "tip" on a fake platform that shows made-up profits, so you invest more and can never withdraw. Stop, keep your money, and keep the evidence.

**I sent money to someone claiming to be a soldier - can I get it back?**

Possibly. Tell your bank immediately. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, and eligible UK transfers since 7 October 2024 may fall under APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions. Cryptocurrency recovery can be difficult.

**How do I report a military romance scam in the UK?**

Report the profile to the app, then report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Forward scam emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk` and scam texts to 7726.

## Pig Butchering Scam UK: Dating Apps & Fake Crypto

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/pig-butchering-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A dating match slowly steers the conversation toward crypto investing? That pattern has a name — here's how to recognise and avoid it.

### What a pig butchering scam looks like

This scam starts with contact on a dating app, or sometimes an unexpected "wrong number" text or message, that develops into what feels like a genuine relationship over weeks or months — usually without ever meeting in person. An example of the style, once trust is built: `I've been doing really well with a crypto trading platform a friend showed me. You should let me show you how it works.` The "relationship" is the mechanism, not a side effect.

### Why it's called "pig butchering" and why it works

The term is commonly used for scams where a target is gradually built up with trust and fake profits before the final loss. UK reporting guidance treats this as overlapping with romance fraud and cryptocurrency investment fraud: the emotional relationship creates the trust, and the fake investment platform extracts the money. Weeks of apparently genuine connection, with no red flags beyond never quite meeting in person, lowers your guard far more than a cold approach could.

### Signs you may be targeted by a pig butchering scam

- You met on a dating app, or through an unexpected message, and the relationship has moved fast emotionally.
- Despite weeks or months of contact, you've never met in person, and there's always a reason it can't happen yet.
- The person introduces a cryptocurrency trading "opportunity" or app.
- You're shown a dashboard of growing profits and encouraged to invest more.
- Attempts to withdraw money are met with excuses, fees, or the account being frozen.

### How the scam works step by step

First, contact begins on a dating app or via an unsolicited message, and a relationship develops over an extended period with no in-person meeting. Second, once trust is established, a cryptocurrency trading platform or app is introduced, often described as something the other person has personally profited from. Third, an initial small investment shows fake but convincing growth. Fourth, you're encouraged to invest increasing amounts, until a withdrawal attempt is blocked, a large fee is demanded, or contact stops altogether.

### How to protect yourself

Be cautious of any online relationship that moves toward a specific investment platform, however genuine the relationship feels.

- Never invest based on a relationship alone. Check any trading platform or firm independently using the FCA Financial Services Register.
- Treat an inability to ever meet in person, combined with an eventual investment pitch, as a serious warning sign.
- Remember that showing you fake "profits" on an app or platform proves nothing about whether the money is real or withdrawable.

### If you've already sent money

Stop sending any further money immediately, even if told a fee is needed to release a withdrawal. Be alert to a follow-up "recovery" approach — a separate scam where someone offers, for an upfront fee, to get your lost money back.

### How to report a pig butchering scam (UK)

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. This pattern can sit under romance fraud and cryptocurrency investment fraud. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**What does "pig butchering" actually mean?**

It describes a scam where a fake relationship or friendship is built over time before the victim is steered into a fraudulent investment.

**Is this just a romance scam, or something different?**

It overlaps with romance fraud, but the end goal is usually a fake cryptocurrency or investment platform rather than a direct request for money.

**I've already invested money with someone I met this way — what do I do?**

Stop sending any further money, even if told a fee is needed to release funds. Watch out for a follow-up recovery scam, and report what happened.

**Can I get my money back from a pig butchering scam?**

There's no guarantee, but contact your bank as soon as possible to ask about your options, and report it to Report Fraud, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Acting quickly gives the best chance.

**How do I report this kind of scam in the UK?**

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Tinder Scams UK: How to Spot a Fake Profile or Romance Con

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/tinder-scam-uk/
Category: Romance & Dating Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A Tinder match who moves fast, won't video-call, then needs money or pushes 'crypto'? How to spot a romance scam and protect yourself — without the shame.

### Three high-risk decision points on Tinder

Three moments on Tinder carry most of the financial risk, and each has a clean decision attached to it.

- A new match asks you to prove you are real by using a link they send you. Decision: never open it. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you.
- A match wants your number in the first handful of exchanges. Decision: slow down. That is a red flag rather than conclusive proof of fraud, and Tinder's own safety tips say to keep conversations on Tinder while you are getting to know someone.
- Weeks in, a warm and attentive person mentions a trading platform they use. Decision: treat that as fraud from its first mention, however long you have been talking. Tinder's safety tips put it plainly: do not let a match talk you into investing or opening an account with a service or website they share.

None of this requires you to be suspicious of people in general. Each one is a discrete choice with a right answer, which is why it is worth settling them in advance rather than mid-conversation with someone you are enjoying.

### What the Photo Verified badge actually proves

From 26 March 2026 Tinder began rolling Face Check out to new UK users, and describes it as required for all new UK users. You record a short video selfie in the app; Tinder's system tests that a real, physically present person took it and compares the face with the profile photos, then awards the Photo Verified badge. In earlier Face Check markets Tinder reported more than a 60 per cent fall in exposure to potential bad actors and more than a 40 per cent fall in bad-actor reports — those are Tinder's own measured results. Separately, Tinder offers an optional ID + Photo Verification process, which checks a government-issued ID against a selfie and profile likeness and confirms age; Tinder says expressly that it does not guarantee the ID's validity or a user's safety.

Read the badge for exactly what it is. The badge shows that Tinder's liveness and face-matching checks succeeded. Tinder also uses Face Check to detect the same face across multiple accounts, but neither the badge nor that detection guarantees a person's name, biography, location, relationship status or intentions.

The mandatory Face Check announcement applies to new users, so an older account should not be assumed to have completed it.

Face Check is a floor, not a character reference. Tinder's safety tips suggest a phone or video call as a screening step before meeting, and somebody who keeps producing reasons never to take one has told you something the badge cannot. Note, though, that Tinder's in-app Face to Face video chat has been discontinued, so any such call will run on a separate service. Arrange it if you want to, and carry on talking in Tinder afterwards rather than abandoning the in-app record.

### The 'get yourself verified first' link is always a scam

One pattern is close to universal on Tinder. An enthusiastic new match explains that she only meets people who are safety-verified, then sends a link to a site with a name in the style of `safe-dating-verify.com` or `datesafe-id.net`. The page imitates a background-check service. It wants your name, date of birth, email address and card number, and promises the card is only there to confirm you are an adult.

An unsolicited verification page like that may steal personal or payment information, and nothing on the page tells you which. There is no upside to filling it in.

The rule to hold on to is narrow and it is reliable. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you. Never use a verification link sent by a match. Start any genuine account or age-verification process only from Tinder's own app, site or help flow.

It is worded that way on purpose, because Tinder itself can send you outwards: an account restricted on age grounds may be directed from an in-app prompt to a third-party age-verification service. What matters is where the journey starts. A link that arrives in a chat is not a Tinder flow, and the response is to report the account rather than reason with it. If the same lure reaches you by email, forward it to report@phishing.gov.uk.

### Tinder's safety prompts, and what they do not tell you

Several Tinder features fire on their own. Read them as safety prompts, which is what Tinder calls them — not as findings about the person you are talking to.

- Contact Exchange Alerts appear when Tinder detects contact details being shared in a chat. The prompt surfaces safety information; it does not mean the app has judged the timing, or the person, abnormal.
- Are You Sure? asks a sender to reconsider a message that looks inappropriate, and Does This Bother You? offers the person receiving it an immediate route to report.
- Photo Verified Chat, when you enable it, restricts incoming messages to Photo Verified members. Tinder does not claim it removes any particular share of throwaway or bot accounts.
- Block Contacts lets you pre-block people from your phone's contact list. It is best-effort by Tinder's own account: Tinder says it cannot prevent two people seeing each other if the uploaded contact details do not match the details used to create the account.

None of these stops a patient, funded operator. What they do is interrupt you for a second, which is the only thing a prompt can do — the decision still belongs to you.

### When Telegram and a trading app enter the conversation

The most expensive Tinder pattern is not the urgent-emergency story. It is the slow one, where there is no crisis, no request and nothing to refuse. Across several weeks a match becomes a fixture of your day, mentions in passing that an uncle or a mentor handles money for the family, and eventually shares an app or web platform with a tidy interface and a balance that ticks upward.

A small opening deposit appears to grow. That screen is fabricated. Attempt a withdrawal and a charge appears: tax, a compliance fee, an account-upgrade minimum, an unlocking payment. Every one of those is another deposit into the same fraud, and paying one always reveals another.

Two details are specific to how this reaches you through Tinder. First, the chat usually leaves the app early, for WhatsApp or Telegram. Tinder holds the messages that remain in its own service and cannot review a conversation on another platform at all, so moving off-platform takes everything that follows out of Tinder's in-app moderation view unless you preserve it and supply it yourself.

Second, check the named platform on the FCA Firm Checker at `register.fca.org.uk` before any money moves, not afterwards. Look the firm up, read what it is actually authorised to do, and confirm that every contact detail you have been given matches the register. A fraudulent platform may be missing from the register altogether — but a scammer may equally impersonate an authorised firm or quote a genuine firm's real details, so a name that does appear is not a clean bill of health. Start the check from the FCA's own page, never from a link the match supplies. To pressure-test the site itself, our guide at /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### Screenshot first, then unmatch, block and report

Order matters. Capture screenshots first: the profile, the photos, the whole chat, any usernames, numbers, links or wallet addresses. The moment you unmatch, the conversation disappears from your side of the app.

Then open the three-dot menu on the profile or in the chat and choose to report — there is also a report button at the foot of every profile you can see. Follow the on-screen prompts, pick a reason, and add the details that help. Who submitted a report and what it said stay confidential, but Tinder does say a reported person may receive a generic notification that a report led to their account being reviewed, so do not assume nobody is told anything. Blocking removes their profile from your feed and stops them contacting you again.

If you unmatched first and only later realised what was happening, you have not lost the chance. Tinder's Safety Center carries an online route for reporting someone you unmatched, or who unmatched you, so the report is still possible once the connection is gone. Make it anyway: yours may be the report that closes an account currently working through dozens of other people.

### If you have already paid

Being targeted says nothing bad about your judgement. These are staffed, scripted operations run at industrial scale, working through many people at once with material that has been tested on other targets before it reached you.

Work in this order.

- Ring your bank today and use the phrase authorised push payment fraud. Money sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS from a UK account on or after 7 October 2024 may be reimbursable under the rules currently in force, to a maximum of £85,000, with a possible excess of up to £100 and a 13-month window to claim. Every case is assessed individually, so treat this as a claim worth making rather than a refund to expect.
- Card payments run on a separate track: ask your issuer about disputing the transaction.
- Ask Cifas about Protective Registration if you handed over identity documents or personal details.
- Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the full sequence, including what to preserve as evidence and who to tell in what order.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does a Photo Verified badge mean my Tinder match is genuine?**

It means Tinder's liveness and face-matching checks succeeded — a live person recorded a selfie that matched the profile photos. It guarantees nothing about their name, biography, location, relationship status or intentions. Tinder says Face Check is required for new UK users from 26 March 2026, so the badge is now ordinary rather than remarkable.

**A match sent a link to get me 'safety verified' before we meet. Is it real?**

No. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you, so a verification link that arrives in a chat is never legitimate. The page may steal personal or payment information. Start any genuine account or age-verification process only from Tinder's own app, site or help flow, and report the account instead of replying.

**Tinder showed a safety warning when we swapped numbers. Should I worry?**

That is Contact Exchange Alerts working as designed. It is a safety prompt triggered by contact details being shared, not a judgement about the timing or the person, so it is not an accusation and not evidence. Use the pause it gives you: Tinder's own tips suggest staying in the app while you get to know someone.

**I unmatched before I thought about reporting. Is it too late?**

No. Tinder's Safety Center has an online route covering someone you unmatched, or who unmatched you, so a report is still possible. Whatever you screenshotted beforehand will make it far more useful to their moderators.

**My match steered me into a trading app and now I cannot withdraw. What now?**

Stop paying. Withdrawal taxes, release charges and upgrade minimums are all part of the same fraud. Phone your bank the same day, look the platform up on the FCA Firm Checker starting from the FCA's own site, and report it. Recovery is uncertain, particularly with cryptocurrency, but speed genuinely improves the odds.

## Amazon Prime Scam UK: Spot a Fake Renewal Email

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/amazon-prime-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Got an email saying your Amazon Prime membership failed to renew or payment failed? How to spot a fake Prime renewal scam and report it in the UK.

### What a fake Amazon Prime renewal email looks like

An Amazon Prime scam email pretends your membership has expired, your payment failed, or your account will be charged, so you click a link and hand over login or card details. An example of the style is: `Your Amazon Prime membership payment of £8.99 has failed. Update your payment details within 24 hours to avoid losing access: amazon-prime-billing.example`.

The link opens a fake Amazon login or payment page. Amazon does send genuine renewal and payment emails, so the red flag is an unexpected message asking you to click a link and enter details rather than checking your account directly.

### Why these emails fool people

Many people have Amazon Prime and expect occasional billing emails, so the message feels routine, and the threat of losing access or an unexpected charge creates urgency. The sender name and link can both be made to look genuine.

The reliable check is to go to the source yourself: open the Amazon app or type `amazon.co.uk` into your browser and check Your Account, Prime membership, and Message Centre there, rather than clicking the email link.

### Signs an Amazon Prime email is a scam

- It claims your payment failed or membership will be cancelled unless you act.
- It asks you to "update" or "confirm" card or login details through a link.
- The link is not `amazon.co.uk` or another genuine Amazon domain.
- It gives a short deadline before you "lose" Prime benefits.
- It uses a generic greeting or has spelling and formatting errors.
- It arrives when you have not made any recent changes to your account.

### How the scam works

First, an email claims a Prime payment or renewal problem. Second, urgency pushes you to click the link. Third, a fake Amazon login or payment page captures your details.
