Fourth, criminals use them for account takeover or card fraud. Fifth, they may follow up with more emails or calls pretending to be Amazon.

Checking Your Account directly on `amazon.co.uk` or in the app, rather than clicking the email link, breaks the chain.

### How to check an Amazon Prime email safely

Do not click links or open attachments in an unexpected Prime email.

- Open the Amazon app or type `amazon.co.uk` yourself and check Your Account, Prime membership, and Message Centre there.
- Never enter your Amazon password or card details on a page you reached from an email link.
- Treat any "payment failed" or "membership expiring" message with suspicion until checked directly.
- Contact Amazon only through the app or `amazon.co.uk`, not a number or link in the email.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, and our /guides/amazon-order-scam-email-checklist/ and /guides/amazon-phone-call-scam-uk/ guides cover related Amazon scams.

### If you clicked the link or shared details

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report an Amazon Prime scam email (UK)

Report a suspicious Amazon message to Amazon at `amazon.co.uk/reportascam`. If the same scam reached you as a text message, forward that text to 7726 so your mobile provider can investigate. A scam email can also be sent to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep the original email and any screenshots.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Amazon email about Prime payments, or is every such email a scam?**

Amazon does send genuine Prime billing emails, so the topic alone is not proof. Treat any email asking you to click a link and enter card or login details as phishing, and check your account directly at `amazon.co.uk` instead.

**The email says my Prime payment failed and I'll lose access - is it real?**

Check it yourself in the Amazon app or at `amazon.co.uk` rather than clicking the link. A genuine payment issue should show in Your Account or Message Centre, not only through an emailed link with a short deadline.

**I entered my card or Amazon login after clicking the link - what now?**

Contact your bank using the number on your card, change your Amazon password by typing `amazon.co.uk` yourself, and turn on two-step verification or a passkey if available. Ask about a chargeback if money left your account.

**How do I check if my Amazon Prime membership is really expiring?**

Open the Amazon app or type `amazon.co.uk` yourself and check Your Account under Prime membership. Never rely on a link in an email to judge whether a renewal problem is real.

**How do I report a fake Amazon Prime email?**

Report it to Amazon at `amazon.co.uk/reportascam`, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`, and if you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Concert Ticket Scam UK: Where They Happen and How to Avoid Them

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/concert-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake ticket sellers target sold-out gigs on Facebook Marketplace, Instagram and copycat sites. Where the scams happen and how to buy resale safely.

### Where these scams happen — the three main venues

Facebook Marketplace and event groups are a common source of concert ticket fraud in the UK. Sellers create profiles in advance of a popular event, list tickets at face value or slightly above to appear legitimate, and ask for payment by bank transfer. After payment, they block the buyer or simply stop responding. Searching for an event on Marketplace typically surfaces dozens of listings, with no way to verify which, if any, are genuine.

Instagram and X (Twitter) accounts with a handful of followers suddenly post selling two tickets to an event — "DM me for details". These accounts are often fraudulent. Using an established resale platform gives you buyer protection that a social media sale cannot; an unsolicited direct message offering tickets is a strong warning sign.

Replica or unofficial resale websites are designed to look like Ticketmaster, See Tickets, or Eventim but are registered to unrelated owners. They collect card details and do not issue tickets. Always check the full domain name before entering payment details — not just the logo or page design.

### Why sold-out events attract more scammers

Scammers deliberately target events that sell out quickly — major festivals, stadium tours, and finals — because the buyer's urgency overrides normal caution. When an event is officially sold out, any listing feels like a lucky find, which is exactly the emotional state fraudsters exploit.

Glastonbury is a particularly high-risk example. The festival registers tickets to the original buyer's name and photo ID. These tickets cannot be transferred at the door, meaning resold Glastonbury tickets are very likely to be refused entry regardless of whether they look genuine. Anyone selling Glastonbury tickets outside the official registration system is either running a scam or selling tickets that will not work.

### Warning signs before you pay

- The seller asks for payment by bank transfer, PayPal Friends and Family, or gift cards. None of these offer buyer protection, and they are the payment methods of choice for ticket fraudsters specifically because the money cannot easily be recalled.

- The listing was created recently, the seller has no transaction history, or the profile photo is a generic image.

- The price is at face value for a sold-out event from an unverifiable social profile. This can feel like a lucky find, but when a stranger on social media offers tickets at face value and asks for bank transfer, that combination is a warning sign. (Face-value resale through verified platforms like Twickets is legitimate — context matters.)

- The seller sends a ticket confirmation email that appears to come from the ticketing company. These are straightforward to fake using the correct logos and formatting. A confirmation email proves nothing before the event.

- The seller claims to be abroad, in a hurry, or unable to meet in person.

### Platforms that offer real protection — and ones that do not

The safest options are official resale channels operated by the original ticketing platform. Ticketmaster's Fan-to-Fan exchange, See Tickets resale, and Eventim resale all verify that the seller actually holds the ticket before it can be listed. Twickets operates on a face-value basis — sellers cannot charge above the original ticket price plus a small fee — and handles disputes between buyers and sellers.

The Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers (STAR) is the UK trade body for legitimate ticketers. STAR members follow a code of practice and offer dispute resolution; their website lists approved members.

Facebook Marketplace, Instagram, Gumtree, and classified ads have no dedicated ticket-purchase protection — if a transaction goes wrong, you are reliant on your bank's chargeback process rather than any platform guarantee. StubHub is a legitimate marketplace; check its current buyer guarantee terms before purchasing, as these differ from official resale channels.

Where possible, pay by credit card. A qualifying purchase with a cash price over £100 and up to £30,000 is protected under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act, provided there's a genuine credit agreement and a direct link between you, the card issuer, and the party actually supplying the ticket — making your card provider jointly liable for non-delivery. Buying through a resale agent or marketplace that takes payment on the seller's behalf can break that link, putting Section 75 in a grey area, so for resale purchases specifically, chargeback via your bank (available on debit or credit cards, though discretionary rather than a legal right) is often the more reliable route.

### Already paid and no tickets appeared — what to do now

Act as quickly as possible:

1. If you paid by bank transfer, call your bank immediately on the number on the back of your card and report it as fraud. The bank may try to trace or recall the transfer, but recovery is not guaranteed.

2. For a qualifying credit purchase with a cash price over £100 and no more than £30,000, ask the card issuer whether Section 75 applies. The debtor-creditor-supplier relationship can be broken by some reseller or payment-intermediary arrangements. For an eligible debit- or credit-card transaction, also ask about chargeback. Card-scheme deadlines vary, so ask promptly rather than assuming a fixed cutoff.

3. Do not send further money. Scammers sometimes contact victims again claiming they can refund you if you pay a processing fee. This is a secondary fraud on top of the first.

4. Report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Also report the seller to the platform where you found them — Facebook, Instagram, or whichever site was used.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it safe to buy concert tickets from Facebook Marketplace?**

It is a high-risk way to buy tickets. Facebook Marketplace has no buyer protection for ticket purchases. Legitimate fans do occasionally sell there, but so do the majority of ticket fraudsters. If you do attempt to buy through Marketplace, insist on meeting in person at the venue and only exchanging cash for the ticket once you have confirmed it scans at the door — never pay in advance by bank transfer.

**The seller sent me an email that looks like it came from Ticketmaster. Does that prove the tickets are real?**

No. Ticket confirmation emails are straightforward to fake using the correct logos, formatting, and plausible reference numbers. The only reliable proof is a ticket that scans at the venue's official scanners on the night. If you are buying in advance, you cannot fully verify the ticket through an email alone — this is why using official resale channels that verify seller ownership is so much safer.

**What is the safest way to buy resale tickets if an event has sold out?**

Use the official resale function of the original ticketing platform where one is available, and check the platform's current buyer terms before paying. Twickets operates on a face-value model; check its current protection and dispute terms too. A qualifying credit purchase with a cash price over £100 and no more than £30,000 may receive Section 75 protection, but intermediary arrangements can break the required relationship. Avoid paying an unknown seller by bank transfer.

**Someone is selling Glastonbury tickets above face value — is that legal, and will the tickets work?**

Selling Glastonbury tickets at any price above face value breaches the ticket's terms and conditions. More importantly, Glastonbury registers tickets to the buyer's photo ID — anyone who purchases a resold Glastonbury ticket is very likely to be refused entry at the gate, even if the ticket itself is genuine. It is effectively impossible to legitimately resell a Glastonbury ticket, making any listing an extremely high risk.

**I bought tickets from a reseller and they did not scan at the door. What do I do right now?**

Stay at the venue and speak to box office or venue staff immediately — do not leave. Explain the situation and ask them to log the incident; this helps with any subsequent fraud report. Then contact your bank as soon as possible to raise a chargeback or Section 75 claim, and report the fraud to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland. Keep all payment records and any messages from the seller as evidence.

## F1 British GP Ticket Scam UK: Spot a Fake Silverstone Seller

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/f1-british-gp-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Offered British Grand Prix tickets below face value from a seller on social media? How to spot a fake Silverstone ticket scam and buy safely.

### What an F1 British GP ticket scam looks like

Criminals advertise British Grand Prix tickets on social media, resale sites, and classified ads, taking payment for tickets that do not exist, cannot be transferred to you, or are not valid for entry. An example of the style is: `Selling 2x British GP grandstand tickets, below face value as I can no longer go. Bank transfer only, first come first served.`

Silverstone uses digital tickets in its Silverstone Tickets app. A seller who only sends a screenshot, PDF, or vague promise of a transfer is high risk: Silverstone says screenshots of digital tickets will not scan because the QR code is live. This guide shows the warning signs, how to buy safely, and what to do if you have already paid.

### Why these scams are convincing

Grandstand tickets sell out fast and are in high demand, so a below-face-value deal from someone who "can no longer go" sounds plausible and appealing. Genuine-looking screenshots, barcodes, or account-transfer messages can be faked or copied, and urgency around a high-demand event pushes buyers to skip proper checks.

The fact that protects you: Silverstone's own guidance says tickets are managed and transferred through the Silverstone Tickets app, and guests receive an email to accept the ticket on their own device. A screenshot or private payment promise is not the same as a completed transfer.

### Signs an F1 ticket seller is a scam

- They want payment by bank transfer to a personal account, with no buyer protection.
- The price is below face value for a sold-out or high-demand grandstand.
- They send only a screenshot, PDF, or barcode instead of completing the official app transfer.
- They cannot or will not explain how the ticket was bought and how it will be transferred.
- You are pressured to pay quickly because "someone else is interested".
- The seller found you through an unofficial group or an unsolicited social-media message.
- They cannot answer basic questions about the seat, grandstand, or purchase route.

### How the scam works

First, an advert or message offers tickets below face value or when demand is high. Second, you pay, often by bank transfer. Third, you receive a screenshot, PDF, or promise of a transfer that may be fake or never completed. Fourth, at the gate the ticket is refused because it is a duplicate, already used, or not held on your device through the proper process. Finally, the seller is unreachable.

Buying through official channels, and relying only on a completed Silverstone app transfer where that is the required delivery route, breaks the chain.

### How to buy F1 tickets safely

Use official routes wherever possible for high-demand events.

- Buy directly from Silverstone or F1's official ticketing links wherever possible.
- If buying resale, use a platform with clear buyer protection and avoid private bank transfers to strangers.
- Do not rely on screenshots of Silverstone digital tickets; Silverstone says screenshots will not scan.
- Confirm any ticket transfer is completed through the Silverstone Tickets app before you rely on it.
- Be very wary of below-face-value deals for a sold-out or high-demand event.
- Prefer paying by card or a protected platform rather than a bank transfer to a stranger.

If you are unsure, our /guides/concert-ticket-scam-uk/ and /guides/stubhub-ticket-scam-uk/ guides cover the same pattern at other events.

### If you have already paid

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report an F1 ticket scam (UK)

Report the seller or advert to the platform you found it on. If the scam reached you by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if by text, forward it to 7726.

If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep all your evidence, including any ticket files or screenshots.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it safe to buy F1 tickets from someone on social media?**

Treat it as high risk, especially for a high-demand event. Buy from Silverstone or F1's official ticketing links where possible, or use a resale route with clear buyer protection rather than a private seller.

**Can I use a screenshot of a Silverstone ticket?**

No. Silverstone says screenshots of digital tickets will not scan because the QR code is live. A seller sending only a screenshot is a major red flag.

**The seller is offering tickets below face value for a sold-out event - is that a red flag?**

Yes. A below-face-value deal for a sold-out grandstand is a common scam lure. Confirm any transfer through the official process before paying.

**I've paid for tickets that turned out to be invalid - can I get my money back?**

Possibly. If you paid by card, ask your bank about a chargeback. Eligible UK transfers since 7 October 2024 may fall under APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions.

**How do I report an F1 ticket scam?**

Report the seller or advert to the platform, then if you lost money, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Fake Festival Ticket Scam UK: How to Buy Safely

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-festival-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Tempted by a cheap festival ticket you spotted on social media? Here's how to spot a fake seller and buy safely before you pay a penny.

### What a fake festival ticket listing looks like

This scam is a social media post, marketplace listing, or lookalike website offering festival tickets that don't exist, are duplicated, or never arrive. An example of the style is a social post reading: `Selling my festival ticket, can't go anymore, must sell today — bank transfer only.` The urgency and 'bank transfer only' framing are the two biggest tells.

### Why these scams are convincing

Genuine fan-to-fan resale does happen, and popular festivals do sell out, so an urgent 'one ticket left' post doesn't look unusual on its own. A screenshot of a real-looking e-ticket is also trivial to copy and send to more than one buyer, so having 'proof' in your inbox doesn't confirm anything.

### Signs a festival ticket seller is a scam

- You're pushed to pay by direct bank transfer rather than through the platform's own payment or transfer system.
- The seller won't or can't prove the ticket is genuinely theirs to sell, beyond a screenshot.
- The price is drastically below face value, paired with pressure to decide immediately.
- The seller or site isn't listed with STAR (the Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers) and isn't the festival's own official outlet.
- You're asked to move the conversation off the platform you found the listing on.

### How the scam works step by step

First, a listing or direct message offers a ticket, often at a discount, with pressure to act fast. Second, you pay directly — usually by bank transfer — to secure it. Third, either the seller disappears once paid, or the same screenshot ticket is sold to several buyers, and only whoever the venue scans first is admitted. By the time you find out, the seller is uncontactable.

### How to buy a festival ticket safely

Buy only through the festival's own official ticket outlet, or a reseller accredited by STAR (the Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers) — you can check a seller against STAR's member list at `star.org.uk`.

- Genuine ticket transfers for major festivals normally go through the official ticketing platform or app, not a private message.
- Treat 'bank transfer only, must be quick' as a decisive warning sign on its own.
- If in doubt, a screenshot alone is never proof a ticket is genuine or hasn't already been sold to someone else.

### If you've already paid for a fake ticket

If you paid by credit card, ask your card provider about a Section 75 claim for payments of more than `£100` and up to `£30,000`. If you paid by debit card, ask about chargeback; it is a card-scheme process rather than a legal right, and your bank will explain the time limits and evidence needed. Stop all further contact with the seller. If the event is still ahead, contact the festival's official box office to ask whether there's anything they can do, though a ticket bought this way often can't be salvaged.

### How to report a fake festival ticket scam (UK)

Report the listing to the platform it appeared on (Facebook, Instagram, or the marketplace itself), and report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it ever safe to buy a resold festival ticket?**

Yes — through a reseller accredited by STAR (the Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers) or the festival's own official platform. The risk is concentrated in off-platform social media sales paid by direct bank transfer.

**What is STAR and how do I check a seller?**

STAR (Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers) is a self-regulatory body for the UK ticketing industry with a government-approved Alternative Dispute Resolution service. You can check whether a seller or site is an accredited member at `star.org.uk` before paying.

**I've already paid for a ticket that turned out to be fake — can I get my money back?**

If you paid by credit card, ask about a Section 75 claim for amounts more than `£100` and up to `£30,000`. If you paid by debit card, ask your bank about a chargeback. Report the scam to Report Fraud either way, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

**I bought a ticket and the festival is tomorrow — what can I do right now?**

Contact the festival's official box office directly to ask if anything can be verified or done, but be realistic that a ticket bought through an unofficial channel often can't be recovered in time. Focus on the chargeback or Section 75 route afterwards.

**How do I report a fake festival ticket seller?**

Report the listing to the platform it appeared on, and report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Glastonbury Ticket Scam UK: Spot a Fake Seller

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/glastonbury-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-05

Offered a Glastonbury ticket outside the official route? Check the festival and See Tickets directly before paying a private seller.

### What a fake Glastonbury ticket offer looks like

This scam is a social media post, message, or lookalike website offering a Glastonbury ticket outside the festival's own registration and ticketing system. An example of the style is a message reading: `I've got a spare Glastonbury ticket, can't go anymore — bank transfer only, first come first served.` Offers of special access, VIP-style passes, backstage access, or a "concierge" route should be treated as high-risk unless you can verify them directly through Glastonbury's official channels.

### Why Glastonbury tickets are different from other festivals

Glastonbury uses a registration-led ticketing system and directs buyers through official channels. That makes it a harder ticket to resell safely than many events, because a private seller's promise isn't the same as an official transfer or sale route. A seller offering a ticket outside the official process is asking you to trust them more than the festival's own ticketing system.

### Signs a Glastonbury ticket offer is a scam

- You're offered a ticket outside the official sale or resale route.
- You're asked to pay by direct bank transfer to a private individual rather than through an official channel.
- The offer includes "VIP", "backstage", "concierge", or special-access language that you can't verify on official Glastonbury pages.
- The seller is vague about how the ticket will actually transfer to you.
- There's pressure to pay immediately because "someone else is interested".

### How the scam works step by step

First, a seller advertises a ticket via social media or a direct message, often at or near face value to seem credible. Second, you pay by bank transfer, sometimes before being given any official ticketing details at all. Third, because the sale has happened outside the official process, the seller may disappear, the ticket may never arrive, or the ticket may not get you into the festival.

### How to buy or resell a Glastonbury ticket safely

Use Glastonbury's official channels and the official See Tickets Glastonbury route. Don't rely on a private seller's screenshot, story, or promise.

- Check the current Glastonbury ticket information directly, because sale and resale details can change by year.
- Treat any special-access claim as unverified unless it appears on official Glastonbury or See Tickets channels.
- If you're unsure whether a seller or site is genuine, check Glastonbury's own official channels directly rather than trusting what a seller tells you.

### If you've already paid for a fake ticket

If you paid by credit card, ask your card provider about a Section 75 claim for qualifying payments of more than `£100` and up to `£30,000`. If you paid by debit card, ask about a chargeback. Stop all further contact with the seller, and don't send any further payment even if told the first one "didn't go through".

### How to report a fake Glastonbury ticket seller (UK)

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. You can also check Glastonbury's current official contact page for festival-specific reporting routes.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it ever safe to buy a resold Glastonbury ticket?**

Only use the official Glastonbury route for the relevant year's sale or resale. A private ticket offer outside that system is a strong warning sign.

**Do VIP or backstage Glastonbury tickets really exist?**

Don't trust a private seller's claim. Treat VIP, backstage, concierge, or special-access offers as unverified unless you can confirm them on official Glastonbury or See Tickets channels.

**I've already paid for a ticket that turned out to be fake — can I get my money back?**

If you paid by credit card, ask about a Section 75 claim for qualifying amounts more than `£100` and up to `£30,000`. If you paid by debit card, ask your bank about a chargeback. Report the seller either way.

**Why might a resold ticket not work at the gate?**

A private seller's screenshot or story isn't the same as an official sale or transfer. Glastonbury ticketing is registration-led, so always check the official rules for the current year.

**How do I report a fake Glastonbury ticket seller?**

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland), and use Glastonbury's current official contact channels for festival-specific reporting.

## Is Viagogo Safe to Buy Tickets in the UK? What You Need to Know

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/viagogo-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Viagogo is a real resale marketplace, not a scam company, but hidden fees and refund problems are common. What UK buyers should know before paying.

### What Viagogo is — and why it has such a bad reputation

Viagogo is a secondary ticket marketplace, meaning it connects people who have tickets to sell with people who want to buy them. It is a real company that has operated in the UK since 2006. However, it built a lasting bad reputation through a practice called drip pricing: listing tickets at an attractive base price, then adding large booking fees, order processing charges, and delivery costs at the checkout stage, by which point many buyers had already committed emotionally to the purchase.

In 2018, the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) secured a court order against Viagogo — one of the few times the CMA had to go to court after a company refused to offer undertakings voluntarily. The order required Viagogo to show the total ticket price upfront and to provide clearer information about sellers. The CMA subsequently monitored compliance and threatened contempt proceedings before suspending further action once changes were made. Buyer complaints about fees, refunds, and invalid tickets have continued to be reported since then.

### The fees: what you actually pay versus the listed price

The advertised price and the final payable total can differ because compulsory fees and delivery charges may apply. Check the total, currency and delivery terms before entering payment details.

The CMA’s enforcement action required clearer pricing and seller information. That does not make every listing good value or every ticket valid, so compare the final total with the face value and any official resale option.

### Are Viagogo tickets valid? What can go wrong

Many buyers receive valid tickets and attend their event without issue. However, several things can go wrong:

- Duplicate or cancelled tickets. A seller may list the same ticket to multiple buyers, or the original ticket may be cancelled by the promoter. Viagogo should replace these under its buyer guarantee, but the process takes time and can be difficult if the event has already passed.

- Nominative or restricted tickets. Some events link tickets to the original buyer or restrict resale. The promoter’s terms may allow cancellation or refusal of entry, even where the ticket itself is genuine.

- Late or non-delivery. Viagogo often releases tickets close to the event date, though timing varies by event. If tickets have not arrived, contact Viagogo support through the platform before assuming fraud.

### Your rights if something goes wrong

Viagogo publishes a buyer guarantee that may provide replacement tickets or a refund when a ticket is invalid, subject to its current terms and deadlines. Contact the platform promptly; disputes are harder after an event has passed.

For stronger protection:

- Pay by credit card where practical. Section 75 may apply to a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and not more than £30,000, but the required credit and supplier relationship must be present; ask the card issuer to assess the facts.

- Chargeback. If you paid by card and the seller does not deliver, contact the card issuer promptly and ask whether the card-scheme rules allow a chargeback. Time limits vary.

- If a seller contacts you and asks for payment outside the Viagogo platform — by bank transfer, PayPal Friends and Family, or gift cards — stop immediately. This is a scam separate from Viagogo's own practices, and no buyer protection applies. Report it to Viagogo, and to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

### When it is definitely a scam — not just Viagogo being Viagogo

Separate from Viagogo's own controversial practices, fraudsters exploit Viagogo's reputation in specific ways:

- Fake Viagogo websites. Scammers build replica sites with near-identical URLs (viag0go.com, viagogo-tickets.co.uk, or similar) to harvest payment details. Always confirm the URL is viagogo.com exactly before entering any information. Type the address directly into your browser rather than clicking a link from an email or social media.

- Off-platform sellers. Someone contacts you on social media, by email, or via a classified ad claiming to have Viagogo tickets and asking for direct payment. Viagogo does not operate this way. Any seller asking you to pay outside the platform is conducting a fraud.

- Fake order confirmation emails. Phishing emails can imitate booking confirmations and direct you to a lookalike sign-in or payment page. Check the order by opening Viagogo yourself rather than using the email link.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Viagogo a scam or a legitimate company?**

Viagogo is a real, registered company, not a scam operation. It is a secondary ticket resale marketplace that has operated since 2006 and has been subject to formal enforcement by the UK Competition and Markets Authority. The company changed some of its practices following that action. Legitimate and risk-free are not the same thing with Viagogo — buyers should understand the fee structure, refund limitations, and ticket validity risks before purchasing.

**Are Viagogo tickets genuine and will they work at the door?**

Many buyers receive valid tickets and attend without issue. However, there is a meaningful risk that tickets are invalid, duplicated, or nominative (linked to the original buyer's name, which venues can refuse). The risk is higher for very high-demand events where promoters actively cancel resold tickets.

**Can I get a refund from Viagogo if the event is cancelled?**

Check Viagogo’s current terms and contact it promptly. A qualifying credit-card purchase may also give you a Section 75 route, but eligibility depends on the payment and supplier arrangements.

**What did the CMA do about Viagogo?**

In 2018, the UK Competition and Markets Authority secured a court order against Viagogo after the company refused to offer undertakings voluntarily — unlike StubHub, GetMeIn, and Seatwave, which offered undertakings at an earlier stage. The court order required Viagogo to show full prices upfront and provide clearer seller information. The CMA then monitored compliance before suspending further proceedings. The CMA case is publicly documented on gov.uk.

**Is there a safer alternative to Viagogo for resale tickets?**

Yes. Twickets is a face-value resale platform where sellers cannot charge above the original ticket price. Ticketmaster's Fan-to-Fan exchange and the official resale functions on See Tickets and Eventim allow sellers to list tickets with verified ownership within the original platform. Buying directly from the venue or the event's official ticketing partner avoids the resale market, and with it the risks specific to resale — but check the web address carefully first, because fake “official” ticket sites exist too. The Society of Ticket Agents and Retailers (STAR) maintains a list of approved members who follow a consumer protection code of practice.

## StubHub Ticket Scam UK: Spot a Fake Seller

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/stubhub-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Shopping Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Buying resale tickets on StubHub and offered a deal that bypasses the platform? How to spot a fake StubHub seller, buy safely, and report it.

### What a StubHub ticket scam looks like

StubHub is a genuine ticket resale platform, but criminals exploit it with fake listings, cloned websites, or messages that try to move you off-platform where its protections do not apply. An example of the style is: `I have 2x tickets on StubHub but I'll do a better price if you pay me directly by bank transfer instead of through the site.`

Once payment happens outside StubHub, StubHub's FanProtect protection is unlikely to help because the private payment is not a StubHub order. This guide shows the warning signs, how to buy safely, and what to do if you have already been caught out.

### Why these scams are convincing

A slightly better price for paying "directly" sounds like a reasonable saving, and a cloned website that copies StubHub's branding closely can look identical to the real thing. Pressure around sold-out or high-demand events pushes buyers to skip proper checks.

The rule that protects you: complete any StubHub purchase entirely within the platform. Its protections, including guarantees around valid tickets, apply to qualified orders made and paid for through StubHub itself.

### Signs a StubHub deal is a scam

- The seller wants to move payment off StubHub, by bank transfer or another method.
- You reached a "StubHub" site through an unfamiliar link rather than typing stubhub.co.uk yourself.
- The web address is a lookalike, not the genuine StubHub domain.
- You are pressured to pay quickly because the event is sold out or in high demand.
- The seller avoids using StubHub's own messaging system.
- The price seems unusually low for a sold-out or popular event.

### How the scam works

First, you find a listing or are contacted about tickets, genuinely on StubHub or through a cloned site. Second, the seller offers a discount to pay directly, off the platform. Third, you pay by bank transfer or another unprotected method. Fourth, the tickets never arrive, are invalid, or the seller disappears. Finally, because the payment happened outside StubHub, its guarantees do not apply.

Completing every step of the purchase inside the genuine StubHub platform breaks the chain.

### How to buy StubHub tickets safely

Keep the whole purchase on the platform.

- Type stubhub.co.uk yourself rather than following a link from an email, text, or ad.
- Keep the purchase and payment entirely on StubHub - never move to a bank transfer or private payment.
- Be suspicious of any discount offered specifically for paying off-platform.
- Check the exact web address before entering any payment details.
- Prefer paying by card within the platform, which combines with StubHub's own guarantees.

If you are unsure, our /guides/concert-ticket-scam-uk/ and /guides/f1-british-gp-ticket-scam-uk/ guides cover the same resale-ticket pattern at other events.

### If you have already paid off-platform

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report a StubHub scam (UK)

Report the seller or listing directly to StubHub through its help centre. If the scam reached you by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if by text, forward it to 7726.

If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep all your evidence, including the listing and any messages.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is StubHub a scam, or just used by scammers?**

StubHub is a genuine, established ticket resale platform. The scam risk comes from sellers trying to move you off-platform or from cloned websites, not from StubHub itself.

**A seller offers a discount if I pay them directly instead of through StubHub — should I?**

No. Always pay and communicate entirely within StubHub. Its buyer protections only apply to purchases made through the platform, not to private payments arranged outside it.

**How do I make sure I'm on the real StubHub website?**

Type stubhub.co.uk into your browser yourself rather than following a link from an email, text, or advert, and check the exact web address before entering any payment details.

**I paid a StubHub seller directly and the tickets never arrived — can I get my money back?**

Possibly, but StubHub's own guarantees are unlikely to apply to an off-platform payment. If you paid by card, ask your bank about a chargeback.

**How do I report a StubHub scam?**

Report the seller or listing to StubHub through its help centre, then if you lost money, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Facebook Ad Scam UK: Check the Ad Library First

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/facebook-ad-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake investment and counterfeit-goods ads run on Facebook using copied branding. Meta's own Ad Library shows what's really running.

### What the Facebook ad scam looks like

This scam is a paid advert on Facebook or Instagram using a real or near-identical brand's name and logo, promising something that doesn't hold up — a guaranteed investment return, heavily discounted branded goods, or a work-from-home job with unrealistic pay. An example of the style: `LIMITED STOCK: [Brand] clearance sale, up to 80% off, today only — click to order.` The ad often links to a professional-looking site or asks you to message a page directly, where the real request — a deposit, personal details, or upfront payment — follows.

### Warning signs to look for

- The brand name or logo is slightly different from the real company's, or the ad claims a discount far beyond what that retailer ever genuinely offers.
- The advertiser's Facebook Page is new, has few followers, or its "About" details don't match the real company.
- The ad promises guaranteed earnings or returns ("make £5,000 a week from home") with no clear, checkable explanation of how.
- Clicking through leads to a site that only accepts bank transfer or an unusual payment method, not a normal checkout.
- You're asked to message the Page directly and move the conversation to WhatsApp or email before completing any purchase.
- The advertiser doesn't appear in Meta's public Ad Library, or appears there with different branding or claims to what you saw in your feed.

### How this scam works step by step

A paid ad appears in your Facebook or Instagram feed, often looking identical to a genuine retailer or investment brand. Clicking through takes you to a site or a direct message conversation designed to extract payment or personal details quickly, before you have time to check further. If it's a goods scam, payment is taken and nothing arrives, or a cheap counterfeit turns up instead. If it's an investment or job scam, an initial payment or deposit is requested, followed by further requests once you've engaged, before contact stops entirely.

### How to check an ad before you click

Search Meta's Ad Library (`facebook.com/ads/library`) for the advertiser's Page name. Meta describes it as a public tool for viewing active ads currently running across its apps and services; for social issues, election, or political ads, Meta provides additional transparency information. A Page with no active ads matching what you saw, or running ads inconsistent with the brand it claims to be, is a strong warning sign. Separately, go to the brand's official website directly — not through the ad's link — and compare prices, contact details, and offers. For further verification steps, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### What to do if you've already paid

Contact your bank or card provider as soon as possible and explain what's happened — a card payment may be eligible for a chargeback if goods never arrive or are significantly not as described. Report the ad and the Page directly to Facebook or Instagram using the Report Ad or Report Page option. Keep screenshots of the ad, the Page, and any payment confirmation as evidence.

### How to report a Facebook ad scam in the UK

Report the ad in-app using Report Ad, and report the Page itself. Report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland — in Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. If you paid by card, ask your bank about a chargeback claim.

### Frequently asked questions

**How can I check if a Facebook ad is genuinely from the brand it claims to be?**

Search Meta's Ad Library (facebook.com/ads/library) for the advertiser's Page. It shows active ads currently running across Meta apps and services; additional transparency details apply to social issues, election, or political ads. Also visit the brand's official website directly, not through the ad's link, and compare details.

**Is Meta's Ad Library a real, current tool I can actually use?**

Yes — it's Meta's own public transparency tool for active ads across Meta apps and services, with extra information for social issues, election, or political ads.

**I paid for something advertised on Facebook and it never arrived — what now?**

Contact your bank or card provider and ask about a chargeback claim, since a card payment for goods that never arrive is often eligible. Report the ad and the Page to Facebook using Report Ad, and report the scam to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

**How do I report a scam Facebook ad?**

Use Report Ad on the advert itself and report the Page separately. Report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Instagram Fake Giveaway Scam UK: How to Spot and Report It

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/instagram-fake-giveaway-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Instagram fake giveaway scams trick users into following fake accounts, sharing personal details, or sending money for 'entry fees'. We explain how to verify genuine giveaways, what to do if you've already engaged, and how to report the scam.

### What is an Instagram fake giveaway scam?

An Instagram fake giveaway scam is when a fraudster creates a fake account impersonating a real brand, celebrity, or influencer, then posts a fake giveaway to trick people into engaging. The scammer might claim you've won a prize (iPhone, holiday, cash) and ask you to click a link, follow the account, share personal details, or pay an 'entry fee' or 'shipping cost' to claim it. The account looks convincing — it may copy the real brand's profile picture, bio, and posting style — but it is controlled entirely by the scammer. A blue tick is not proof a giveaway is genuine: some ticks are older notability-based verifications, and others simply mean the account pays for a Meta Verified subscription with an identity check — so a Meta Verified tick can be bought, and some legitimate brands go without one. Once you engage, you either lose money, have your account compromised, or your personal data is sold to other criminals. Real brands rarely run giveaways via Instagram DMs or ask winners to pay upfront.

### Red flags that an Instagram giveaway is fake

- The account is not the brand's genuine profile. Don't rely on the blue tick either way — a tick can be a paid Meta Verified subscription rather than an old-style notability verification (scammers can buy one, and some real brands don't have it), so confirm the account by finding the brand's official profile through their own website.
- The account has very few followers or was created recently. Scammers often set up new accounts; check the 'About' section or look at when the account was created if possible.
- The giveaway asks you to pay money upfront — for 'shipping', 'processing', 'entry fee', or 'tax'. Legitimate giveaways never charge winners to claim prizes.
- The post asks you to click a link outside Instagram or visit a suspicious website. Real brands run giveaways within Instagram or direct you to their official website only.
- The giveaway asks for sensitive personal information like your full address, bank details, passport number, or National Insurance number before you've won anything. Legitimate brands should not ask for sensitive financial or identity information before you have independently confirmed the giveaway and its terms.
- The account name is slightly different from the real brand — for example, 'Apple_UK_Official' instead of 'Apple'. Scammers use similar names to confuse you.
- The giveaway promise is too good to be true — a brand-new iPhone, £5,000 cash, or a luxury holiday with no clear entry mechanism. If the prize seems unrealistic, it almost certainly is.
- The post has poor grammar, spelling errors, or awkward phrasing. Many scammers operate from outside the UK and their English may be noticeably off.

### How the scam unfolds from first contact to loss

The scam typically starts when you see a post from what looks like a real brand or influencer offering a generous prize. The post asks you to 'like, follow, and comment' or click a link to enter. If you click the link, you're taken to a fake website that mimics Instagram's login page or a fake entry form. If you log in with your Instagram credentials, the scammer captures your username and password and can take over your account, lock you out, or use it to run the same scam to your followers. Alternatively, the fake entry form asks for your name, address, phone number, and email — data the scammer sells to other criminals or uses for identity theft. If the scam involves a 'shipping fee' or 'processing cost', you're asked to pay via bank transfer, gift card, or cryptocurrency. Once you pay, the scammer disappears and you never receive the prize. In some cases, the scammer may contact you via DM claiming you've won and asking you to 'verify' your details or pay a fee to release the prize. By this point, your account may already be compromised or your personal data is in criminal hands.

### How to verify if an Instagram giveaway is genuine

Before engaging with any giveaway, take these steps to confirm it's real. First, don't treat the blue tick as proof — a tick may be an older notability-based verification or just a paid Meta Verified subscription with an identity check, which scammers can also buy, and some genuine brands go without one, so a tick is not a green light and a missing tick is not proof of a scam. Second, visit the brand's official website or their official Instagram account directly (search for them fresh, don't click links from the giveaway post) and check their recent posts — do they mention this giveaway? Real brands promote genuine giveaways on their own official accounts and website. Third, look at the account's history: how long has it existed, how many followers does it have, and what kind of posts does it usually make? A brand-new account with 50 followers claiming to give away iPhones is almost certainly fake. Fourth, check the giveaway terms: does it ask for payment, sensitive personal data, or your Instagram login details? Legitimate giveaways never do. Fifth, if you're unsure, contact the brand directly using the contact details on their official website — not via the suspicious account — and ask if they're running this giveaway. Finally, be wary of giveaways that ask you to click external links; real brands usually run giveaways entirely within Instagram or direct you to their official domain only.

### What to do immediately if you've already engaged

If you've clicked a suspicious link or entered your Instagram login details, change your Instagram password right now using a device you trust. Go to Instagram Settings > Security > Password and create a new, strong password that you haven't used elsewhere. If you've already lost access to your account, use Instagram's account recovery process: go to the login page, tap 'Need more help?', and follow the prompts to regain control. If you've paid money via bank transfer, contact your bank immediately and explain you've been scammed. For eligible bank (Faster Payments) transfers made on or after 7 October 2024, banks must reimburse most victims of authorised push payment (APP) scams, subject to conditions and a cap — ask your bank to treat it as an APP scam claim and to try to recall the payment. If you paid via gift card or cryptocurrency, unfortunately the money is almost impossible to recover, but report it anyway (see below). If you've shared personal details like your address or phone number, monitor your credit report for signs of identity theft and consider Cifas Protective Registration if your identity is at heightened risk. If the scammer has taken over your account and is using it to run the same scam to your followers, change your password, enable two-factor authentication (Settings > Security > Two-Factor Authentication), and notify your followers via other channels that your account has been compromised. Do not click any links the scammer posts.

### How to report an Instagram fake giveaway scam in the UK

Report the scam through multiple channels to maximise the chance of action. First, report the fake account directly to Instagram: go to the account, tap the three dots, select 'Report', and choose 'It's a scam' or 'Impersonation'. Instagram will review and may remove the account. Second, report the scam to Report Fraud, the national fraud reporting service for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting their website. They log reports and share data with law enforcement and banks. If you live in Scotland or the crime happened there, contact Police Scotland on 101. Third, if the scam involved a phishing link (a fake login page), submit the web address through the NCSC's scam-website reporting form at ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website, and forward any scam email itself to report@phishing.gov.uk. Fourth, if you received a suspicious text message as part of the scam, forward it free of charge to 7726, the number most UK mobile networks use to report scam texts. Fifth, if you've lost money, report it to your bank and ask them to file a report with their fraud team. Finally, for guidance on next steps if you've been financially harmed, contact the consumer service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262. Keep records of all screenshots, account names, and links involved.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does a blue verification tick mean an Instagram giveaway is genuine?**

No. A blue tick can be an older notability-based verification or simply a paid Meta Verified subscription with an identity check — scammers can buy Meta Verified, and some genuine brands don't have a tick — so a tick is not an endorsement of any giveaway and a missing tick doesn't by itself prove a scam. The reliable check is to find the brand's real profile another way: visit their official website and follow the Instagram link they publish there, then compare the username character by character. Treat any giveaway you reached from a random post or DM with caution, however professional the account looks.

**I clicked a link from a fake giveaway and entered my Instagram password. What should I do?**

Change your Instagram password immediately from a device you trust — go to Settings > Security > Password and create a new, strong password. Then enable two-factor authentication (Settings > Security > Two-Factor Authentication) so the scammer cannot log back in even if they have your old password. Check your account activity for any unauthorised logins or posts, and if you see any, report them to Instagram. If you've already lost access to your account, use Instagram's account recovery process to regain control. Monitor your email for any password reset requests from Instagram or other services, as the scammer may try to compromise other accounts.

**I paid a 'shipping fee' for a fake giveaway prize. Can I get my money back?**

Contact your bank immediately and explain that you've been scammed — how you paid matters. If you paid by bank (Faster Payments) transfer on or after 7 October 2024, banks must reimburse most victims of authorised push payment (APP) scams, subject to conditions and a cap, so ask your bank to treat it as an APP scam claim. If you paid by debit or credit card, chargeback covers card payments (not ordinary bank transfers) — ask your card provider whether chargeback or other protections apply. If you paid via gift card or cryptocurrency, recovery is extremely unlikely because these payments are very difficult to reverse, but still report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, and tell your bank so they have a record. Do not send any more money to the scammer, even if they claim they need a 'processing fee' or 'tax' to release your prize — this is a common follow-up tactic.

**The fake account is still running the scam to other people. How do I report it?**

Report the account to Instagram directly: visit the account, tap the three dots, select 'Report', and choose 'It's a scam' or 'Impersonation'. Instagram reviews reports and may remove the account if it violates their terms. You can also report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, so it's logged with UK law enforcement. If the account is impersonating a specific brand or person, encourage them to report it too — brands and public figures have more direct channels with Instagram. Share screenshots of the scam with your followers so they don't fall for it, but do not engage with the fake account or click any of its links.

**Can scammers actually take over my Instagram account if I give them my password?**

Yes. If a scammer has your Instagram password, they can log in, change your email address and password, lock you out, and use your account to run scams to your followers or steal your personal data. This is why you should never enter your Instagram login details on any website outside of Instagram itself — even if it looks identical to the real Instagram login page. If you've already given your password to a scammer, change it immediately and enable two-factor authentication. If you've lost access to your account, use Instagram's account recovery process to regain control as quickly as possible.

## Instagram Investment Scam UK: Fake Trader Profiles

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/instagram-investment-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake 'trader' profiles DM UK Instagram users promising guaranteed crypto or forex returns, backed by edited screenshots. Here's how to check first.

### What the Instagram investment scam looks like

This scam is an Instagram profile presenting itself as a successful independent trader, fund manager, or crypto specialist, who contacts you directly rather than you finding them. An example of the style: `I've helped over 200 people this year turn £500 into £4,000+ trading forex — I only take on a few new clients at a time.` The profile shows screenshots of trading platforms and "client" testimonials, almost always edited or entirely fabricated, and asks for an initial deposit to "manage" on your behalf.

### Warning signs to look for

- The account contacted you first, unprompted, rather than you seeking out an adviser — genuine regulated advisers don't cold-DM strangers.
- The profile is recent, or investment content only appears after a sudden change from unrelated posts.
- Profit screenshots look inconsistent, or don't match how a genuine trading platform's interface actually looks.
- You're asked to send money to a personal bank account or personal crypto wallet, not a firm's segregated client account.
- They can't, or won't, give a Financial Conduct Authority reference number you can check independently.
- Financial promotions on social media may be unlawful unless they are made or approved by an authorised person and comply with FCA rules — an unauthorised "finfluencer" account offering to manage your money directly is a serious warning sign.

### How this scam works step by step

Contact starts with a follow or a direct message, often targeting accounts that engage with finance content or mention investing in their bio. The scammer builds rapport over several messages, sharing edited screenshots of supposed profits and sometimes fake testimonials from other "clients". You're asked to send an initial amount, commonly a few hundred pounds, to be "invested" on your behalf. A dashboard or further screenshots may show your balance apparently growing, encouraging a larger second deposit. When you eventually ask to withdraw, you're met with excuses, a request for a further "release fee", or silence, and the account is often deleted shortly after.

### How to verify a trader is genuine

Never invest based on an Instagram profile alone. Ask for a Financial Conduct Authority reference number and check it yourself on the FCA Firm Checker (`fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker`) — do not use a link or number the account gives you. A genuine, regulated adviser operates through a proper firm with a client agreement, not personal Instagram messages, and will never ask you to send money to a personal account. Treat unsolicited investment contact on social media as a red flag by default, regardless of how convincing the screenshots look.

### What to do if you've already sent money

Stop all further contact and payments immediately, even if promised a fee will "unlock" your balance. Report the profile to Instagram directly: open their profile, tap the three-dot menu, select Report, then Fraud or Scam. If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank straight away and explain what happened. Keep every message and screenshot as evidence — these matter for both your bank's investigation and any report you make.

### How to report an Instagram investment scam in the UK

Report the profile through Instagram's own reporting tool (three-dot menu → Report → Fraud or Scam). Report the scam itself to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland — in Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Report an unauthorised individual claiming FCA status to the FCA on 0800 111 6768.

### Frequently asked questions

**Are all Instagram trading/investment accounts scams?**

Not automatically, but any account that DMs you first with guaranteed returns and asks you to send money to a personal account should be treated as a scam by default. Genuine regulated advisers don't cold-message strangers offering to manage their money.

**Can someone legally promote investments to me on Instagram?**

Only if the promotion is properly made or approved under FCA rules — the FCA has specifically acted against unauthorised social media "finfluencers" promoting financial products. An account offering to personally invest your money for you, without a checkable FCA reference, should be treated as a serious red flag.

**I've already sent money to an Instagram 'trader' — what now?**

Stop sending anything further, and report the profile to Instagram (three-dot menu → Report → Fraud or Scam). If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank immediately, and report the scam to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

**How do I report an Instagram investment scam?**

Report the account in-app (Report → Fraud or Scam) and to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). Report an unauthorised firm or individual to the FCA on 0800 111 6768.

## TikTok Shop Scams UK: Spot Fake Sellers & Bad Deals

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/tiktok-shop-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A TikTok Shop deal that's too good, or a seller wanting PayPal 'friends and family'? How to spot a TikTok Shop scam and keep your money protected.

### What a TikTok Shop scam looks like

TikTok Shop is a real shopping feature, but scams can still happen around it. The main danger is a seller or message pushing you away from the official checkout, or a fake prize or shop link asking for personal, login, card, or bank details.

An example of the giveaway style is: `You've won our TikTok giveaway! Claim your prize here: tiktok-prize.example`. Another red flag is a seller offering a discount if you pay by bank transfer, gift card, or PayPal Friends and Family instead of using TikTok Shop checkout. Keep the order inside the official shop flow wherever possible.

### Why TikTok Shop scams catch people out

TikTok shopping is fast, visual, and trend-led, which makes impulse buys easy. Scammers can copy brand imagery, ride viral products, and use direct messages to create urgency. TikTok's own business page describes TikTok Shop as a shopping journey that lets customers check out directly within TikTok, so a request to leave that flow is a warning sign.

If you pay outside the official checkout, you may lose the platform order trail and have to rely on the outside payment method. PayPal says eligible purchases are protected when you send money via Goods and Services, which is why Friends and Family is the wrong payment type for buying from a seller.

### Signs of a TikTok Shop scam

- A seller asks you to pay outside TikTok Shop checkout by bank transfer, gift card, crypto, or PayPal Friends and Family.
- A branded item is priced far below normal retail price.
- You are pushed to buy immediately before a limited deal ends.
- A direct message says you have won a giveaway and links you off TikTok to claim.
- The seller has little history, weak review signals, or only stock-style images.
- You are asked for card, bank, password, or verification-code details outside the normal checkout.
- Errors can be clues, but a polished shopfront or message can still be unsafe.

### How the TikTok Shop scam works

First, a viral listing, livestream, comment, or direct message offers a bargain or prize. Second, it moves you away from the normal checkout or pushes you to an external link. Third, you pay by a method with weak purchase protection, or you enter personal and financial details on a fake page. Fourth, the item never arrives, is not as described, or the prize was only a way to harvest your details.

TikTok's phishing guidance says TikTok will not contact you to ask for your password, verification codes, or other sensitive personal information. Treat any message asking for those details as phishing.

### How to check and buy safely on TikTok Shop

Keep the purchase inside the official shop flow.

- Pay through TikTok Shop checkout where the product is listed, not through bank transfer, crypto, gift card, or PayPal Friends and Family.
- If using PayPal for a purchase, use Goods and Services where eligible, not Friends and Family.
- Treat an impossible branded bargain as a red flag for a fake, counterfeit, or non-delivery risk.
- Check the seller's ratings, reviews, return information, and whether the content matches the actual product.
- Ignore giveaway DMs that link you off TikTok to claim a prize.
- Never enter card, bank, password, or verification-code details from a DM or external link.

If you are unsure whether a linked site is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks, and our /guides/is-temu-a-scam-uk/ guide covers similar cheap-marketplace risks.

### If you paid or shared details

Act quickly. If the order exists inside TikTok Shop, use the order help, refund, or report options available in the app. If you paid by card or PayPal Goods and Services outside TikTok, contact the card issuer or PayPal and ask about a dispute or chargeback. If you paid by PayPal Friends and Family, recovery is much harder because PayPal's purchase-protection wording is tied to eligible Goods and Services payments.

### How to report a TikTok Shop scam (UK)

Use TikTok's in-app report options for the message, account, shop, or order where available. TikTok's help page for direct messages says you can report a specific message or report the chat, then choose a reason and submit the report.

If a scam reached you by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if it came by text, forward it to 7726. If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is TikTok Shop a scam, or just some sellers?**

TikTok Shop is a genuine shopping feature. That does not make every seller, message, or off-platform link genuine. Check the seller and keep payment in the official shop flow.

**A seller wants PayPal Friends and Family instead of normal checkout - is that safe?**

No. Friends and Family is not the right PayPal payment type for buying goods from a seller. PayPal says eligible purchases are protected when you send money via Goods and Services, subject to terms and limits.

**I got a TikTok message saying I won a giveaway - is it real?**

Treat it as suspicious if it asks you to leave TikTok, enter payment details, share login details, or provide a verification code. TikTok says it will not ask for passwords, verification codes, or sensitive personal information in this way.

**I have already paid a TikTok Shop scammer - can I get my money back?**

Possibly, depending on how you paid. Use TikTok's order help if the order is in TikTok Shop. Contact your card issuer or PayPal for card or eligible Goods and Services payments. Eligible UK bank transfers made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall under APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions.

**How do I report a TikTok Shop scam?**

Report the message, account, seller, or order inside TikTok where available. Forward scam emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk` and scam texts to 7726. If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

## WhatsApp Investment Scam UK: The Private-Chat Con

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/whatsapp-investment-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Unlike a public Instagram pitch, a WhatsApp investment scam builds a personal 'relationship' privately over days. Here's how to spot it.

### What the WhatsApp investment scam looks like

This scam is a direct WhatsApp message from someone claiming to be an investment professional, fund manager, or trader, often saying a mutual contact recommended you or that they found your number through a networking site. An example of the style: `Hi, I was given your number by a mutual connection — I run a small private trading group and thought you might be interested in what we're seeing in the markets right now.` What follows is usually days of relationship-building in a private chat, unlike a public Instagram pitch — building trust one-to-one before any money is mentioned.

### Warning signs to look for

- You don't know the person, and they contacted you first through WhatsApp with an investment opportunity.
- The account is recently created, or has a generic or stock profile photo.
- They claim exclusive access to a private trading group, fund, or opportunity not available to the public.
- Conversation moves from friendly and personal to investment-focused over several days, building trust before any money is mentioned.
- You're eventually asked to send money to a personal bank account or personal crypto wallet, not a firm's client account.
- They discourage you from mentioning the "opportunity" to family, a financial adviser, or your bank.

### How this scam works step by step

Contact begins with a friendly, low-pressure message, often claiming a personal connection or referral. Over subsequent days, the conversation shifts toward investing, with the contact presenting themselves as experienced and successful, sometimes sharing screenshots of trading platforms or supposed returns. Once trust is established, you're invited to invest a sum — commonly starting small — with a promise of managing it on your behalf. Screenshots or a dashboard may show apparent growth, encouraging further deposits. When you ask to withdraw, excuses, a demand for a further fee, or silence typically follows, and the contact often blocks you or disappears.

### How to check who you're really talking to

Ask for a Financial Conduct Authority reference number and verify it yourself using the FCA Firm Checker (`fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker`) — never through a link or number the contact provides. A genuine regulated adviser works through a proper firm with formal paperwork, not a personal WhatsApp number, and won't discourage you from checking with your bank or a professional adviser. If you can, verify the identity of whoever supposedly "referred" you directly, rather than taking the WhatsApp contact's word for it.

### What to do if you've already sent money

Stop sending anything further immediately, even if told an extra payment will release your balance. Report the WhatsApp contact using the in-app Report option (open the chat, tap the contact's name, then Report — you can block at the same time). If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank straight away and explain what's happened. Keep the full conversation as evidence.

### How to report a WhatsApp investment scam in the UK

Report the contact in WhatsApp itself (tap their name in the chat → Report). Report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland — in Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Report an unauthorised individual claiming FCA status to the FCA on 0800 111 6768.

### Frequently asked questions

**Why would a scammer use WhatsApp instead of a public platform?**

A private chat lets a scammer build a personal relationship over days without public scrutiny, unlike a visible Instagram or Facebook post. That slower, one-to-one trust-building is exactly what makes the WhatsApp version convincing to people who'd be suspicious of an obvious public ad.

**Someone said a mutual contact gave them my number — does that make it genuine?**

Not by itself. Verify this directly with the person supposedly named, rather than taking the WhatsApp contact's word for it — this claim is easy to fake and commonly used to lower your guard.

**I've sent money to a WhatsApp 'trader' — what should I do?**

Stop sending anything further, report the contact in WhatsApp (tap their name → Report), and contact your bank immediately if you paid by transfer. Report the scam to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

**How do I report a WhatsApp investment scam?**

Report the contact in-app (tap their name in the chat → Report) and to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). Report an unauthorised firm to the FCA on 0800 111 6768.

## WhatsApp Stranger Scam UK: How to Spot and Stop It

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/whatsapp-stranger-scam-uk/
Category: Social Media Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A stranger messaged you on WhatsApp? Learn the warning signs, how to verify who they are, protect your accounts, recover money and report the scam.

### What is a WhatsApp stranger scam?

A WhatsApp stranger scam starts with an unexpected message from an unknown person, or from someone claiming to be a person or organisation you know. The criminal may use a newly registered number, take control of a genuine WhatsApp account, or try to trick you into linking your own account to their device. Their aim may be to obtain money, passwords, one-time codes, identity documents, access to your WhatsApp account, or information they can use in a later scam.

The approach varies. Some criminals impersonate a family member with a “new number”; others begin with an apparent wrong-number message and build a relationship over days or weeks. Job, investment, parcel, business-support and romance stories can all move onto WhatsApp. The shared feature is not the subject of the message but the attempt to make you rely on the chat instead of verifying the request independently.

Receiving an unexpected message does not itself prove fraud. The safe response is to pause before sharing information, opening links, linking a device or sending money.

### Warning signs of a WhatsApp stranger scam

No single clue proves that an account is fraudulent. Several of these appearing together are a strong reason to stop and verify:
- A person claiming to be a friend or relative contacts you from a new number and quickly asks for money, gift cards, cryptocurrency or a bank transfer.
- A familiar account makes a request that is out of character. A real account can be compromised, so recognising the number or profile photo is not enough.
- The sender creates urgency, asks you to keep the request secret, or discourages you from checking with another person.
- A supposed job requires an upfront payment, a deposit, paid “tasks”, use of your bank account, or movement to a cryptocurrency platform.
- An investment contact promises guaranteed or unusually high returns, shows profits you cannot independently withdraw, or requires another payment to release funds.
- The sender asks for a six-digit WhatsApp code, a device-linking code, a QR-code scan, screen sharing, a password, PIN or one-time bank code. Do not provide or approve any of these.
- A link leads to a sign-in, payment or identity-check page you did not navigate to through the organisation’s official app or website.
- The sender asks for a passport image, date of birth, bank details or other sensitive information without a purpose you have independently confirmed.
- Details, tone or answers do not fit the person being impersonated. Treat that as a prompt to verify, not proof by itself; privacy settings, travel and language differences make profile photos, country codes and writing style unreliable tests.

### How the scam unfolds from first contact to the request

An impersonation scam may move quickly. A message claims to be from a relative who has lost or damaged their phone, then introduces an urgent bill and asks you to pay a new account. A business impersonator may claim that an account, delivery or payment needs immediate attention.

Other scams develop more slowly. A wrong-number conversation, romantic approach, job offer or investment group builds familiarity before introducing a payment or asking for personal information. The criminal may move the conversation through several services so that no single platform sees the whole scheme.

The first payment is not necessarily the end. Criminals often invent another fee, tax, emergency or withdrawal charge after someone has paid. If information rather than money was taken, it may be used to target email, banking, social-media or credit accounts. Stop when the request becomes suspicious; do not pay again in the hope of recovering an earlier payment.

### How to verify who is really contacting you

Use a route that did not come from the suspicious chat. If the sender claims to be someone you know, contact that person through a saved number, another established account or in person. Ask about the request itself. A voice note from the suspicious account is weaker evidence because an account may be compromised and voices can be imitated.

If the sender claims to represent a business, bank or public body, close the chat. Open the organisation’s official app or type its known website address yourself, then use the contact details published there or on a card or statement you already hold. Do not call a number, follow a link or install an app supplied in the message.

Do not rely on a profile photo, country code, familiar display name or WhatsApp business presentation as proof. Those details can be copied, hidden by privacy settings or attached to a compromised account. WhatsApp does not show you how old another person’s account is.

Never share a WhatsApp registration code, device-linking code, PIN or bank one-time code. Do not scan a QR code or approve a linked device because an unexpected contact asks you to. Meta warns that criminals use false voting, support and verification stories to link a victim’s WhatsApp account to a criminal’s device.

### What to do if you replied, paid or shared information
