- Be on guard for a follow-up call claiming to be your bank — this is part of the scam. Your real bank will never ask you to move money to a 'safe account'. Hang up and call back on the card number.
- Keep the message and any payment confirmation as evidence, then report it.
- Monitor your statements and consider checking your credit file for applications you don't recognise.

### How to report a DPD scam text in the UK

Forward a suspicious SMS free of charge to 7726 — which spells `SPAM` on a phone keypad — then delete it; this alerts your mobile provider so it can investigate and block the sender. For an iMessage, RCS or app message, also use the service's built-in junk or spam reporting tool. If you lost money or shared personal or card details, report the scam to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040; in Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101. Forward suspicious emails impersonating DPD to the National Cyber Security Centre at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does DPD charge a redelivery fee by text?**

DPD does not charge consumers to reattempt a standard delivery. However, DPD's international support guidance says it may notify a recipient by SMS or email with a secure payment link when genuine import duties or taxes are due. Do not decide from the message alone: use the parcel number from your retailer's confirmation and open the official DPD site or app yourself to verify the charge.

**What does a genuine DPD text look like?**

A genuine DPD notification should match a parcel you are actually expecting and a parcel number you can verify through the official DPD site or app. Delivery notifications commonly give tracking or delivery-window information. A separate duties-or-taxes notification can be genuine for an international parcel, but verify it independently before paying. DPD will not need your card PIN, online-banking password, or one-time banking code.

**I paid a DPD 'redelivery fee' — what should I do now?**

Contact your bank straight away on the number printed on the back of your card, explain you entered card details on a scam site, and ask them to block the card and monitor for fraud. Change any password or code you entered. Be especially wary of a follow-up call claiming to be your bank's fraud team — that is the next stage of the scam. Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

**How do I report a fake DPD text message?**

Forward the text free to 7726 so your mobile network can investigate the sender, then delete it. If you lost money or shared personal or card details, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). You can also report the fake DPD website to the NCSC.

## DVLA Vehicle Tax Text: Is It Genuine or a Scam?

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/dvla-vehicle-tax-text-scam/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A DVLA text says vehicle tax failed or a refund is waiting? DVLA says it will not ask for bank or payment details this way. Check only through GOV.UK.

### What the fake DVLA tax text says

Fake DVLA texts commonly claim a vehicle-tax payment failed, tax is overdue, a penalty is imminent, or a refund is waiting. They direct the recipient to a GOV.UK-style copycat page that collects card, bank or identity details. In its April 2025 scam-awareness news story, DVLA said almost 20,000 customers called its contact centre in 2024 to report fraudulent activity.

DVLA's current advice makes the answer narrower and more reliable than judging the sender name: a message asking for bank or card details, confirmation of payment details, or a vehicle-tax refund through a link is the scam sign. DVLA will not ask for your bank-account details or ask you to confirm payment details, and vehicle-tax refunds are issued automatically — never via an email with a link. Genuine reminders do exist, so check and tax the vehicle only through GOV.UK.

### Why a "DVLA" text is easy to fake

Scammers can use official-looking sender names, GOV.UK-style design, and urgent wording. Sender IDs can be spoofed, so `DVLA` showing as the sender proves nothing — the fake can even land in the same thread as a genuine message. Timing can also make a fake feel real if it arrives near a renewal date.

The key facts are clearer than the message: DVLA has said the only place to access official information on DVLA and its services is GOV.UK, that it never sends text messages about vehicle-tax refunds, and — per a DVLA official — that it never asks for bank or credit-card details by text message or email.

The same criminals run a phone version — an automated call claiming your tax payment failed — covered at /guides/dvla-phone-scam-uk/.

### What genuine DVLA reminders actually look like

Knowing the real process makes the fake obvious.

- The standard tax-due reminder is a letter — the V11 — posted to the address on your V5C log book. GOV.UK also refers to reminders arriving by email or text, so a reminder in your inbox is not automatically fake — but a genuine one never asks for bank details.
- If a Direct Debit payment fails through lack of funds, DVLA says the account holder gets an email and it retries within 4 working days; if that fails too, a further email says the Direct Debit is cancelled and the vehicle is no longer taxed. Note what is missing: no request for bank details, no urgent payment link.
- A genuine refund is a cheque, issued automatically for any full months left once you tell DVLA the vehicle is sold, scrapped, exported or SORNed, sent to the address on the log book — nothing to claim, no link, no bank details.

### Signs a "DVLA" text is a scam

- It asks you to pay, update payment details, or claim a refund through a link.
- The link is not on `gov.uk`, or it uses a lookalike, extra words, or a shortened URL.
- It threatens a fine, penalty, or deadline if you do not act immediately.
- It asks for card numbers, bank details, or personal information.
- It claims a refund is waiting — genuine refunds arrive as automatic cheques, not links.
- It asks you to upload or confirm driving-licence or V5C details. DVLA warns against sharing these online (identity-theft risk).
- It looks official but asks you to use a route outside GOV.UK.

### How the vehicle-tax scam works

First, a text claims a vehicle-tax payment failed, tax is due, or a refund is available. Second, it pushes you to a link. Third, the link opens a fake page styled to look like GOV.UK or DVLA. Fourth, it asks for card, bank, or personal details. Fifth, the criminals use those details to take money, attempt further card transactions, or target you again.

Some pages ask for a small "fee" to seem believable while harvesting details for larger fraud later.

### How to check with DVLA safely

Close the message and type `gov.uk` yourself. Use:

- `gov.uk/check-vehicle-tax` to check free whether a vehicle is taxed or SORNed — you only need the registration number. Records can take up to 2 working days to update after you tax.
- `gov.uk/vehicle-tax` to tax a vehicle officially, using the reference from your V11 reminder, your V5C log book, or the green new-keeper slip.
- `gov.uk/vehicle-tax-refund` to understand when a refund is issued automatically.

DVLA says it may ask a person to confirm personal details by email or text when there is a live enquiry, so 'DVLA never texts' is not a safe universal rule. The red line is a message asking for bank details, confirmation of payment details, or a vehicle-tax refund claim. If a message refers to a real enquiry, confirm it through a GOV.UK service or contact route you open yourself.

### If you paid or shared card details

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to stop the card if needed, and ask about disputing the transaction. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

Then take stock of what the fake page collected. Card details: watch statements for small "test" transactions. Name, address, date of birth or licence details: consider Cifas Protective Registration and monitor your credit reports with the agencies MoneyHelper lists — Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three main agencies, plus Crediva. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) walks through this in order.

### How to report a DVLA text scam (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. Ofcom says forwarding scam texts to 7726 is free and alerts your mobile provider to investigate and block the number.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If a similar scam arrived by email, forward it to `report@phishing.gov.uk`; DVLA also suggests reporting misleading copycat adverts to the search engine.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does DVLA send texts about vehicle tax refunds?**

DVLA has said it never sends text messages about vehicle-tax refunds — a genuine refund is an automatic cheque to the address on your V5C. Treat any "refund waiting" link as a scam.

**Does DVLA ask for bank or card details by text or email?**

DVLA says it will never ask you for your bank-account details or ask you to confirm payment details. Use GOV.UK instead.

**Does DVLA ever send genuine emails or texts at all?**

Yes — which is why the sender name proves nothing. GOV.UK refers to tax reminders arriving by letter (the V11), email or text, and DVLA emails you if a Direct Debit fails. None of those ask for bank or payment details.

**The text arrived when my tax was due - could it be genuine?**

Timing proves nothing — scam texts go out in bulk. Ignore the link and check directly on GOV.UK.

**A message says my Direct Debit for vehicle tax failed - what should I do?**

Do not use anything in the message. Check the vehicle yourself at `gov.uk/check-vehicle-tax`, and retax at `gov.uk/vehicle-tax` if the tax really has lapsed.

**I entered card details on a DVLA-style site - what now?**

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on your card. Ask them to secure the card and dispute the payment. If you also gave personal details, consider Cifas Protective Registration. Then report the scam.

**How do I report a fake DVLA text?**

Forward it to 7726 (free). If you lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## EE Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Message

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/ee-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-06

A text claiming to be EE asks for your PIN or password? EE says it doesn't ask for either by text. Here's how to check a suspicious message safely.

### What a fake EE text looks like

This scam is a text message designed to look like it's from EE, claiming a payment has failed, your account is suspended, or a device delivery needs confirming. An example of the style: `Your EE bill payment was declined. Update your payment details now to avoid service interruption.` It usually includes a link to a fake EE-branded login page.

### Why these texts are convincing

EE does genuinely text customers about billing and account matters, so a message on these topics isn't unusual by itself. The threat of losing service creates urgency that pushes people to click and act quickly, rather than pause to check the message independently.

### Signs an EE text is a scam

- It asks you to click a link and enter your PIN or password. EE says it will never ask for either by text or email.
- It asks you to make a payment or transaction by following a link.
- There's pressure to act immediately or risk losing service.
- The sender isn't a number or short code you recognise as EE's own.

### How the scam works step by step

First, a text arrives claiming a problem with your EE account or a payment. Second, a link opens a page built to look like EE's genuine login. Third, whatever you enter — your login details, PIN, or payment information — is captured. Fourth, the criminal can access your real EE account or use the payment details elsewhere.

### How to check an EE text is genuine

Don't click the link. Log into the EE app directly, or type ee.co.uk into your browser yourself, and check your account there instead.

- EE offers two-factor authentication (2FA) on your online account as an extra security step. EE says that once 2FA is set up on your account, you won't be able to remove it.
- If you're unsure about a message, check your account directly rather than replying to the text or following its link.

### If you've already entered your details

Log into your EE account directly and change your password immediately. If you entered card or payment details, contact your bank and explain what happened.

### How to report a fake EE text (UK)

Forward it free to 7726, and you can also forward phishing emails referring to EE to `phishing@ee.co.uk`. If you've lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Will EE ever ask for my PIN or password by text?**

No. EE says it will never ask you for your PIN or password by text or email. Treat any message asking for either as a scam.

**I clicked the link and entered my EE login details. What should I do?**

Log into your EE account directly through the app or by typing ee.co.uk yourself, and change your password immediately.

**Does EE have an email address for reporting phishing?**

Yes. Forward phishing emails referring to EE to `phishing@ee.co.uk`, and forward suspicious texts to 7726.

**Should I turn on two-factor authentication for my EE account?**

Yes, it's a genuine extra layer of security EE offers. Be aware that EE says once 2FA is set up, you won't be able to remove it.

**How do I report a fake EE text in the UK?**

Forward it to 7726, and report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland) if you've lost money or shared details.

## Evri Scam Texts: How to Spot a Fake Parcel Text (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/evri-delivery-scam-guide/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

An Evri text about a missed delivery or a small fee? How to tell a genuine Evri message from a scam text, and how to track your parcel safely.

### What a fake Evri text looks like

An Evri parcel scam text is a smishing message that imitates the courier so you tap a link and hand over card or personal details. An example of the style is: `Evri: We missed you. Reschedule delivery and pay the £1.79 fee: evri-reschedule.example`.

The hook is a small, believable fee - usually a redelivery, release, or address-check fee - because the amount looks too minor to question. The link opens a fake courier page that captures whatever you type. This guide shows how to spot the fake, track your parcel safely, and report it.

### Why Evri texts are easy to fake

Evri launched in March 2022 after Hermes UK rebranded, and scammers still use both the old and new names. Our /guides/evri-delivery-scam-guide/ guide covers the same scam under the old brand.

Evri says it may contact customers by email or text to say a parcel is in its network, and that a genuine text may include a tracking link to `Evri.com`. Evri also says its text messages will only come from `Evri`, will only ever send a tracking link, will never ask you to reschedule a delivery or ask for payment to do so, and will never prompt you to install an app.

That means the safest check is not the sender name. It is what the text asks you to do. If it asks for payment, card details, personal information, or an app install, do not use the link.

### Signs an Evri text is a scam

- It asks you to pay a small fee to redeliver, reschedule, release, or confirm a parcel.
- It asks you to reply with a letter such as `Y` so a link can be opened.
- The link is not a direct Evri tracking link on `evri.com`, or it uses a lookalike or shortened address.
- It asks for card details, bank details, personal information, or a security code.
- It tells you to install an app or download a file.
- It pressures you with a deadline before the parcel is returned.
- You were not expecting a parcel, or the tracking number does not match anything you ordered.
- Spelling and spacing errors can be clues, but a polished text can still be a scam.

### How the Evri parcel scam works

First, a text claims a delivery failed or a small fee is due. Second, it pushes you to a link to pay, reschedule, or confirm your address. Third, the link opens a fake Evri page that asks for your address and card details. Fourth, the criminals capture what you enter.

The first payment may be small, but the card and personal details can be used for larger fraud. Some victims are then contacted by someone pretending to be their bank about the payment. Do not continue that call; hang up and contact the bank yourself using a trusted number.

### How to check an Evri text safely

Do not tap the link or call a number from the text.

- Open the official Evri app or type `evri.com` into your browser yourself.
- Use a tracking link from the retailer you ordered from if you have one.
- Check for a tracking-only Evri update rather than a payment, app install, or personal-details request.

Evri says its texts only send tracking links to its website, and it attempts deliveries up to three times. If the text asks for payment to reschedule a delivery, asks you to install an app, or asks for card or bank details, treat it as a scam. When you are unsure whether a linked site is a copycat, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### If you paid or shared card details

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to stop the card if needed, and ask about disputing the transaction. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

### How to report an Evri scam text (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. The NCSC says most UK phone providers let customers report suspicious texts for free this way, so the provider can investigate.

If the suspicious message mentions Evri, use the reporting options on Evri's cyber-security page so Evri can investigate and work with partners to take down fraudulent websites. If a similar scam arrived by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Evri the same as Hermes?**

Evri launched in March 2022 after Hermes UK rebranded. Scammers use both names, so treat either brand the same way: do not tap payment links; check directly in the Evri app or at `evri.com`.

**Does Evri charge a redelivery fee by text?**

Evri says its text messages will never ask you to reschedule a delivery or ask for payment to do so. It says genuine Evri texts only send a tracking link to `Evri.com`.

**I paid the fee - can I get my money back?**

Possibly. Contact your bank or card issuer straight away using the number on your card, report it as a scam, and ask them to stop the card and dispute the payment. Watch for follow-up calls pretending to be from your bank.

**I clicked the link but did not enter anything - am I at risk?**

The risk is lower than if you entered details, but do not continue. Close the page, do not download anything, and run a security scan if the site prompted a download. If you typed card or personal details, treat them as compromised and contact your bank.

**How do I report an Evri scam text?**

Forward it to 7726. If the message mentions Evri, also use Evri's cyber-security reporting route. If you lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Fake Halifax Text? Scam Checks, 159 and Safe Reporting

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/halifax-bank-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Received an unexpected Halifax fraud or payment text? Do not share a passcode or move money. Check it in the app, through the card number or via 159.

### What a fake Halifax text looks like

A Halifax scam text impersonates the bank to make you tap a link, disclose banking details, share a passcode or move money. Common stories include a blocked payment, new payee, locked account or suspicious login. An example of the style: `HALIFAX: A new device was registered to your account. Not you? Verify now: halifax-secure-check.example`. The wording is not proof either way.

Use this page when a message arrived unexpectedly. If an expected verification text did not arrive, that is a service problem - see /guides/bank-text-codes-not-arriving/ instead.

### Why a Halifax text can look convincing

Scammers can use familiar-looking sender names and wording that copies real bank alerts, and a fake can sit right beside genuine Halifax messages on your phone - sender display and message grouping prove nothing either way.

Halifax's official fraud contact page says Halifax will never ask you to tell them your account details, share your Personal Security Number, tell them your PIN or card expiry date, or move money to another account. If a text asks for any of those, it is a scam.

### The Halifax-to-Lloyds brand change: a new hook for scammers

Halifax is being rebranded as Lloyds: announced on 1 July 2026, closed to new customers since 16 July 2026, with existing customers moved to the Lloyds app and rebranded accounts in stages over the coming months. Sort codes, account numbers, cards, PINs and payments carry on unchanged.

Fraudsters exploit announcements like this with urgent texts: "confirm your details for the switch", "re-register for the Lloyds app". Halifax says it will only contact customers about the transition by email, letter or a banking message - it will not call or text you about it, will not ask you to log in through a link or QR code, and will not ask for your PIN.

So a text about the change that asks you to tap, log in, verify or move money is a scam. Customers who have already moved approve Halifax-card payments in the Lloyds app - type `halifax.co.uk` yourself for the current instructions.

### Signs a Halifax text is a scam

- It pressures you to act fast: an account "locked", payment "held", or deadline.
- It asks you to tap a link to "verify", "secure", log in, or re-enter card details.
- The link uses a lookalike or unusual domain. Never use text links for banking.
- It asks for your password, PIN, Personal Security Number, card details, or one-time passcode.
- It tells you to move money to a new, holding, or "safe" account.
- It mentions the change to Lloyds and asks you to log in, register or confirm anything - Halifax says it will not text you about the transition.

### How the Halifax text scam works

First, a text appears to come from Halifax, warning of a blocked payment, new payee, suspicious login or a problem with the move to Lloyds. Second, it pushes you to a link to fix it. Third, the link opens a copycat page that asks for banking or card details. Fourth, the criminals capture what you enter. Fifth, they may trigger a real one-time passcode and ask for it - Halifax says a passcode is like a PIN: never shared. Finally, they try to move money, add payees, or use the details in further fraud. The safest point to break the chain is before tapping the link.

### How to check if a Halifax text is genuine

Do not reply, use the link or call a number in the message. Check independently:

- Call 159. Stop Scams UK's participant list includes Halifax, Lloyds Bank and Bank of Scotland, and it says 159 covers more than 99% of UK retail current accounts.
- Open the official Halifax or Lloyds app for your account and check activity and secure messages.
- Call the number printed on the back of your card.
- Type the bank's address yourself, or use a trusted bookmark.

Halifax also says it will not ask you to share personal details or move money by phone, email or text - a passcode request, app approval or "safe account" transfer is reason enough to hang up and check. Not every genuine text appears in-app; if you cannot confirm the claim, contact the bank directly. If a linked website looks suspect, /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### If you tapped the link, shared details or moved money

If you entered login details, card details, or a passcode, call 159 or the number on your card immediately and say you may have been phished. Ask Halifax to secure the account and check for activity you do not recognise. Change your Halifax password only through the official app or by typing the address yourself, and anywhere else you reused it. If you shared card details, ask for the card to be stopped and reissued.

If you sent money by UK bank transfer on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory APP fraud reimbursement rules may apply to Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers, subject to a 13-month claim window, a maximum claim of £85,000, and a possible excess of up to £100 - ask the bank to assess the claim. The [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) covers the wider steps.

If you shared personal details such as your date of birth or address, be alert to identity-theft attempts and consider a Cifas Protective Registration. If you bank elsewhere, the same checks apply — see /guides/lloyds-bank-scam-text/.

### How to report a Halifax scam text in the UK

Forward the text to 7726. The NCSC says most UK phone providers let customers report suspicious texts for free this way.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If the scam arrived by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. Tell Halifax through the app or the number on your card.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is a Halifax text with a link always a scam?**

No. A link alone is not proof either way. Never use a text link to log in, confirm details, enter a one-time code, or move money. Check independently.

**Will Halifax text me about the change to Lloyds?**

No. Halifax says it will only contact customers about the brand change by email, letter or a banking message - never by call or text - and will not ask for a login via link or QR code, or your PIN.

**What number should I call to check a Halifax text safely?**

Call 159 or the number printed on the back of your card. Do not call a number supplied in the suspicious text.

**I tapped the link and entered my details - what should I do now?**

Contact Halifax immediately via 159, the app, or the number on your card. Change your password through the official app, stop your card if needed, and report any payment you did not make.

**How do I report a fake Halifax text in the UK?**

Forward it to 7726. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Halifax Text Not Arriving? Bank Verification Code Fixes

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/bank-text-codes-not-arriving/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Halifax or another bank verification text not arriving? Check the registered number, app, signal and message filters, then use a safe alternative route.

### First identify which bank text is missing

A single missing bank code can have several possible causes and is not proof of fraud or a SIM swap — start with the normal delivery and account checks below. Banks send different kinds of messages: one-time passcodes for a payment or login, security checks, and optional account alerts. Confirm which message you expected and whether the bank still has your current mobile number. Do not keep requesting codes repeatedly; use one fresh request after completing the checks below.

### Run these low-risk checks first

Check that the phone has signal and Airplane Mode is off, restart it, and look in blocked, filtered or junk-message folders. Confirm that the inbox has space and that you can receive an ordinary text or call from someone you know. Then request one new code and wait for the newest message; older codes may expire when a replacement is issued. Menu names vary, so use the phone manufacturer's official help if you cannot find a setting.

### Halifax text messages not arriving: the relevant checks

Check that Halifax has your current mobile number — it needs this to send passcodes, and extra security checks may use an app, an SMS passcode or a phone call depending on the task and account. Halifax is transitioning its brand to Lloyds and says customers who have moved will approve Halifax-card payments in the Lloyds app, so type `halifax.co.uk` yourself and follow the current instructions shown for your account rather than assuming which branded app applies. If you cannot complete the check, contact the bank through the official app or the number printed on your card. This is a service-access problem; the separate /guides/halifax-bank-scam-text-uk/ guide covers unexpected messages claiming to be Halifax.

### Check the bank account and mobile number

Sign in through the bank's official app or a website address you typed yourself. Check that the registered mobile number is correct, including after a recent number change, new SIM or account update. Look for an in-app notice about maintenance or a security hold. If the app offers another verification route, follow only the instructions shown inside the official app; availability differs by bank and transaction.

### Contact the bank without using a message link

If other calls and texts arrive but only the bank message is missing, contact the bank through its official app or the number printed on your card. Ask it to confirm the registered number, whether the attempted action generated a code, and which alternative verification methods are available for your account. Do not use a support number from a search advert, unexpected text or caller.

### When it may be a bank or network delivery issue

Check the bank's official service-status or help page, then ask the bank and mobile provider whether they can see a current delivery problem — don't diagnose the cause from social-media posts alone. SMS passes through systems operated by the sender, messaging suppliers and mobile networks, so a delay can occur outside your phone; the NCSC advises organisations to understand and audit that supply chain because message content, sender details and delivery can be affected.

### Separate a missing code from possible SIM-swap warning signs

A missing bank code alone does not establish a SIM swap. The NCSC describes SIM-swap attacks as an attacker transferring a victim's number to another SIM so the attacker can receive calls and messages intended for that number — make urgent checks if you also notice unexpected loss of normal calls and SMS, an unrecognised mobile-account or number-port change, or unauthorised financial activity; these are escalation prompts, not a definitive diagnostic list.

### What to do if there are SIM-swap warning signs

Use another phone or a secure internet connection to contact the mobile network and bank through official routes. Ask the network whether a SIM replacement or number port was requested, ask the bank to protect the account, and secure the email account used for recovery. Keep records of alerts and unauthorised changes. Report suspected fraud to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Do not describe a routine bank-code delay as a confirmed SIM swap.

### Frequently asked questions

**Why is my bank verification text not arriving?**

Check signal, Airplane Mode, blocked or filtered messages, and whether the bank has your current mobile number. Request one fresh code. If ordinary calls and texts work but the bank code still does not arrive, contact the bank through its app or the number on your card.

**Why are my Halifax text messages not arriving?**

Halifax says it needs your up-to-date mobile number to send a passcode and may use an app, SMS or phone call for extra checks. It is transitioning customers to the Lloyds brand, so follow the current instructions shown at `halifax.co.uk` or in your account rather than assuming which app applies. Contact the bank through the official app or the number on your card if the check still fails.

**Does a missing bank code mean my SIM was swapped?**

No. A missing code alone has several routine explanations. Contact the network and bank urgently if the phone also loses service, ordinary calls and texts stop, or you discover a SIM replacement or number-port request you did not make.

**How do I know whether a bank text is genuine?**

A familiar sender name or message thread is not proof because SMS origin information can be imitated. Do not use an unexpected link or share a code with a caller. Open the bank's app yourself or call the number on your card; forward a suspicious text to 7726.

## HMRC Tax Refund Text Scam: Spot the Fake (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/hmrc-tax-refund-text-scam-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-24

An HMRC text saying you're owed a tax refund — click to claim? Real refunds aren't claimed by text link. How to spot the scam and check safely on GOV.UK.

### What a fake HMRC refund text looks like

An HMRC tax-refund scam text is a smishing message that pretends to be from HM Revenue & Customs so you tap a link and hand over bank, card, or personal details. An example of the style is: `HMRC: You are due a tax refund of £274.50. Claim now: hmrc-taxrefund.example`.

The promise of a refund is the hook, and the amount is often specific to make the message look official. The link opens a fake GOV.UK-style page that asks for details to process the refund, but captures them instead.

### Why HMRC refund texts are convincing

Scammers can spoof a sender name such as `HMRC` or `GOV.UK`, so the sender label is not enough to prove the message is genuine. The important nuance is that HMRC does send some genuine text messages. GOV.UK lists recent genuine HMRC text-message campaigns, and some genuine texts can include links to GOV.UK information or HMRC webchat.

The fact that cuts through the scam is this: HMRC says it will never ask for personal or financial information when it sends text messages, and GOV.UK's advice on any text offering a tax refund is blunt — do not open the link. For Self Assessment tax refunds, a genuine HMRC text may confirm that a refund is being processed and when you can expect it, but it will not ask for personal or financial information or provide website links.

For P800 tax-overpayment refunds, your tax calculation letter tells you how to claim. GOV.UK says you may be able to claim online, through your Personal Tax Account or the HMRC app, by contacting HMRC, or you may automatically get a cheque if your letter says so. You do not claim a refund through a random text link.

### Signs an HMRC text is a scam

- It offers a tax refund or rebate that you can claim by tapping a link.
- It asks for bank details, card details, your National Insurance number, or other personal information.
- It says you must act quickly or lose the refund.
- It links to a lookalike GOV.UK page, a shortened URL, or a page outside the route you reached yourself by typing `gov.uk`.
- It announces a rebate out of the blue. A genuine Self Assessment refund text only confirms a refund you already requested is being processed, and a P800 overpayment refund starts with a tax calculation letter — not a text link.
- It threatens a fine, arrest, or legal action unless you pay immediately.
- It looks official but asks you to use a route outside GOV.UK, the HMRC app, or your HMRC online account.

### How the HMRC refund scam works

First, a text claims you are owed a refund or, in the threatening variant, that you owe tax and face action. Second, it pushes you to a link to claim or pay. Third, the link opens a fake GOV.UK-style page asking for bank, card, or personal details. Fourth, the criminals capture everything you enter.

Those details can then be used for card fraud, bank fraud, identity misuse, or further impersonation scams. Checking only through GOV.UK, the HMRC app, or your HMRC online account breaks the chain.

### How to check with HMRC safely

Do not tap the link or call a number from the text.

- Type `gov.uk` into your browser yourself and search for `Personal Tax Account`.
- Use the official HMRC app if you already use it.
- Follow the instructions on a tax calculation letter you received by post.
- If you recently requested a Self Assessment refund, check whether the text only confirms processing and timing, without links or requests for details.

A genuine HMRC text should not ask for personal or financial information or include a refund-claim link. If you are not sure, check GOV.UK's list of genuine HMRC contacts and contact HMRC only through numbers or services published on GOV.UK. When you are unsure whether a linked site is a copycat of GOV.UK, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### If you clicked or shared details

If you gave bank or card details, contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to secure the account, and ask about disputing any payment. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

### How to report an HMRC scam text (UK)

Forward suspicious HMRC texts to 60599. GOV.UK says texts to this number are charged at your network rate. You can also forward scam texts to 7726 so your mobile provider can investigate.

Forward suspicious emails that mention HMRC to `phishing@hmrc.gov.uk`, then delete them. If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does HMRC send tax refund texts?**

HMRC may send some genuine texts, including Self Assessment refund-processing confirmations if you requested a refund. Those texts should not ask for personal or financial information or include website links. Treat any text that asks you to claim a refund through a link as a scam.

**Does HMRC ask for bank details by text?**

No. GOV.UK says HMRC will never ask you to disclose personal or payment information by text message.

**I clicked the link and entered my details - what now?**

If you gave bank or card details, call your bank using the number on your card and ask them to secure the account. Then report the scam text to 60599 and, if useful, 7726. If you shared personal details, consider Cifas Protective Registration and monitor your credit reports.

**I gave my National Insurance number but not bank details - am I at risk?**

Your National Insurance number alone does not give someone direct access to your bank account, but it can help criminals impersonate you. Watch for unexpected letters, accounts, or credit applications, and consider Cifas Protective Registration.

**How do I report an HMRC tax refund scam text?**

Forward the text to 60599. You can also forward it to 7726. Report scam emails claiming to be from HMRC to `phishing@hmrc.gov.uk`. If you lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Is This NHS Appointment Text Genuine? Checks and Scam Signs

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/nhs-appointment-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

The NHS does send appointment texts and NHS App fallback messages. Check the appointment independently and beware links asking for payment or details.

### What a fake NHS text looks like

An NHS scam text imitates an appointment reminder, cancellation, waiting-list check or health-service message to collect personal or payment details. But a text is not automatically fake: NHS services and their messaging suppliers can use SMS, including when an NHS App message is not delivered or read.

NHS England's current messaging guidance gives one specific fallback example: a text from `NHSApp` telling the named patient that a secure message is waiting in the NHS App or at `https://www.nhs.uk/inbox`. Other legitimate provider messages can differ. The safe test is to open the NHS App or NHS account yourself, or contact the named GP surgery or hospital through independently found details, and match the message to a real appointment or communication.

### Why a fake NHS text is convincing

Scammers use sender names, timing, and health-related urgency to make a message feel important. A missed appointment or cancelled treatment can make people act quickly. Some texts also offer a grant, refund, or payment to lure people into entering bank details.

Two facts help. First, the NHS App lets people manage healthcare and, where available, book or manage appointments and view messages. Second, the NHS Constitution says NHS services are free of charge except limited circumstances sanctioned by Parliament. A surprise text asking you to pay a fee to keep, rebook, or receive an NHS appointment should be treated as a scam until you have checked directly.

Real NHS charges do exist. In England the everyday examples are prescription charges, paid at the pharmacy or covered by a prepayment certificate, and NHS dental band charges, paid to the dental practice. What those genuine charges have in common is that none of them is collected through a payment link in an unexpected text about your appointment.

### Signs an NHS text is a scam

- It asks you to pay a fee to keep, rebook, or receive an NHS appointment.
- It asks for bank or card details through a text link.
- It offers a grant, refund, or payment that you must claim through a link.
- It asks for full personal information to "confirm" or "verify" your appointment.
- The link is not an `nhs.uk` address, or it is a shortened or lookalike link.
- It pressures you to act immediately or lose your appointment.
- You cannot match it to a real appointment in the NHS App or with your GP surgery or hospital.
- Errors can be clues, but a tidy, official-looking text can still be a scam.

### How the NHS text scam works

First, a text claims your appointment has changed, or that you are eligible for a payment, treatment, or priority booking. Second, it pushes you to a link to rebook, confirm, or claim. Third, the link opens a fake NHS-style page asking for personal details and often card or bank information. Fourth, the criminals use those details for payments, identity fraud, or follow-up scams.

Because a health message feels urgent, the safest move is to pause and check through the NHS App, your NHS account, your GP surgery, or the hospital using contact details you find yourself.

### How to check an NHS text safely

Do not start from an unexpected link. Instead:

- Open the NHS App yourself and check Messages, Appointments, referrals and hospital appointments.
- NHS England says App notifications can fall back to SMS within a few hours if they are not delivered or read, so check whether the same secure message exists in the App.
- Contact the named GP surgery, hospital or clinic through a number on an appointment letter or its official `nhs.uk` page.
- A surprise demand for a fee to keep or rebook ordinary NHS care, or a request for bank details to receive a grant or refund, needs direct verification before any response.
- A non-`nhs.uk` link is not automatically fraudulent because some trusts use patient portals, but never trust it solely because it arrived by text. Confirm the provider and portal independently.

### If you clicked or shared details

Act quickly. If you entered card details or made a payment, contact your bank or card issuer using the number on your card. Tell them it was a scam and ask them to stop the card, monitor the account, and discuss any dispute or chargeback options.

### How to report an NHS scam text (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. It is free, and it reports the message to your mobile provider, which can investigate and block the sender. You can also send a screenshot or screen recording to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If the scam reached you by email, forward it to `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

You can also tell the relevant GP surgery, hospital trust, or NHS organisation using contact details you find yourself.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does the NHS send appointment texts?**

Yes, NHS services can send genuine messages, including text messages. That means a text is not automatically fake. The red flag is a link asking you to pay, claim money, or provide bank, card, or sensitive personal details.

**The NHS is free - so why would an NHS text ask for payment?**

Be cautious. The NHS Constitution says NHS services are free of charge except limited circumstances sanctioned by Parliament. A surprise text asking you to pay to keep, rebook, or receive an NHS appointment is not a normal way to handle care and should be checked directly. The genuine exceptions include prescription charges and NHS dental charges in England, which you pay at the pharmacy or to the dental practice — not through a link in a text demanding money to hold an appointment.

**Can the NHS really cancel my appointment by text?**

Genuine reminders or updates can come by message or text, depending on the service. If a text says your appointment is cancelled or changed, check it in the NHS App or contact your GP surgery or hospital directly. Do not use the link in the message.

**I clicked the link and entered my details - what now?**

If you entered card or bank details, call your bank using the number on your card and ask them to stop the card and watch the account. If you shared personal information, consider Cifas Protective Registration. Then report the scam text to 7726 and to Report Fraud if money, sensitive details, or hacking were involved. Report Fraud covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland. If you live in Scotland or the crime happened there, contact Police Scotland on 101.

**How do I report an NHS scam text?**

Forward it to 7726 for free. If you have a screenshot or email, send it to `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Lloyds Scam Texts: How to Spot a Fake Lloyds SMS (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/lloyds-bank-scam-text/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Got a Lloyds text about a new payee or 'suspicious activity'? How to tell a genuine Lloyds SMS from a scam — and how to check it safely on 159.

### What a fake Lloyds text looks like

A Lloyds scam text is smishing: a fake SMS that pretends to be from the bank so you tap a link and give away banking details, card details, or a one-time passcode. An example of the style is: `LLOYDS: A new payee was added to your account. If this wasn't you, cancel here: lloyds-verify-account.example`.

The hook changes - a new payee, blocked card, payment on hold, suspicious login, or account restriction - but the aim is to make you panic and tap before you verify.

### Why the fake can look real

Scammers can use familiar-looking sender names and copy the tone of real bank alerts. A fake text can appear near genuine bank messages on your phone, so you cannot rely on the display name or conversation thread.

Lloyds' official fraud contact page says Lloyds Bank will never ask you to tell them account details, share your Personal Security Number, tell them your PIN or card expiry date, or move money to another account. If a text asks for any of that, treat it as a scam.

Lloyds' current scam-messages page also says it may send you links to its secure app or to pages with more information, but that it will never link directly to its Internet Banking log on page or to a page asking for your logon, banking or personal details. So the presence of a link is not the test — what the page then asks you for is.

### Signs a Lloyds text is a scam

- It rushes you: a payee "added", card "blocked", or deadline to avoid losing access.
- It links you to "cancel", "verify", "secure", log in, or re-enter card details.
- The link goes to a lookalike or unfamiliar domain. Do not use text-message links for banking.
- It asks for banking details, card details, a passcode or your Personal Security Number. Lloyds says it will never ask you to share any of these, and the same goes for your log-on password, user ID or memorable information.
- It tells you to move money to a new, holding, or "safe" account.
- A generic greeting can be a clue, but it is weaker in SMS than email.
- Errors can be clues, but a tidy text is not proof.

### How the scam plays out

First, an unexpected text appears to come from Lloyds about a new payee, blocked payment, or login. Second, it pushes you to tap a link. Third, the link opens a copycat page that asks for banking or card details. Fourth, the criminals capture what you enter. Fifth, they may trigger a real one-time passcode and ask for it on the fake page. Finally, they try to move money, add payees, or use the details for further fraud.

### Check it safely, without tapping anything

Never dial a number or open a link that the text itself supplied. Reach Lloyds by a route you chose:

- Hang up and dial `159` yourself. Stop Scams UK says the route you reach by dialling `159` cannot be spoofed or impersonated, and `159` will never call you. Lloyds Bank is one of the participating banks.
- Open the official Lloyds app and read your activity and secure messages there.
- Type `lloydsbank.com` into the browser yourself, or use a bookmark you saved earlier.
- Ring the number printed on the back of your Lloyds card.

Not every genuine text is mirrored as an in-app message, so silence in the app is not by itself a warning sign. If nothing independent confirms the claim, contact Lloyds directly.

If you are unsure whether a linked website is a copycat, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks.

### If you tapped the link or shared details

If you entered banking details, card details, a passcode or your Personal Security Number, call 159 or the number on your card straight away and ask Lloyds to secure the account. Change your Lloyds password only inside the official app or on an address you typed yourself, and change it anywhere else you reused it.

Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) takes the rest in order: stopping and reissuing the card, spotting payments, payees and account changes you did not authorise, and the money-recovery routes.

If you bank elsewhere, the same checks apply — see, for example, our /guides/halifax-bank-scam-text-uk/ guide.

### How to report a Lloyds scam text (UK)

Forward the text to 7726. The NCSC says most UK phone providers let customers report suspicious texts for free this way.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

Tell Lloyds what happened using the app or your card number, and screenshot the message before you delete it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is a Lloyds text with a link always a scam?**

No. Genuine Lloyds messages can carry links, so the link alone settles nothing. Judge the request instead: never use a text link to sign in, confirm details, key in a one-time passcode, or move money.

**Can a scam text appear with real Lloyds messages?**

Yes. A spoofed sender ID drops the fake into the same thread as genuine alerts, so where a message sits in the thread is not evidence. Confirm it in the Lloyds app, on 159, or using your card.

**What number should I call to check a Lloyds text safely?**

Call 159, or the number printed on the back of your Lloyds card. Never ring a number that the suspicious text supplied — it may connect you straight to the criminals.

**I tapped the link and entered my details - what now?**

Contact Lloyds immediately using 159, the app, or the number on your card. Change your password through the official app or site, stop your card if needed, and report any payment you did not make.

**Can I get my money back if I paid a Lloyds scammer?**

Possibly. Eligible UK bank transfers over Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions. Card payments have different protections, such as chargeback.

## Nationwide Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Building Society SMS

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/nationwide-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Got a Nationwide text about suspicious activity, a blocked account, or a payment to verify? How to spot a fake Nationwide SMS and report it in the UK.

### Check before you pay, not after

The most useful thing Nationwide offers a member staring at a suspicious text is used before any money moves. Its Scam Checker Service invites you to run a payment past staff first — the wording on nationwide.co.uk is to talk to the society if you are unsure about a payment you are about to make, and it will look into it. The freephone line published on the Scam Protection Promise page runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, branch staff will do the same review in person, and the service covers payments set up through the app, the Internet Bank and Open Banking.

The Scam Protection Promise is attached to that conversation and inseparable from it. If you talked to Nationwide through Scam Checker before making the payment, and it did not tell you not to proceed, it says it will give you back every penny should the payment turn out to be a scam. It is not an after-the-event refund guarantee for a payment you made without asking. The Promise applies to Faster Payments, CHAPS and electronic transfers between Nationwide accounts. Card payments, cash withdrawals, cheques and overseas payments sent by SWIFT or SEPA fall outside it, and Nationwide says it may change or withdraw the Promise, telling members in branch and on its website if it does.

That pre-payment conversation is precisely what an urgent SMS is designed to rush you past.

### Call Checker: proving who is on the line

Since January 2026 the Nationwide banking app has carried Call Checker, which answers a question 159 cannot. Dialling 159 reaches the society on a line you opened yourself; it tells you nothing about the person already talking to you. Call Checker does exactly that.

Stay on the call, open the app, go to More and pick the Call Checker tile. The screen states either that you are on a call with a named Nationwide colleague or that you are not on a call with the society. If it says the second thing, the caller is impersonating Nationwide, no matter how much they appear to know about your accounts.

Nationwide launched the tool because impersonation runs through so much of the fraud its members report, and a scam text is very often the reconnaissance step for that call.

### Four things Nationwide will never ask a member to do

The society publishes a short list. It will never ask you to:

- Give it your full one-time code or card reader code.
- Transfer your money to a safe account.
- Log into the Internet Bank through a link in an email, text or social media message.
- Use, re-enable or re-sync your card reader over the phone.

The third entry decides most texts on its own. A message telling you to sign in through its link is requesting the one thing Nationwide states it never requests.

### Member-shaped bait: Fairer Share and restriction warnings

Membership hands fraudsters hooks a high-street bank cannot offer. The Fairer Share Payment is the obvious one: in 2026 more than four million eligible members received £100 between 10 and 30 June, paid automatically into an open Nationwide current account, with nothing to apply for.

Because no application or claim process exists, the fraudulent discriminator is a request to do something with the payment. A message asking you to claim it, confirm your details for it, sign in to receive it or release it is invented — for example `Nationwide: your Fairer Share payment could not be processed. Confirm your details: nationwide-member.example`. A text that merely links to genuine Fairer Share information is not, by itself, proof of fraud; it is the demand for an action on your side that gives it away.

The other family leans on loss instead of reward: unusual activity, a restriction about to be applied, a card about to be stopped. Both want the same outcome, which is you signing in somewhere that is not the society's own app.

Open that app and look for yourself. Your genuine balance, your genuine payment history and any action Nationwide actually needs from you all appear there, and no real restriction is ever lifted by completing a web form you arrived at from an SMS.

### Reporting it as a member

Nationwide asks members to send suspicious emails, texts and messages to `phishing@nationwide.co.uk`. It does not reply to each one, but it says it reviews what arrives, and the detail helps shut down the infrastructure behind a campaign. Forward the SMS to `7726` as well so your mobile network sees the sender, and pass an emailed version to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

Where money has actually gone, or you have given away enough for someone to impersonate you, add a police record: Report Fraud takes reports at `reportfraud.police.uk` and on 0300 123 2040, while in Scotland that report goes to Police Scotland on 101 instead.

### If you have already replied, tapped or paid

Ring the society immediately. Its 24-hour fraud number is published in the app, on nationwide.co.uk and on the back of your card. 159 routes participating callers to Nationwide — Stop Scams UK describes the service as connecting customers of more than 99% of UK retail bank current accounts, which is not a guarantee for every handset or network, so use the published number if 159 does not connect for you. Say which of three things happened: you entered credentials, you approved a one-time code, or you sent a payment. They trigger different responses inside the society.

Nationwide's Scam Protection Promise may apply only if you used its Scam Checker and talked to the society before making the covered payment, and it did not tell you not to proceed. Separately, the mandatory reimbursement rules may apply to eligible Faster Payments or CHAPS transfers made from 7 October 2024. Those rules cap an eligible claim at £85,000 and allow 13 months from the payment to raise a case, and they are conditional every time rather than automatic.

While a claim is open, work through the payment, account and identity actions in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Where is Call Checker in the Nationwide app?**

Stay on the call, open the banking app, tap More and choose the Call Checker tile. It has been available since January 2026 and shows either that you are on a call with a named Nationwide colleague or that you are not on a call with the society.

**I got a text about my Fairer Share payment — can it be genuine?**

Not one that asks you to claim it, confirm details for it, sign in for it or release it. Nationwide pays Fairer Share automatically into an open current account; the 2026 payment of £100 landed between 10 and 30 June with no application process. A message that only links to genuine information is not by itself proof of fraud — the request for an action from you is.

**Does the Scam Protection Promise guarantee my money back?**

Nationwide says it will refund every penny of a covered scam payment if you talked to it through Scam Checker before paying and it did not tell you not to proceed. The Promise covers Faster Payments, CHAPS and electronic transfers between Nationwide accounts; listed exclusions include cards, cash, cheques and SWIFT/SEPA payments. Nationwide may change or withdraw the Promise.

**Would Nationwide ever ask me to move money to a safe account?**

Never. It sits on the society's published list of things it will never ask a member to do, alongside handing over a full one-time code, signing in through a link, and re-syncing a card reader over the phone.

**Where do I report a Nationwide scam text?**

Send it to `phishing@nationwide.co.uk` and forward it to `7726`. If a payment left your account, ring the society's 24-hour fraud line or 159 first, then log the case with Report Fraud — Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

## NatWest Scam Texts: How to Spot a Fake NatWest SMS (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/natwest-fraud-text-message-scam-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Got a NatWest 'fraud alert' text about a payment or new device? How to tell a genuine NatWest SMS from a scam — and how to check it safely on 159.

### The fake NatWest text - and what it is really after

A NatWest fraud-text scam is smishing: a fake SMS that pretends to be from the bank so you tap a link and give away login details, card details, or a one-time passcode. An example of the style is: `NatWest: We blocked a £420 payment from a new device. If this wasn't you, confirm here: natwest-secure-login.example`.

The story varies - a blocked payment, payment on hold, new device, frozen card, or suspicious activity - but the aim is to frighten you into acting before you check.

### Why it slips past your guard

Scammers can use familiar-looking sender names and bank-style wording. A fake may appear near genuine messages on your phone, so sender display and message position are not reliable proof.

NatWest's official text-scam guide says it will never ask you to call a number in a text message to confirm or cancel payments. It also warns not to click links or download files from sudden text messages, and not to share bank account details, passwords, or one-time passcodes.

### Red flags in a NatWest scam text

- It creates urgency: a payment "blocked", a device "added", or access lost unless you act now.
- It sends you to a link to "confirm", "restore", "secure", log in, or re-enter card details.
- It tells you to call a number in the text to confirm or cancel a payment.
- It asks for bank account details, passwords, PINs, card details, or one-time passcodes.
- It tells you to move money to a new, holding, or "safe" account.
- The link goes to a lookalike or unfamiliar domain. Do not use text-message links for banking.
- Errors can be clues, but a polished text can still be fraudulent.

### Step by step: how the scam works

First, a text appears to be a NatWest alert about a blocked payment, new device, or suspicious login. Second, it pushes you to a link or phone number. Third, the link opens a copycat page or the caller asks for security details. Fourth, the criminals capture what you provide. Fifth, they may trigger a real one-time passcode and ask for it. Finally, they try to access the account, approve a payment, or use your details for further fraud.

### How to check a NatWest text safely

Do not use a number or link from the text. Use one of these independent routes:

- Call 159. Stop Scams UK lists NatWest as a 159 participant.
- Open the official NatWest app and check activity, messages, or My Security Profile.
- Type `natwest.com` yourself, or use a trusted bookmark.
- Use the phone number on your card or a recent statement.

NatWest's own guidance says to check transactions in the mobile app or call the number on the back of your card.

The email version of this impersonation is covered in our /guides/natwest-phishing-email-uk/ guide; to judge the linked site itself, see /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/.

### Already responded? Do this now

If you gave away login details, card details, or a one-time passcode, call 159 or the number on your card now and tell NatWest the account may be compromised. Reset your NatWest password only from inside the app or from an address you typed yourself, and replace it anywhere you reused it.

Work through our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) for the rest, including getting the card stopped and reissued, reviewing payments and payees, and the routes to recover money.

If you bank elsewhere, the same checks apply — see, for example, our /guides/barclays-bank-text-scam-uk/ guide.

### Where to report a NatWest scam text

NatWest says suspicious texts referring to NatWest can be forwarded to 88355, the bank's own reporting route; standard network rates apply and it is not a premium-rate number. Scam texts can also be forwarded free of charge to 7726, the spam-reporting shortcode run by the UK mobile networks.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If the same scam also reached you by email, send it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. Keep screenshots before anything is deleted, and let NatWest know through the app.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is a NatWest text with a link always a scam?**

NatWest says it will never ask you to call a number in a text to confirm or cancel a payment, or ask you to disclose your full PIN, full password or security code. A genuine code message is not permission to give the code to a caller or enter it on a page reached from an unexpected text.

**Can a fake NatWest text land with real alerts?**

Yes. Sender IDs can be forged, so a fake can sit in the same thread as real NatWest alerts. Its position there is not evidence — check in the app or on 159 instead.

**What is the safest number to call to check?**

159, or the number on your NatWest card. Do not ring a number the text gave you, however official the number looks.

**Can I get my money back after a NatWest text scam?**

Possibly. Eligible UK bank transfers over Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by APP reimbursement rules, subject to limits and exclusions. Card payments have different protections, such as chargeback.

**How do I report a NatWest fraud text?**

Forward suspicious texts referring to NatWest to 88355, which is NatWest's own reporting route. Any scam text can also go to 7726, the spam-reporting shortcode run by the UK mobile networks. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## O2 Warning: How to Spot Fake 'Important' Texts and What to Do

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/o2-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Fake O2 texts claim your account needs urgent verification or a payment has failed, linking to bogus login pages. How to spot and report them.

### The 'important account notice' text — what it looks like

A common pattern in O2 phishing texts is: `IMPORTANT: Your O2 account requires immediate verification. To avoid suspension, confirm your details here: [link].` Another variant targets your payment: `Your O2 direct debit of £XX has failed. Update your payment method within 24 hours or your service will be suspended: [link].` A third variant promises something: `Congratulations — you are eligible for a free handset upgrade. Claim before midnight: [link].`

All three share the same three features: a false sense of urgency, a link you're pressured to click, and a claim that something bad will happen — or something good will be lost — if you don't act immediately. That urgency is the mechanism. The goal in every case is to get you to enter your O2 login credentials, card details, or personal information on a fake website.

### What real O2 texts look like — and what O2 says it will never ask for

O2 does send genuine texts — data usage alerts, bill-ready notifications, and upgrade reminders — so the presence of a text from 'O2' is not suspicious by itself. What matters is what the message asks you to do.

If a text asks you to log in and verify your details via a link, do not use it — go directly to o2.co.uk yourself instead. O2's published commitment is specific: it says it will never call, text, or email you asking for a one-time code, password, or other security information. Be careful with broader assumptions — O2 does send genuine billing and payment texts, so a payment-problem message is not automatically fake. The test is not the topic but the action: log in directly at o2.co.uk or through the official app to check an account or billing issue. If the position is not clear there, contact O2 using contact details you found independently rather than replying to the message.

Genuine O2 texts tend to come from a named sender rather than a random mobile number, but sender names can be spoofed — a message displaying as 'O2' is not proof on its own that it is genuine. Check any claimed account issue by logging in directly at o2.co.uk, independently of any text message, and if the position is not clear there, contact O2 through contact details you found independently.

### Five seconds to check before you tap any link

Before clicking any link in an O2 text, run through these checks:

1. Check the sender field. Genuine O2 texts tend to come from a named sender rather than a mobile number, but sender names can be spoofed — so treat this as one signal, not proof.

2. Preview the link before tapping. On iPhone, press and hold the link to see the destination URL. On Android, long-press to copy and then inspect it. If the domain is not o2.co.uk or o2.com, treat it as suspicious.

3. Log in separately. Open your browser and type o2.co.uk yourself. If there is a genuine account issue, it will be shown on your account dashboard — no link required.

4. Never call a number in the text. Scammers include fake O2 support numbers in some messages. From your O2 phone, dial 202 (free) if you're Pay Monthly, or 4445 (free) if you're Pay As You Go — or use the O2 app to reach genuine support. From any other phone, use the O2 customer service number on your bill or o2.co.uk.

5. If in doubt, do nothing. Scammers rely on urgency to override your normal caution. If the message is real, the account issue will still be there in ten minutes when you have checked independently.

### Already clicked or entered your details? Do this in order

If you clicked a link in a suspected scam text and entered information, act in this sequence:

1. Change your O2 password immediately — go directly to o2.co.uk on a different device if possible, log in, and change your password. Do this before anything else to close off access to your account.

2. If you entered card or bank details on the fake site, call your bank on the number on the back of your card right away. Tell them you gave your details to a phishing site. They can monitor for fraud and may be able to block the card before it is misused.

3. If the password you entered on the fake O2 site is one you use on other accounts — email, Amazon, banking — change it on every one of those services now. Scammers use harvested credentials to attack other accounts, a technique called credential stuffing.

4. Enable two-factor authentication on your O2 account so that future logins require a code sent to your phone — even if someone has your password, they cannot log in without the code.

5. Monitor your O2 bill for unfamiliar charges over the next few months. Premium-rate services can be added to an account without your knowledge once credentials are compromised.

### How to report an O2 scam text

You can forward a suspicious SMS text to 7726 free of charge. For RCS, iMessage and messages received through apps, use the relevant built-in reporting tool.

If the text contained a phishing link, report the link to the National Cyber Security Centre: forward phishing emails to report@phishing.gov.uk, or use the NCSC's report-a-scam-website form at ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website.

If you have lost money or given financial details, file a full report with Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or call 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or contact Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Keep the original text message as evidence — take a screenshot before you delete it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does O2 send texts about account problems, or is any O2 text a scam?**

O2 does send genuine texts — bill reminders, data alerts, and upgrade offers — so receiving a text from O2 is not automatically suspicious. What matters is what it asks you to do. O2 says it will never call, text, or email you asking for a one-time code, password, or other security information. Whatever a message claims — billing problem, suspension, upgrade — check it by logging in directly at o2.co.uk rather than using any link in the text.

**The text came from a number labelled 'O2' in my phone — how can it still be fake?**

SMS sender names can be spoofed. A scammer can send a message that displays as 'O2' or 'O2 Alerts' just as easily as the real company can. This is called SMS spoofing. The displayed sender name is not proof the text is genuine. The reliable approach is to ignore the link entirely and log in yourself at o2.co.uk; if the position is not clear there, contact O2 using contact details you found independently.

**I'm getting an O2 text saying I'm due a free handset upgrade — is this real?**

It may be genuine, but treat it with caution. Check your upgrade eligibility by logging in directly at o2.co.uk or by dialling 202 (Pay Monthly) or 4445 (Pay As You Go) from your O2 phone — do not use the link in the text. If you are genuinely eligible for an upgrade, it will show in your account independently of any message.

**I forwarded the text to 7726 — what happens next?**

Your network operator investigates the sender and, if confirmed as a scammer, blocks it and can alert other UK networks. You will normally receive an auto-reply asking for the sender's number — reply with it. You do not need to do anything further unless you lost money or entered personal details, in which case also report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk, or to Police Scotland on 101 if you are in Scotland.

**I clicked the link but didn't enter anything. Am I at risk?**

Usually not — on a modern, updated smartphone, simply clicking a link without entering information rarely causes harm. As a precaution: close the tab, clear your browser cache, and check that your O2 account password has not been changed by logging in directly at o2.co.uk. If your phone has not received any recent security updates, consider running a malware scan with a reputable tool.

## Parcel Scam Texts Around Bank Holidays & Christmas

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/bank-holiday-parcel-scam-wave-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-06

A 'missed delivery' text arrives after a public holiday or during the Christmas rush? Real delays can make fake parcel texts seem plausible.

### What this scam wave looks like

This scam is a text claiming a parcel couldn't be delivered, needs rescheduling, or needs a fee to release. It may arrive around a public holiday or a busy shopping period such as Christmas, when genuine delivery disruption or high parcel volume makes the story sound plausible. An example of the style: `We attempted delivery but no one was in. Reschedule your parcel here.` The courier name changes, but the pattern — a link, a small fee, and urgency — stays the same.

### Why public holidays and busy periods are exploited

Royal Mail says it doesn't usually deliver or collect on public or local holidays, so people often expect some delivery disruption around those dates. That gives fake 'missed delivery' messages useful cover. Reliable sources support that operational mechanism, but not a distinct, documented scam spike tied specifically to UK bank holidays. Treat bank-holiday timing as context, not proof.

Evri also warns that its texts will never ask customers to reschedule a delivery or ask for payment to do so. If a text claims otherwise, use the courier's official site or app instead of the link in the text.

### Signs a delivery text is part of a scam wave

- It arrives around a public holiday or busy shopping period, claiming a missed or held delivery.
- It asks for a small fee to release or reschedule the parcel.
- The link doesn't go to the courier's genuine website.
- You weren't expecting a delivery, or can't match it to a recent order.

### How the scam works step by step

First, a text arrives at a time when a delivery delay feels believable, claiming a parcel is held or a fee is needed. Second, the link opens a lookalike version of a courier's website. Third, you're asked to pay a small fee and enter personal or card details. Fourth, the details are captured, and no genuine parcel was involved.

### How to check a delivery text safely

Don't tap the link. If you're expecting a parcel, find the tracking number in the retailer's own confirmation email, then go to the courier's official website or app by typing the address yourself.

- Only install a delivery app from an official app store, never a link in a text.
- A genuine delay around a public holiday or Christmas doesn't require you to use a text link. Check through the courier's own tracking instead.

### If you've already paid or entered details

Contact your bank immediately if you entered card details, and ask them to watch for unauthorised transactions. If you entered a password you've reused elsewhere, change it.

### How to report a parcel scam text (UK)

Forward it free to 7726. If you've lost money or shared sensitive details, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Why do fake delivery texts seem to fit around bank holidays?**

Royal Mail says it doesn't usually deliver or collect on public or local holidays, so genuine delays can make a fake 'missed delivery' text sound plausible. No reliable evidence was found for a specific bank-holiday scam spike, so don't rely on timing alone.

**How do I know if a 'missed delivery' text is genuine?**

Find the tracking number in the retailer's own order confirmation, then check it directly on the courier's official website or app. Don't use a link in the text itself.

**I paid a small 'redelivery fee' from a text like this. What do I do?**
