Contact your bank immediately, explain it was a scam, and ask them to watch for further unauthorised transactions.

**Do genuine couriers ever charge a fee by text to release a parcel?**

Don't pay through a text link. Evri says its texts never ask customers to reschedule a delivery or pay to do so. For any courier, use official tracking, the official app, or the retailer's order page.

**How do I report a fake delivery text?**

Forward it to 7726, and report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland) if you've lost money or shared details.

## Parking Fine Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake PCN SMS

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/parking-fine-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

Got a text about an unpaid parking fine or PCN with a pay-now link? How to spot a fake parking fine text, check the real issuer, and report it.

### What a fake parking fine text looks like

A parking fine scam text is a smishing message claiming you have an unpaid parking fine or Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) and must pay through a link to avoid extra charges or court. An example of the style is: `You have an unpaid parking fine of £60. Pay within 48 hours to avoid a court summons and extra costs: pcn-payment.example`.

The link opens a convincing payment page that captures your card and personal details. A key tell: do not rely on a pay-now link in an unsolicited text. Check any alleged parking fine through the issuer you find independently.

### Who actually issues parking fines (and who does not)

GOV.UK lists different parking and traffic penalties by issuer, including local council PCNs, Dart Charge, Transport for London red route and charging notices, Fixed Penalty Notices from police, local councils or DVSA, and tickets from private parking companies. DVLA is not the body listed for issuing parking fines, so a "DVLA parking fine" text is a strong red flag.

Because a genuine notice should have a reference and an official payment or appeals route, you can check it through the real issuer instead of a text link.

### Signs a parking fine text is a scam

- It demands payment through a link to avoid a court summons or rising costs.
- It claims to be from the DVLA about a parking fine.
- It gives a short deadline, often 24 or 48 hours.
- The link is a lookalike address, such as `pcn-payment.example`, not an official issuer's site.
- It asks for card details and personal information on the linked page.
- It cannot name the location, date, or vehicle, or the details do not match.
- You cannot match it to a written notice, reference, or official issuer.

### How the scam works

First, a text claims you owe a parking fine. Second, a deadline and the threat of court push you to pay fast. Third, the link opens a fake payment page. Fourth, criminals capture your card and personal details for fraud. Fifth, they may follow up pretending to be your bank.

Checking directly with the council, operator, transport authority, or GOV.UK - never the text link - breaks the chain.

### How to check a parking fine safely

Do not tap the link or pay from the text.

- Use GOV.UK's parking fines page at `gov.uk/parking-tickets` to find the right route for council PCNs, Dart Charge, TfL notices, Fixed Penalty Notices, and other ticket types.
- For a private parking charge, contact the operator using details you find yourself, not the text.
- Look for the genuine written notice, reference, payment route, and appeal instructions.
- Never enter card details on a page you reached from a text.
- Treat any "DVLA parking fine" text as a scam.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, and our /guides/council-tax-scam-text-uk/ and /guides/dvla-vehicle-tax-text-scam/ guides cover related government-impersonation texts.

### If you tapped the link or paid

Act now using the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report a parking fine scam text (UK)

Forward the scam text to 7726 so your mobile provider can investigate. If the same scam reached you by email, forward it to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. If a genuine fine turns out to exist, deal with it only through the council, operator, transport authority, or GOV.UK.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does the DVLA send parking fine texts?**

Treat a "DVLA parking fine" text as a scam. GOV.UK lists parking and traffic penalty routes for councils, Dart Charge, TfL, police, DVSA, and private parking companies; DVLA is not the parking-fine issuer.

**How do I check if a parking fine is real?**

Use GOV.UK's parking fines page at `gov.uk/parking-tickets`, your council's official website, or the private parking operator's real contact details. A genuine notice should have a reference and an appeals process; never pay through a link in a text.

**The text threatens a court summons within 48 hours - is that genuine?**

Treat it as suspicious. Real parking penalties have a written process with time to pay or appeal. A short text-link deadline is pressure designed to rush you.

**I paid a parking fine through a link in a text - what now?**

Contact your bank using the number on your card, ask them to secure the account, and ask about a chargeback. If you shared personal details, consider Cifas Protective Registration and monitor your credit reports.

**How do I report a parking fine scam text?**

Forward it to 7726, and if you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Royal Mail Scam Texts: Spot a Fake Delivery Text (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/royal-mail-text-scam-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-18

A Royal Mail text about a 'fee to pay' or redelivery? How to tell a genuine Royal Mail message from a scam — and pay any real fee safely.

### What a fake Royal Mail text looks like

A Royal Mail scam text is a smishing message that pretends to be from Royal Mail so you tap a link and hand over card or personal details. An example of the style is: `Royal Mail: Your parcel has an unpaid shipping fee of £2.99. Pay to reschedule delivery: royalmail-redelivery.example`.

The fee is usually small and believable. The link opens a fake Royal Mail page, often styled around a missed delivery, customs fee, or postage shortfall. This guide shows how to tell a fake from a genuine Royal Mail fee message, how to pay safely, and how to report the scam.

### Why Royal Mail texts are easy to fake

Scammers can set a sender name to read `Royal Mail`, so the displayed sender is not enough to prove the message is genuine. They also exploit a real detail: Royal Mail can charge legitimate fees.

Royal Mail's own guidance says an underpaid item surcharge is notified by a grey `Fee to Pay` card. For customs fees, Royal Mail says it will contact the recipient by SMS or email and will also leave a grey `Fee to Pay` card. It says an SMS or email about a customs fee will link to the Royal Mail `Fee to Pay` site.

That nuance matters. A text about a Royal Mail customs charge is not automatically fake, but you should verify it independently. Type `royalmail.com/pay-a-fee` or `royalmail.com/track-your-item` yourself, use the official Royal Mail app, and match the barcode or tracking details before paying.

### Signs a Royal Mail text is a scam

- It asks for a redelivery or release fee that you cannot match to a real item, tracking number, barcode, or `Fee to Pay` card.
- It links to a lookalike or shortened address instead of a Royal Mail route you reached yourself.
- It asks for card details, bank details, or personal information on a copycat page.
- It pressures you with a deadline before the item is returned to sender.
- It claims a customs or postage fee but gives no verifiable item reference.
- The wording, spelling, or layout looks odd, though a polished text can still be a scam.
- It asks you to use a payment route outside Royal Mail's official `Fee to Pay` process.

### How the Royal Mail fee scam works

First, a text claims your parcel needs a small fee paid before delivery. Second, it pushes you to a link to pay or reschedule. Third, the link opens a fake Royal Mail page asking for your address and card details. Fourth, the criminals capture them.

The first amount may look small, but the details can be used for further card fraud. Some victims later get a call pretending to be from a bank fraud team about the payment. Hang up and contact your bank yourself using a trusted number.

### How to check a Royal Mail text safely

Do not use a payment link from an unexpected text.

- Type `royalmail.com/pay-a-fee` or `royalmail.com/track-your-item` into your browser yourself.
- Use the official Royal Mail app, or follow the grey `Fee to Pay` card left at your address.
- For customs charges, check that the SMS or email matches a real Royal Mail item and the official `Fee to Pay` route.
- For underpaid postage, rely on the grey `Fee to Pay` card and Royal Mail's site.

If the message cannot be matched to a real item, treat it as a scam. When you are unsure whether a linked site is a copycat, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ walks through the checks, and our /guides/dpd-delivery-scam-text/ guide covers the same trick from other couriers.

### If you paid or shared card details

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on the back of your card. Tell them it was a scam, ask them to stop the card if needed, and ask about disputing the transaction. A card payment may be recoverable through chargeback, depending on the circumstances and card scheme rules.

### How to report a Royal Mail scam text (UK)

Forward suspicious texts to 7726. The NCSC says most UK phone providers let customers report suspicious texts for free this way, so the provider can investigate.

Royal Mail asks customers to report suspicious Royal Mail emails by forwarding them to `reportascam@royalmail.com`. Check Royal Mail's scam-protection page for current reporting options if the scam came through another channel. If a suspicious email contains a phishing link, you can also forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If you lost money, shared sensitive information, or were hacked, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Royal Mail charge a fee by text?**

Sometimes. Royal Mail says customs-fee notifications may arrive by SMS or email and will also be backed up by a grey `Fee to Pay` card. Underpaid item surcharges are notified by grey `Fee to Pay` card. The safe method is to type `royalmail.com/pay-a-fee` yourself and verify the item before paying.

**How do I tell a genuine Royal Mail fee from a scam?**

Match it to a real item using Royal Mail Track & Trace, the official app, or the barcode on the grey `Fee to Pay` card. Use the official `Fee to Pay` route rather than a link in an unexpected text.

**I paid the fee - can I get my money back?**

Possibly. Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the number on your card, report it as a scam, and ask them to stop the card and dispute the payment. Watch for follow-up bank impersonation calls.

**I clicked the link but did not pay - am I at risk?**

The risk is lower than if you entered details, but do not continue. Close the page, do not download anything, and run a security scan if the site prompted a download. If you entered card or personal details, treat them as compromised and contact your bank.

**How do I report a Royal Mail text scam?**

Forward it to 7726. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Scam Royal Mail emails can be forwarded to `reportascam@royalmail.com`.

## TSB Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Bank SMS

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/tsb-bank-scam-text-messages-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Got a TSB text about suspicious activity, a blocked account, or a payment to confirm? How to spot a fake TSB SMS, check safely, and report it in the UK.

### TSB publishes one set of checks for email and different advice for texts

The two are routinely run together and that is how people reach the wrong answer. TSB's published SMS advice contains no identifier that marks a text as genuine. What it does say is that scam texts often carry spelling and grammar mistakes, that links may take you to a website built to steal your details, and that you should not reply or click on anything.

So the test for a text is behavioural rather than forensic. Treat a message as unverified whenever it arrives unexpectedly, carries a link, manufactures a deadline, or asks for security information — something along the lines of `TSB: a payment of £450 is pending. Cancel now: tsb-secure-login.example`, which is an illustration rather than a real campaign. Then settle it independently, away from the message: open the TSB app yourself, or go through an official contact route you already hold, such as the number printed on the back of your card.

One aside, clearly labelled because it is the part most often misapplied. TSB does publish identifiers for its genuine emails: it says an email will greet you personally by name and will include the last four digits of your TSB current account number, the last four digits of another TSB product you hold, or the last three digits of your postcode, and that its email addresses end in `tsb.co.uk`. Those are email checks. A text is not fraudulent merely because it lacks them, and finding something that looks like one inside a text proves nothing either way.

### What TSB says a fraudster asks for

TSB frames these three on its fraud-prevention pages as warnings about telephone calls:

- A caller asking for your PIN. TSB says it will never ask you for it.
- A caller asking for your full password or memorable information.
- A caller saying your money is not safe and telling you to move it into a "safe" bank account.

The scope of that source is calls, so it should not be quoted as a statement about texts. The substance still travels, though, because the underlying banking facts do not change with the channel: no genuine process needs your PIN or your full password, and no genuine instruction moves your money into another account for safekeeping. A text asking for those secrets, or pushing you towards a safe account, is fraudulent however convincing the sender name looks.

### The Fraud Refund Guarantee ended in 2024 — what applies now

TSB launched the UK's first Fraud Refund Guarantee in April 2019. It is no longer running. TSB confirms the guarantee ended at midnight on 6 October 2024 and now applies only to eligible fraud transactions that took place before that moment.

Money sent from 7 October 2024 onwards falls under the mandatory reimbursement rules instead, and those are narrower than the old promise:

- They cover authorised push payment fraud — money you were tricked into sending yourself — made by Faster Payments or CHAPS. International payments, card payments, cash and cheques sit outside them.
- Reimbursement is capped at £85,000 for each eligible claim.
- You have 13 months from the payment to report it.
- A firm may deduct an excess of up to £100 per claim; TSB's published position is that it will not apply that excess on claims it refunds.
- An approved claim is repaid within five business days.

None of that amounts to a guaranteed refund. Claims are assessed individually and reimbursement can be reduced or refused, so the decision that actually protects your money is the one you take before the payment leaves, not the argument afterwards.

### The call that usually comes next

A smishing text is often the opening move rather than the whole scam. Whatever a fake login page harvests makes the follow-up call convincing: the voice already knows your name, your balance and a recent transaction, and wants you to move funds somewhere safe.

TSB is one of the institutions reachable on 159, the Stop Scams UK number that cannot itself be spoofed or impersonated. Use it in one direction only. 159 is a number you dial out on; it says nothing about whoever is already talking to you. TSB's published guidance tells customers to end a suspicious call and contact it through 159. Hang up first, then dial 159 or use the number on the back of the card.

### Where to send the text

- `emailscams@tsb.co.uk` — TSB's mailbox for suspicious emails and texts. TSB says screenshots of a text message can be sent here, which is the practical way to pass an SMS on.
- `7726` — the free shortcode that puts the sender in front of your mobile network.
- `report@phishing.gov.uk` — the NCSC's address, if the same bait also landed in your inbox.

Losses, or credentials you have already handed over, belong with Report Fraud too: `reportfraud.police.uk`, or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scottish reports go to Police Scotland on 101. Hold on to the original message until every report is filed.

### If you already tapped through

Speed matters more than tidiness here. Ring TSB on the number on the back of your card, or 159, and say plainly that you entered details on a page you reached from an SMS — that gets the account flagged rather than merely watched. If a payment went out, say so in the same call: the 13-month reporting window is generous, but a Faster Payment raised within minutes stands the best chance of being stopped at the receiving end.

Then work through the payment, account and identity steps in our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/). Where identity details such as your date of birth or address history went across alongside banking credentials, Cifas Protective Registration adds an extra check to applications made in your name.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is TSB's Fraud Refund Guarantee still running?**

No. TSB confirms it ended at midnight on 6 October 2024 and now covers only eligible fraud transactions from before then. Anything from 7 October 2024 is assessed under the mandatory reimbursement rules — conditional, capped at £85,000, and limited to Faster Payments and CHAPS.

**Will TSB take the £100 excess out of a fraud claim?**

The rules allow a firm to deduct up to £100 per claim, and TSB's published position is that it will not apply that excess on claims it refunds. That does not make repayment automatic: the claim still has to be accepted on its facts.

**How do I tell a genuine TSB message from a fake?**

TSB publishes its name and partial-account/postcode checks for email, not SMS. For texts, it warns about spelling or grammar errors and links that may steal details, and says not to reply or click. Check the TSB app independently, forward a suspicious text to `7726`, and send TSB a screenshot at `emailscams@tsb.co.uk`.

**Someone rang claiming to be the TSB fraud team — how do I check?**

TSB's published guidance tells customers to end a suspicious call and contact it through 159. Hang up first, then dial 159 or use the number on the back of the card.

**How do I report a TSB scam text?**

Screenshot it, email it to `emailscams@tsb.co.uk`, then forward the message itself to `7726`. Where money moved or credentials went across, add a Report Fraud case at `reportfraud.police.uk`, or dial 101 for Police Scotland.

## TV Licensing Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Licence SMS

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/tv-licensing-scam-text-message-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Got a TV Licensing text about a failed payment, an expired licence, or a refund? How to spot a fake TV Licensing SMS and report it in the UK.

### What a fake TV Licensing text looks like

A TV Licensing scam text is a fake SMS built to look like TV Licensing, so that you follow its link and type card, bank, or personal details into a page criminals control. An example of the style is: `TV Licensing: Your direct debit failed and your licence is no longer valid. Update your payment to avoid a £1,000 fine: tvlicence-renew.example`.

The pretexts criminals borrow are a Direct Debit that failed, a licence that has expired, and a refund you are owed. The first two are the awkward part: TV Licensing genuinely texts Direct Debit customers about payment problems and genuinely sends renewal reminders, so those subjects do not identify a scam on their own. The refund offer is different - TV Licensing says it does not text to tell you that you are entitled to one.

A fake link opens a convincing TV Licensing-style page that captures whatever you enter. Because TV Licensing sends genuine texts, some of which contain payment links, neither the channel nor the presence of a link settles it. What settles it is checking the same claim with TV Licensing opened independently, rather than through the message.

### Why these texts fool people

TV Licensing is familiar to many UK households, so a payment problem feels plausible, and the threat of a fine adds pressure. A refund offer works the other way, by lowering caution. The sender ID and the link can both be faked to look official. Sender addresses are an email question rather than a text one — our /guides/tv-licence-email-scam-uk/ guide lists the addresses TV Licensing currently identifies as genuine.

What TV Licensing says about its own texts is narrower and more useful. It says it may text a payment-card customer to ask for a payment, link a Simple Payment Plan customer to its payment site, confirm a TVL Pay payment, warn a Direct Debit customer about a payment problem, remind you that a licence is due for renewal, ask a former payment-scheme customer to set up a new way to pay, or confirm contact and ask for feedback. It says it will not text you an offer of a refund, will not ask for your bank details by text, and will not ask for personal details on its website before you have successfully signed in.

### Signs a TV Licensing text is a scam

Warning signs include an unexpected refund claim, a request for bank details by text, or a site that asks for personal details before you have successfully signed in. A payment problem or link is not conclusive by itself; verify the same issue independently in your TV Licensing account.

Alongside those, weigh the pressure tactics rather than the subject line:

- It threatens a fine, court, or an "enforcement officer" unless you act today.
- It pairs a generic greeting with a very short deadline.
- It asks you to reply with your full card number, bank details, or account credentials.
- The claim matches nothing you can find when you open your own account independently.
- It arrives from an odd number - though a familiar sender name proves nothing either way, because sender IDs can be spoofed.

An unfamiliar, misspelled or lookalike address is a warning. TV Licensing currently lists `tvlicensing.co.uk`, `tvl.co.uk`, `spp.tvlicensing.co.uk` and `75plan.tvlicensing.co.uk` as genuine, but visible link text and sender details can be faked. Do not use the message to verify itself: type `tvlicensing.co.uk` independently and check your licence or payment plan there.

TV Licensing's own scam guidance says a genuine Simple Payment Plan text may link to `tvl.co.uk/spppay`, so an address you do not recognise is a prompt to check independently rather than a verdict on its own.

### How the scam works, step by step

First, a text claims a licence or payment problem, or a refund. Second, urgency - a fine or a deadline - pushes you towards the link. Third, a copy of the TV Licensing site asks for card and personal details, typically before any sign-in. Fourth, criminals use them for card fraud, bank fraud, or identity theft. Fifth, a phone call may arrive soon afterwards from someone claiming to be TV Licensing or your bank and quoting the details you just gave.

Opening `tvlicensing.co.uk` yourself interrupts that sequence at the second step - and it is the right move whether the original message was genuine or not.

### How to check a TV Licensing text safely

Do not tap the link or call a number from the text. You can deal with the issue through your account instead of using the message's link.

- Type `tvlicensing.co.uk` into your browser yourself, or sign in from a bill or letter you already have.
- Check your licence status, payment plan, and any outstanding payment there, not through the link.
- Expect to sign in first. TV Licensing says its missed-payment route asks for card details only after you have signed in with your licence number, last name, and postcode.
- A no-licence conviction can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If a court has fined you, use the payment instructions from the court, not a link in a message claiming to be TV Licensing.
- Do not enter card, bank, or personal details on a page you opened from the message.
- If you are unsure, contact TV Licensing through the contact options published on `tvlicensing.co.uk`.

If you are unsure whether a linked page is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, our /guides/tv-licence-email-scam-uk/ guide covers the same scam by email, and /guides/tv-licence-scam-letter-uk/ covers it by post.

### What to do if you tapped the link or typed details

What you do next depends on what the page captured, so work through whichever of these describes your situation.

- Card number typed in: phone the card issuer on the number printed on the card, have it secure or replace the card, and have it review recent spending for anything you did not authorise. A dispute route such as chargeback only becomes relevant if an eligible transaction was actually taken or later shows up - ask the issuer which route fits.
- Online banking credentials typed in: speak to the bank through a route you already trust, such as its app or the number on a statement, and do what it tells you.
- A password typed in: reset it inside the genuine service, and reset it anywhere else you reused it.
- Anything installed or granted: if the page pushed a download, added an app or configuration profile, requested remote access, or the handset has misbehaved since, cut the connection to that session and work through the NCSC's current advice on responding to phishing and recovering a device.
- If identity documents or personal information were exposed, review Cifas's current eligibility wording. Cifas says Protective Registration is only for people whose identities are at heightened risk. It places a warning flag that prompts extra checks on applications; it does not protect existing card transactions and is not insurance.

Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) puts these in order alongside the money and account steps.

### How to report a TV Licensing scam text (UK)

TV Licensing's FAQ 288 currently shows two different spellings for its screenshot-reporting mailbox, so this guide does not ask readers to choose between them. Forward suspicious SMS to `7726`. If you also want to send TV Licensing a screenshot, contact it through its official Contact Us page and ask which current route to use. TV Licensing asks for suspicious emails to go to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk` instead.

For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; `7726` is not the in-app reporting route.

If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. It also has a route for reporting something suspicious where nobody responded and no money was lost, so a suspicious text is still worth reporting. Take a screenshot and note the sender before you report or delete the message.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does TV Licensing send texts, or is every TV Licensing text a scam?**

TV Licensing sends genuine payment, Direct Debit, renewal and account-service texts, and some include links. It says it never texts to tell you that you are owed a refund, never asks for bank details by text, and does not ask for personal details until you have signed in. Verify the message independently at `tvlicensing.co.uk`.

**A text says my TV Licence direct debit failed and I'll be fined - is it real?**

It could be either. TV Licensing does text Direct Debit customers about payment problems, so the subject alone does not answer the question. Open `tvlicensing.co.uk` independently instead of tapping the link and see whether the same payment problem shows on your account. A no-licence conviction can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If a court has fined you, use the payment instructions from the court, not a link in a message claiming to be TV Licensing.

**The text offers a TV Licensing refund - should I claim it?**

No. TV Licensing says it does not text to tell you that you are entitled to a refund, which makes an unexpected refund text one of the few subjects that is a warning sign in its own right. If you think a refund is genuinely due, open `tvlicensing.co.uk` independently and check it in your account.

**I entered my card details on a TV Licensing-looking site - what now?**

Phone the card issuer straight away on the number printed on the card, have the card secured or replaced, and have recent spending reviewed for anything you did not authorise; ask the issuer which dispute route fits any transaction that was actually taken. Reset any password you typed in, and any password you reused elsewhere. If the page pushed a download, added an app or profile, or asked for remote access, follow the NCSC's current device-recovery advice. Consider Cifas Protective Registration only where the exposure puts your identity at heightened risk; check Cifas's current criteria. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the order.

**How do I report a TV Licensing scam text?**

For an SMS, forward the message to `7726`. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; `7726` is not the in-app reporting route. If you also want to send TV Licensing a screenshot, take the mailbox from its current scam advice page or Contact Us route, because FAQ 288 currently shows two different spellings. If money was taken or you handed over sensitive details, add a report to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## UPS Scam Text Messages: Spot a Fake UPS Delivery Text (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/ups-delivery-scam-text-messages-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-31

Fake UPS texts about a missed delivery or 'customs fee' are smishing scams. Here's how to spot a fake UPS text, verify a genuine one, and report it in the UK.

### What is the UPS scam text?

A UPS scam text is a phishing message that impersonates the courier UPS to steal money and personal details. It usually claims a parcel is being held and that you must pay a fee — frequently framed as a 'customs charge', 'import duty', or 'brokerage fee' — or that a delivery was missed and needs rescheduling through a link. UPS handles a large share of international shipments into the UK, and genuine customs charges can apply to parcels from outside the UK, which is exactly why the 'pay this customs fee' version of the scam is so convincing. Scammers send these texts in bulk; they're betting that enough recipients are expecting something from abroad to make the customs story believable. Tap the link and you land on a fake UPS page built to capture whatever you type.

### How the UPS text scam works, step by step

- A text claiming to be from UPS says your parcel is held pending a customs, import, or redelivery fee, with a link to pay.
- The link opens a counterfeit UPS page on a lookalike domain rather than the official ups.com.
- You're asked for personal details and to pay a modest fee by card, made to seem small and reasonable.
- Your card and contact details are captured instantly and can be used or sold on.
- Some victims then receive a follow-up call from a fake 'bank fraud team' that uses the stolen information to sound legitimate and pressure them into authorising larger payments.

### Warning signs of a fake UPS text

- It asks you to pay a customs, import, duty, or redelivery fee via a link in the text. Genuine duties are handled through official channels, not a random SMS link.
- The sender is an ordinary mobile or international number rather than an identifiable UPS sender.
- The web address isn't the official ups.com — look for extra words, hyphens, or unusual endings.
- It uses urgency ('parcel will be returned today') and a generic greeting.
- You aren't expecting an international parcel, or the amount and reference don't match anything you ordered.
- It asks for card details, a one-time passcode, or banking information to 'release' the parcel.

### How a genuine UPS charge or delivery actually works

Real customs charges on parcels from outside the UK do exist, and UPS says some shipments genuinely require funds before or at delivery, so a request for money is not proof of fraud on its own. Legitimate UPS contacts you about them in a verifiable way and lets you check the charge against your specific tracking number on the official ups.com site. To verify any UPS message, don't use its link — find your tracking number in the retailer's dispatch email, then type ups.com into your browser or open the UPS app and enter the number yourself. If you have a UPS My Choice account, check there. A genuine process will match a parcel you're actually expecting and won't ask for your full card number, PIN, online banking password, or a security code by text. If anything doesn't line up, treat the message as a scam and check with the retailer you bought from.

### What to do if you paid a UPS 'customs' or 'delivery' fee

- Phone your bank straight away on the number on the back of your card, tell them you entered details on a scam site, and ask them to block the card and monitor for fraud.
- Change any password or code you entered and treat it as compromised.
- Watch for a follow-up call posing as your bank — it's part of the scam. Hang up and call back on the official number; your bank will never ask you to move money to a 'safe account'.
- Keep the message and payment details as evidence for your report.
- Check your statements and credit file for anything unexpected over the following weeks.

### How to report a UPS scam text in the UK

Forward the text free to 7726 so your mobile network can investigate and block the sender, then delete it. If you've lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (in Scotland, Police Scotland on 101). Phishing links can be reported to the National Cyber Security Centre, and you can alert UPS through the fraud or security section of ups.com so they can act on the fake sites. A quick report helps networks and investigators disrupt the campaign behind the message.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does UPS ask for a customs fee by text?**

Legitimate customs charges on parcels from outside the UK do exist, but UPS does not collect them through a random link in a text message. A text pressuring you to pay a 'customs', 'import', or 'brokerage' fee via a link is almost always a scam. Verify any charge yourself by entering your tracking number on the official ups.com site rather than tapping the link, and check with the retailer if you're unsure.

**How do I know if a UPS text is real?**

A genuine UPS text matches a parcel you're actually expecting and lets you verify everything on the official ups.com site or in the UPS app using your tracking number; it never asks for your full card number, PIN, or a banking passcode by text. Scam texts come from random numbers, use lookalike web addresses, and rush you to pay. When unsure, don't tap the link — go to ups.com yourself.

**I paid a UPS scam text fee — what should I do?**

Contact your bank immediately on the number printed on your card, explain you entered details on a fake site, and ask them to freeze the card and watch for fraud. Change any passwords or codes you shared. Be cautious of a follow-up call claiming to be your bank's fraud team — that's the next stage of the scam. Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

**Where can I report a fake UPS text in the UK?**

Forward the message free to 7726 so your network can investigate the sender, then delete it. If money or personal details were lost, report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland). You can also report the phishing page to the NCSC and notify UPS through ups.com.

## Vodafone Scam Text UK: Spot a Fake Vodafone SMS

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/vodafone-scam-text-uk/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Got a Vodafone text about a billing issue, a refund, or account suspension? How to spot a fake Vodafone SMS, check safely, and report it in the UK.

### What a fake Vodafone text looks like

A Vodafone scam text is a smishing message that pretends to be from Vodafone so you tap a link and hand over card, login, or personal details. Common hooks are a billing problem, a refund, or a threat that your account will be suspended. An example of the style is: `Vodafone: your last payment failed. Update your details within 24 hours to avoid suspension: vodafone-billing.example`.

The link opens a convincing fake Vodafone login or payment page. Vodafone also sends genuine texts, and its missed-payment guidance says it may text a payment link after multiple missed bills when service is restricted. Neither the channel nor the link decides it. The safer check is whether the same issue appears in My Vodafone or is confirmed through a Vodafone contact route found independently.

### Why these texts fool people

A Vodafone billing message can feel plausible to a customer, and the threat of suspension creates urgency. A spoofed sender ID can make a fake appear alongside real brand messages.

That is why the check matters more than the message. Look at billing and account status in the My Vodafone app, or by typing `vodafone.co.uk` yourself, before you act on anything a text asks for.

### Signs a Vodafone text is a scam

- It asks you to confirm login credentials, a full card number, or security details through a link, rather than through an account you sign in to yourself.
- It offers a refund you were not expecting.
- The address is unfamiliar, misspelled, or a lookalike - though visible link text and sender details can be faked, so the displayed address does not settle it either way.
- It gives a short deadline to act, or threatens immediate suspension.
- It uses a generic greeting or unusual formatting.
- Nothing matching the claim appears in My Vodafone when you look independently.
- The sender or number looks odd, but a familiar sender name alone does not prove the message is genuine.

One thing is not a sign by itself: a payment link. Vodafone's current missed-payment guidance says that after multiple missed bills, when service has been restricted, it may text a link to a page where the bill can be paid without using mobile data. Do not decide from the link alone: check whether the same issue shows in My Vodafone, or is confirmed through a contact route you found independently.

### How the scam works

First, a text claims a billing problem, refund, or account issue. Second, urgency pushes you to tap the link. Third, a fake Vodafone page asks for login, card, or personal details. Fourth, criminals capture them for account takeover, card fraud, or identity theft. Fifth, they may follow up by phone pretending to be Vodafone support.

Checking directly in the My Vodafone app or on `vodafone.co.uk`, rather than tapping the link, breaks the chain.

### How to check a Vodafone text safely

Use routes you already control, not the one the message offers.

- Open the My Vodafone app or type `vodafone.co.uk` yourself and check your account and billing there.
- Never enter your login, card, or personal details on a page you reached from a text.
- Treat any unexpected refund or suspension threat with suspicion.
- Contact Vodafone only through the app or contact options published on its official website.

Our /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ guide walks through checking a suspicious page, and the same billing pretext runs on other brands in our /guides/o2-scam-text-uk/ and /guides/tv-licensing-scam-text-message-uk/ guides.

### If you tapped the link or shared details

Vodafone asks anyone who has given away account security details to contact its fraud team straight away and update the affected details, so make that the first move, using contact options in the My Vodafone app or on `vodafone.co.uk`. Change your Vodafone password from the official app or website, never from a link in the message, and change any other account that reused the same password.

If card details went in, contact the card issuer on the number on the card and ask it to secure or replace the card and check for transactions you do not recognise; where an eligible card transaction was actually made or appears, ask which fraud or dispute route applies, because chargeback only comes into play where such a transaction exists. If the page downloaded a file, installed an app or a configuration profile, asked for remote access, or the handset has since behaved unusually, disconnect from the suspicious session and follow current NCSC guidance on responding to phishing and recovering a device.

If identity documents or personal information were exposed, review Cifas's current eligibility wording. Cifas says Protective Registration is only for people whose identities are at heightened risk. It places a warning flag that prompts extra checks on applications; it does not protect existing card transactions and is not insurance. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the payment, account, and identity steps in order.

### How to report a Vodafone scam text (UK)

For an SMS, forward the message to `7726`. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; `7726` is not the in-app reporting route. Vodafone describes `7726` as its free spam text reporting service.

Suspicious emails claiming to be from Vodafone go to `phishing@vodafone.co.uk`, the address Vodafone publishes on its own phishing page, and phishing emails more generally to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

Losses and handed-over details should also go to Report Fraud, online at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. It also takes reports of suspicious contact where nobody responded and no money was lost. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) covers what evidence to keep.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Vodafone send texts, or is every Vodafone text a scam?**

Vodafone sends genuine texts. Its missed-payment page specifically says it may text a payment link after multiple missed bills when service is restricted, so neither the channel nor a payment link proves the message is genuine or fake. Verify the arrears or restriction in My Vodafone, or through Vodafone contact details found independently.

**A text says my Vodafone payment failed and I'll be suspended - is it real?**

Vodafone says it may text a payment link after multiple missed bills when service is restricted. Do not decide from the link alone: check My Vodafone or contact Vodafone through its official site and verify the same arrears or restriction before paying.

**The text offers a Vodafone refund - should I claim it?**

Do not claim a refund through an unexpected text. Open My Vodafone or contact Vodafone through a route you found independently and confirm that a refund is actually due. Do not enter card, login or security details on a page reached from the message.

**I entered my details on a Vodafone-looking site - what now?**

Contact Vodafone's fraud team first and say the account may be compromised — that is Vodafone's own published instruction where account security details have been given away — then update the affected details and your password through the official app or website, and change any other account that reused that password. If card details went in, contact the card issuer on the number on the card and ask which dispute route applies to any transaction that was made or appears. Consider Cifas Protective Registration only where the exposure puts your identity at heightened risk; check Cifas's current criteria. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the order to do these in.

**How do I report a Vodafone scam text?**

For an SMS, forward the message to `7726`. For WhatsApp, Telegram or Signal, preserve the evidence and use the app's report and block tools; `7726` is not the in-app reporting route. If the same scam arrived by email, forward it to `phishing@vodafone.co.uk`, the address on Vodafone's own phishing page. Where money was lost, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. It also takes reports of suspicious messages where nobody responded and nothing was lost.

## Yodel Scam Text Messages: How to Spot a Fake Yodel Text (UK)

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/yodel-scam-text-messages/
Category: Text Message Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake Yodel missed-parcel and redelivery-fee texts are smishing scams. Learn how to check a Yodel by InPost delivery, spot a fake and report it.

### What changed in July 2026, and why scammers benefit

Yodel now operates as Yodel by InPost, and the customer-facing tools moved during July 2026. Yodel's own help centre says the Yodel by InPost app is no longer available from 17 July, and InPost's Yodel help page says Yodel by InPost web accounts also stopped being available from that date. Parcels are handled by InPost, and customers are told to use the InPost app or `inpost.co.uk` to track and manage deliveries.

That transition is exactly the kind of moment smishing gangs wait for. When people are unsure which app, brand, or web address is now correct, a text saying "your Yodel parcel needs attention" is harder to dismiss. InPost also warns that during the move you may receive updates from both Yodel by InPost and InPost, so two genuine senders is now normal — which removes the easy assumption that anything unexpected must be fake.

The practical rule has not changed, though: judge a delivery message by whether you can match it to a real parcel through a route you opened yourself, never by the branding or the link inside it.

### What a fake Yodel text is trying to get

A Yodel scam text impersonates the courier so you tap a link and hand over payment or personal details. It usually claims a delivery failed, a parcel is waiting, or an address needs confirming, then asks for a small 'redelivery' or 'release' fee.

These are sent in bulk to random numbers. The sender has no idea whether you have ordered anything — the bet is simply that many people have a parcel moving at any given time. The small fee is deliberate: a couple of pounds feels too trivial to be worth defrauding someone over, which is what makes people enter a card number. The card details are the actual target, and a follow-up call impersonating your bank is where the large losses happen.

### The one commitment that settles a fee demand

Yodel by InPost's own fraud and information-security page states it will never send emails or text messages asking you to provide your bank details or phone number, and that it will never ask for a fee for redelivery of a parcel.

So a message demanding money to release or redeliver a parcel contradicts the courier's own published commitment, whichever brand name it uses. Note the limit of that rule: it covers redelivery fees and requests for bank details or phone numbers. Genuine delivery notifications do exist, and a retailer or an import charge can legitimately involve money elsewhere in a purchase — so "a message mentioned money" is not the test. "A courier asked me to pay a fee to get my parcel redelivered" is.

### Signs the text is not from the courier

- It asks for any payment to receive or redeliver a parcel.
- It asks for bank details, card details, or your phone number.
- The link is not on `inpost.co.uk` or `yodel.co.uk` — watch for added words, hyphens, or unusual endings.
- It arrives from a random mobile or international number.
- It pressures you with a deadline, a holding fee, or a threat to return the parcel.
- You cannot match it to an order you actually placed.
- It asks for a one-time passcode, password, or date of birth. Yodel's fraud page notes that genuine companies do not email asking for usernames, passwords, dates of birth, or card details.

### Checking a delivery now that tracking has moved

Do not tap the link in the message. Instead:
- Find the tracking number in the dispatch confirmation from the shop you ordered from, not from the text.
- Open the InPost app, or type `inpost.co.uk` into your browser yourself, and enter that tracking number.
- If you still have a Yodel tracking reference, `yodel.co.uk` remains the brand's own site and directs customers to the current InPost route — reach it by typing the address, never through a message link.
- Ask the retailer which courier is carrying the order and whether anything is genuinely out for delivery. The retailer is often the fastest independent check.

A genuine tracking page shows your parcel without asking for a card number, a PIN, a banking password, or a one-time passcode. Yodel's fraud page also says its legitimate emails come from `donotreply@yodel.co.uk` or `noreply@yodel.co.uk`, which is useful context for email — but treat a sender address as a clue, not proof, because sender details can be spoofed.

### If you tapped the link or entered details

Delivery scams have a distinctive second act, so the order of these steps matters.

- Call your bank on the number printed on your card and say you may have entered card details on a fake courier site. Ask them to stop the card and watch the account.
- Expect a follow-up. Criminals who harvest details from a parcel page often ring within days posing as your bank's fraud team, using the real details you just gave them to sound credible. No genuine bank will tell you to move money to a safe account. Hang up and call back on the number on your card.
- Treat any one-time passcode you shared as compromised, and change any password you typed.
- Keep the message and any payment receipt before deleting anything — you will need them to report.

If money has left your account, the payment route decides what protection applies. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) sets out the card, transfer, account and identity steps in order, including how reporting differs in Scotland.

### Reporting a fake Yodel or InPost text

Forward the text free to `7726`. That shortcode is run by the mobile networks and lets them investigate and block the sender.

Yodel's fraud page asks customers to forward suspicious emails to `information.security@yodel.co.uk` rather than clicking anything inside them, so the brand can act on fake domains. Phishing emails can also go to the National Cyber Security Centre at `report@phishing.gov.uk`.

If you lost money or handed over details, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is the Yodel app still available?**

No. Yodel's help centre says the Yodel by InPost app is no longer available from 17 July, and InPost says Yodel by InPost web accounts stopped being available from the same date. Parcels are handled by InPost, so tracking and delivery preferences now live in the InPost app or at `inpost.co.uk`. Reach either by typing the address yourself rather than following a link in a message.

**Does Yodel charge a fee to redeliver a parcel?**

No. Yodel by InPost's fraud page says it will never ask for a fee for redelivery of a parcel, and will never email or text asking for your bank details or phone number. A message demanding a small 'redelivery' or 'release' fee through a link is a scam aimed at your card details.

**A text still says 'Yodel' — does the rebrand make it fake?**

Not by itself. Yodel by InPost is a live brand and you may receive genuine updates from both Yodel by InPost and InPost while the move completes, so Yodel branding alone proves nothing either way. Check whether the message matches a real order by entering the tracking number from your dispatch confirmation into the InPost app or `inpost.co.uk`, opened independently.

**I entered my card details on a courier link — what now?**

Ring your bank on the number on your card, say you entered details on a fake courier site, and ask them to stop the card and monitor the account. Change anything else you typed, and treat a shared one-time passcode as compromised. Be ready for a call claiming to be the bank's fraud team — that is the next stage of the same scam. Then work through the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

**Where do I report a fake courier text?**

Forward it free to `7726` so your network can act on the sender. Suspicious emails can go to Yodel at `information.security@yodel.co.uk` and to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`. If money or details were lost, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Airport Transfer Taxi Scam UK: Spot a Fake or Illegal Ride

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/airport-transfer-taxi-scam-uk/
Category: Travel Scams · Updated: 2026-07-16

Fake transfer sites and illegal touts target airport passengers. Use an official rank or a booking with a licensed operator and verify the vehicle.

### What the scam can look like

One pattern is a bogus transfer website that takes payment for a vehicle that never arrives. Another is an illegal tout approaching passengers in or near arrivals and offering an unbooked ride. An unsolicited approach is not automatically proof that the vehicle is unlicensed, but passengers should use the airport's official rank or a verified pre-booking rather than accepting it.

### The law is not identical across the UK

In England and Wales, a private hire vehicle (often called a minicab) can only be pre-booked through a licensed operator; licensed taxis can also be hailed or hired at a rank in the area where they are licensed. Scotland makes the same practical distinction between taxis and private hire cars under its own legislation.

Taxi and private-hire regulation differs across the UK; there is no single uniform "UK law" here. Northern Ireland does not use the same two-category model. It has Classes A to D: Class C taxis are pre-book only, while some Class A and Class B taxis can be hailed under the published conditions. In England, Wales and Scotland, private-hire vehicles generally must be pre-booked rather than hailed.

### Warning signs

- A driver approaches you and there is no existing booking.
- The vehicle or driver details do not match the booking confirmation.
- The operator cannot be found through the relevant licensing authority.
- The site hides its legal identity or demands an unprotected bank transfer.
- The price or destination changes after you enter the vehicle.

### Check before booking or getting in

Use the airport's official information, taxi rank or a licensed operator. Check the driver, registration and licence details against the confirmation. In London, TfL requires a private-hire booking confirmation to include the vehicle registration, driver's first name, licence number and, where the passenger can receive it, a driver photo.

In England and Wales, taxis display a rear licence plate; most private-hire vehicles display a plate or windscreen/rear-window disc, but exemptions exist. Requirements vary by authority, so absence of one particular design is not a universal test. TfL provides a Licence Checker for London.

At Heathrow, the Authorised Vehicle Area is a waiting area for licensed taxis and private-hire vehicles with pre-booked passengers. It is not a passenger taxi rank and does not make an unsolicited terminal approach legitimate.

### If an online transfer never arrived

Contact the seller through independently verified details and contact the bank or card issuer promptly. A card issuer may be able to use chargeback where a service was not provided, subject to card-scheme rules and time limits; chargeback is not a guaranteed legal right. A qualifying credit-card purchase may also be covered by section 75 where the cash price is more than £100 and not more than £30,000.

### Reporting in the UK

Report an unlicensed vehicle or driver to the local licensing authority, or to TfL in London; call 999 in immediate danger. Northern Ireland has a separate taxi-licensing process. Report a fraudulent booking site to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I hail a minicab or private-hire car?**

Not in England, Wales or Scotland; it must be pre-booked. Northern Ireland uses different taxi classes, so follow the class and local rules there.

**Does every licensed private-hire vehicle display the same plate?**

No. Local designs vary and some vehicles have exemptions. Verify through the relevant authority and the booking confirmation.

## Booking.com Scam UK: Spot a Fake Payment Message

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/booking-com-scam-uk/
Category: Travel Scams · Updated: 2026-07-10

A message uses real booking details and demands payment or card information. Compare it with the confirmation and contact Booking.com directly.

### What the scam looks like

A message refers to a real reservation and claims that payment failed or that card details must be re-entered to avoid cancellation. It may arrive by email, phone, text, WhatsApp or a booking-platform message, and it may contain convincing dates, prices and property details. The link leads away from the expected payment journey or the requested transfer differs from the booking confirmation.

### Do not assume how the data was obtained

A fraudulent message can appear in a genuine thread if an account used to send it has been compromised. Other data exposures or impersonation methods are possible. A single suspicious message does not prove that Booking.com's central systems were breached, nor does it prove that they were not. The useful fact is that a message appearing in a genuine thread is not sufficient authentication.

### Booking.com's published advice

Booking.com says it will not ask travellers to share credit-card details by email, phone, text or WhatsApp, and will not ask for a bank transfer that differs from the payment-policy details in the booking confirmation. It also says Customer Service should ask only for a reservation ID and/or PIN, not an account password or sensitive financial information.

Do not extend that statement into the unsupported absolute that every in-app request concerning a card is automatically fraudulent. Instead, compare the request with the booking terms and confirm it through official Customer Service before taking action.

### Warning signs

- A new payment or card request conflicts with the confirmation.
- The message creates a 24-hour or similarly urgent cancellation threat.
- A link leaves the expected Booking.com payment journey.
- The property asks for a bank transfer or payment method not stated in the booking policy.
- Someone claiming to be Customer Service asks for the account password or full card number.

### Check the request safely

Do not use the link. Open the Booking.com app or site independently, review the confirmation and contact Customer Service through the official account. If the property appears to have sent the message, ask Booking.com to investigate the account rather than relying only on a reply in the same thread.

### If card or login details were entered

Contact the card issuer immediately, change the Booking.com password and any reused password, and report the incident through official Customer Service. Keep screenshots, the URL and the booking confirmation.

### Reporting in the UK

Forward suspicious emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk` and texts to 7726. If money was lost or an account was compromised, report the crime to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does a message in the Booking.com app prove it is genuine?**

No. Compromised provider accounts can be used to send messages through genuine systems. Verify the request against the confirmation and with Customer Service.

**Does the message prove Booking.com itself was hacked?**

No conclusion about the point of compromise can be drawn from the message alone.

## Cruise Scam UK: Spot Fake Deals and Book Safely

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/cruise-scam-uk/
Category: Travel Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Cruise scams use fake deals, "free cruise" prizes and bogus booking sites to take your money. How to spot one, book safely and get your money back.

### What is a cruise scam?

A cruise scam is any fraud built around the promise of a cruise holiday. Some scammers advertise heavily discounted sailings on well-known lines that don't exist, take your payment and vanish. Others run "you've won a free cruise" prize scams — an unsolicited call, email or text tells you that you've been selected for a complimentary cruise, then demands "port fees", "taxes" or booking charges before you can claim it. A third type builds convincing fake booking websites that copy a real cruise line's branding to harvest card details and personal information. What these share is a genuine-sounding travel offer used to rush you into paying by a method that's hard to reverse, usually before you've had a chance to check who you're actually dealing with. Cruises are a natural target because the sums involved are large, the booking is made months ahead, and buyers expect to pay a deposit up front — so a fraudulent "deposit" doesn't feel out of place until the sailing date arrives and there's no cabin.

### Common types of cruise scam in the UK

There are a few patterns worth recognising. The fake deal advertises a cruise far below the going rate — often through a social media ad, a cold call or a spoofed email — and pushes you to pay quickly to "hold the cabin". The free cruise prize claims you've won or been gifted a cruise and asks for an upfront fee, your card details, or a premium-rate call to release it; a genuine prize never requires you to pay to receive it. The clone booking site mimics a real cruise line or travel agent, sometimes reached through a search ad rather than the company's real website, and exists only to collect payment and personal data. The bogus travel agent takes a booking for a real sailing, takes your money, but never actually books it with the cruise line — you only find out when you try to check in. And advance-fee follow-ups target people who've already lost money, posing as a recovery service that can get your cash back for a fee. Knowing which pattern you're looking at helps you pick the right checks and the right reporting route.

### Red flags before you book

- A price that's dramatically below what the cruise line or established agents are charging for the same sailing and cabin type.
- Pressure to pay immediately to "secure" a cabin, with claims that the offer expires today or that only one cabin is left.
- A request to pay by bank transfer, cryptocurrency, gift cards, or a money-transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram — none of these give you the protection a card payment does.
- An unsolicited call, email or text saying you've won or been given a free cruise, especially if it asks for a fee, "taxes", or card details to release it.
- A website reached through an ad or a link in a message rather than by typing the company's address yourself — check the full domain carefully, as clone sites copy the branding but use a slightly different address.
- No verifiable UK company details, no landline, or contact only through a mobile number, WhatsApp or a web form.
- Vague answers about which cruise line operates the sailing, what's included, or what financial protection applies to your booking.
- A "cruise deal" that appears only on social media, with a recently created page or profile and no independent trace of the business elsewhere.

### How to check a cruise deal or seller is genuine

Slow the booking down and verify before you pay. First, find the cruise line's or agent's real website by typing the address yourself or using a trusted search result — not by following the link in an ad, email or text — and confirm the sailing, date and price directly. Second, look up the seller's UK company details on the free Companies House register and check for genuine, verifiable contact information. Third, understand what financial protection actually applies, because this is where cruise bookings are widely misunderstood. ATOL does not protect every cruise: ATOL is the Civil Aviation Authority's scheme and generally covers flight-inclusive package holidays, so a fly-cruise that includes your flights is usually ATOL-protected, but a cruise-only or non-flight booking is not covered by ATOL; it may instead have protection through a bond, insurance, trust arrangement or another scheme, but protection is not automatic for every booking. Ask the seller in writing exactly what protection your specific booking carries and get the answer confirmed before paying. Fourth, ABTA membership can be a reassuring sign, but it is voluntary — plenty of legitimate travel businesses are not ABTA members, so a company not being in ABTA does not by itself prove it's a scam, and equally you should confirm any claimed membership directly with ABTA rather than trusting a logo on a website. Finally, search the company name alongside words like "scam", "complaint" or "review", and check independent sources rather than only the testimonials on the seller's own site.

### How to pay so you're protected

The way you pay makes the biggest difference to whether you can recover your money if something goes wrong. Where possible, pay by credit card. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 makes your card issuer jointly liable with the seller for a qualifying credit-card purchase with a cash price over £100 and no more than £30,000, provided there's a genuine credit agreement and the standard three-party relationship between you, the card issuer and the retailer — so if the cruise is never provided, you may be able to claim against your card provider even if the seller has disappeared. Note that Section 75 comes from the Consumer Credit Act 1974, not the Consumer Rights Act, and the two are often confused. Debit cards are not covered by Section 75, but a chargeback may be available under the card scheme rules — that's a discretionary scheme process rather than a legal right. Avoid paying by bank transfer, cryptocurrency, gift cards or money-transfer services: once that money has moved it's very hard to pull back, and legitimate cruise sellers almost never insist on them. If a booking that started as a card payment suddenly reroutes you to a bank transfer or asks you to email for "alternative payment details", stop — that redirect is a common sign of a scam.

### What to do if you've already paid

If you think you've booked a cruise that doesn't exist, or paid a fee to claim a "free" one, act quickly. First, stop any further payments and don't send more money — recovery-fee follow-ups are a common second scam. Second, contact your bank or card provider straight away using the number on the back of your card. If you paid by credit card, ask about a Section 75 claim; if you paid by debit card, ask about a chargeback. If you paid by bank transfer, tell your bank immediately — where you sent the money by UK bank transfer on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory APP fraud reimbursement rules may apply to Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers, subject to a 13-month claim window, a maximum claim of £85,000, and a possible excess of up to £100, so ask your bank to assess the claim. Third, gather your evidence: the advert or listing, any emails and messages, the website address, payment receipts, and notes of what you were told. Fourth, report the scam through the official channels below. Keep every reference number you're given.

### Reporting a cruise scam in the UK

Report a cruise scam to the police's national fraud service and to the relevant platforms so action can be taken and patterns tracked. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, report to Report Fraud (the current service, formerly known as Action Fraud) at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland by calling 101. Give as much detail as you can: the company name, website, phone numbers, email addresses, the cruise line or sailing claimed, dates of contact, how you paid and how much you lost. If a scam reached you by text message, forward it free of charge to 7726 so your mobile network can investigate. If you came across a fake or suspicious cruise website, report it to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) through its report-a-scam-website service. You can also report the advert or profile to the platform where you saw it — the social network, marketplace or search engine — so it can be taken down. If you need free, independent advice on your consumer rights or a payment dispute, contact the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.

### Frequently asked questions

**Are all cruises ATOL protected?**

No. ATOL is the Civil Aviation Authority's protection scheme and it generally covers flight-inclusive package holidays. A fly-cruise that includes your flights is usually ATOL-protected, but a cruise-only or non-flight booking is not covered by ATOL — it may instead have protection through a bond, insurance, trust arrangement or another scheme, but protection is not automatic for every booking. Don't assume a cruise is ATOL-protected just because it's a big holiday: ask the seller in writing exactly what protection your specific booking carries, and confirm it before you pay.

**The cruise seller isn't an ABTA member — does that mean it's a scam?**

Not on its own. ABTA membership can be a useful sign of an established travel business, but it is voluntary, and many legitimate companies are not ABTA members. A company not being in ABTA doesn't prove it's fraudulent — and a company displaying an ABTA logo isn't automatically genuine either, since logos can be copied. Treat ABTA membership as one check among several: verify any claimed membership directly with ABTA, look up the company on Companies House, and confirm what financial protection your booking has.

**I got a call saying I've won a free cruise — is it real?**

Be very cautious. A genuine prize never requires you to pay a fee, "taxes" or "port charges", make a premium-rate call, or hand over card details to claim it. "Free cruise" prize scams use exactly those demands to take your money or your details. If you didn't enter a competition you have almost certainly not won anything. Don't pay, don't share card or personal details, and if you can, report it — forward a scam text to 7726, and report a call or email to Report Fraud (in Scotland, Police Scotland on 101).

**I've paid a deposit for a cruise that turned out to be fake — can I get my money back?**

It depends on how you paid and how fast you act. If you paid by credit card, ask your provider about a Section 75 claim (a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and no more than £30,000). If you paid by debit card, ask about a chargeback. If you paid by UK bank transfer on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory APP fraud reimbursement rules may apply — ask your bank to assess the claim, within the 13-month window. Report the scam to Report Fraud (or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland) and keep all your evidence and reference numbers.

**How can I tell a fake cruise booking website from the real one?**

Don't reach the site by clicking an ad, email or text link — type the cruise line's or agent's address yourself, or use a trusted search result, and check the full domain carefully, as clone sites copy the branding but use a slightly different web address. Look for verifiable UK company details you can cross-check on Companies House, a genuine landline, and clear answers about which line operates the sailing and what protection applies. If a site pushes you to pay by bank transfer or reroutes you away from a card payment, don't enter your details — report it to the NCSC's report-a-scam-website service.

## Fake Airline Ticket Scam UK: Spot a Bargain Flight Con

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-airline-ticket-scam-uk/
Category: Travel Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Found flights far cheaper than anywhere else, advertised on social media or by a 'travel agent'? How to spot a fake airline ticket scam and report it.

### What a fake airline ticket scam looks like

A fake airline ticket scam advertises flights far cheaper than any genuine airline or travel site, often through social media or an unofficial "agent", then takes payment for tickets that do not exist or never get issued. An example of the style is: `Return flights to Dubai, £89pp all in - limited seats, book direct with me to avoid booking fees.`

You may receive a convincing-looking but fake booking confirmation, only to discover later that no booking exists. This guide shows the warning signs, how to book safely, and what to do if you have already paid.

### Why these scams are convincing

An unusually low price for a popular route is tempting, especially near school holidays or for in-demand destinations, and a fake booking reference or PDF confirmation can look identical to a genuine one. A seller who claims to have bulk or agent-rate tickets sounds like they have inside access to a deal you cannot get elsewhere.

The fact that protects you: only the airline can tell you whether a reservation and a ticket really exist. Its "manage my booking" service is the quick first check, but a reference that does not appear there is a warning rather than a verdict, because some legitimate agent, group, charter and partner bookings are not fully visible in self-service tools. Ask the airline itself before you rely on any confirmation.

### Signs a flight deal is a scam

- The price is far below any genuine airline or comparison site for the same route and dates.
- You are asked to pay by bank transfer to a personal account rather than through the airline or an established travel site.
- The seller found you on social media, or advertises through an unofficial page or group.
- You are pressured to book quickly because seats are "almost gone".
- The airline cannot confirm a reservation or ticket when you contact it using details from its own site.
- The seller avoids identifying the travel company, or for a flight-inclusive package, its ATOL details.

### How the scam works

First, an advert or message offers a bargain flight deal. Second, you pay, usually by bank transfer, to secure the "discounted" seats. Third, you may receive a fake booking confirmation that looks genuine. Fourth, when you check with the airline directly, no booking exists. Finally, the seller stops responding.

Asking the airline itself to confirm the reservation and the ticket, before you rely on any confirmation, breaks the chain.

### How to book flights safely

Book through the airline directly or a recognised travel agent.

- Book through the airline's own website or app, or a well-known travel agent, not a personal seller found on social media.
- Put any booking reference into the airline's "manage my booking" page, and contact the airline directly if it does not appear or the itinerary is incomplete.
- Be suspicious of a price dramatically below every other source for the same flight.
- Prefer paying by card, which offers more practical dispute options than a bank transfer.
- If you are buying a package trip that includes a flight, check whether the travel company is ATOL protected and who the ATOL holder is.

If you are unsure, our /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ and /guides/fake-travel-agent-scam-uk/ guides cover related travel-booking cons.

### If you have already paid

Try the reference and passenger name on the airline's own manage-booking page and screenshot the result. If it is not recognised, contact the airline using details from its official site and ask it to confirm whether a valid reservation and ticket exist. Keep both the lookup result and the airline's response for your bank.

Then contact your bank or card issuer the same day, keep the seller's messages and the confirmation PDF, and follow the payment, account and identity steps in the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### How to report a fake airline ticket scam (UK)

Report the seller's page or advert inside the platform that hosted it, and tell the airline whose name appeared on the confirmation, using the contact route on its own site. Ask it to verify whether any booking exists and let it know its brand is being used to sell tickets.

Money lost belongs in a fraud report: Police Scotland takes reports on 101 in Scotland, and `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Forwarding routes for a scam email or text, and what to do after reporting, are in the [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/).

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it ever genuine to buy flights from someone on social media?**

Treat it as high risk. Book directly through the airline or a recognised travel agent instead. A stranger offering bargain flights on social media is a common scam pattern.

**I have a booking confirmation - does that mean the flight is real?**

No. Check the reference and passenger name on the airline's own site, then contact the airline if the booking is missing or incomplete. Some legitimate agent, group, charter and partner bookings are not fully visible in self-service tools, so a failed lookup is a warning rather than final proof. Ask the airline to confirm whether a valid booking and e-ticket exist.

**Does ATOL cover every flight booking?**

No. A flight bought directly from an airline, where a valid e-ticket is issued in exchange for payment, is not covered by ATOL. Some flight-only bookings made through an ATOL holder can be protected, and the certificate you receive then says "Flight-Only". ATOL's main role is protecting flight-inclusive package trips, so ask the travel company to make the position clear before you book.

**I've already paid for tickets that turned out to be fake - can I get my money back?**
