Tell the caller you will call your supplier back, hang up, and redial using the number on your bill or your supplier's official website. If the call was genuine, your supplier will have a record of it and the next steps will be the same. If no record exists, you have just avoided a scam with no downside.

**What is the customer password scheme and how do I set one up?**

The customer password scheme lets you register a secret word with your energy supplier. Any engineer visiting your home will state this word at the door before you open it fully; if they cannot state it, you can safely refuse entry. Not all suppliers offer this — contact your supplier to ask. If it is available, setting one up is straightforward and costs nothing.

**I let someone into my home to inspect my meter and I am now worried. What should I do?**

Call your energy supplier immediately and report that an individual accessed your meter, asking whether they have any record of an authorised visit. Check your online account for any changes to your direct debit amount or contact details. If you believe you were robbed or the visitor was fraudulent, call the police on 101. Also report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

**The caller said my smart meter is causing a fire or gas risk — should I be worried?**

If you have a genuine concern about a gas emergency — a smell of gas, a visibly damaged meter — call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 using the number you have looked up yourself. For an electricity emergency, call 105. Do not use any number provided by the person who called you. If the only source of the claimed emergency is an unsolicited caller, treat it as a scam and hang up.

**How do I report a smart meter scam call in the UK?**

Report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. If you received a suspicious text about your meter, forward it to 7726. If someone visited your home without authorisation, also report it to the police on 101. The consumer service for your nation can assist with any billing issues that resulted from the scam: Citizens Advice in England and Wales, `energyadvice.scot` in Scotland, or the Consumer Council in Northern Ireland.

## Solar Panel Scam UK: Fake Online Deals & Grants

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/solar-panel-scam-uk/
Category: Utility Scams · Updated: 2026-07-23

A social media ad claims a government scheme covers free solar panels? No checked scheme works that way — here's how to verify before signing.

### What an online solar panel scam looks like

This scam is a social media advert or lead-generation website promising free or heavily subsidised solar panels through a vague "government scheme", asking you to submit your contact details before any real conversation happens. An example of the style: `You may qualify for free solar panels under a new government initiative — enter your postcode to check eligibility.` A related version pressures you into signing a finance or leasing agreement quickly, or contacts you later claiming an urgent paid warranty renewal is due.

### Why these ads are convincing

Genuine UK schemes touching home energy and renewables do exist, including the Energy Company Obligation, the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, and the Smart Export Guarantee. That means a scheme-sounding name isn't automatically fake. What is unsupported is the idea that those schemes hand out free solar panels simply for filling in a quick online form.

### Signs an online solar offer is a scam

- It claims to be a direct government grant covering free solar panels, with no specific scheme named or checkable.
- You're asked to submit contact details on a lead-generation form before any genuine conversation about your property.
- You're pushed to sign a finance or leasing agreement quickly, without time to get independent advice.
- You're contacted later claiming an urgent, paid warranty renewal is needed.
- The installer isn't MCS-certified, or won't confirm it when asked.

### How the scam works step by step

First, an online advert or lead-generation site promises free or heavily subsidised solar panels tied to a vague scheme. Second, you submit your details, triggering a high-pressure sales call pushing a quick decision or a finance agreement. Third, you may be signed into an unsuitable or overpriced leasing arrangement, or simply have your details sold on to other installers and cold-callers. Later, a separate warranty-renewal scam may follow, using a similar sense of urgency.

### How to check a solar offer safely

Check what a scheme genuinely covers directly on gov.uk or Ofgem's own pages, rather than trusting an advert's description of it.

- Confirm any installer is MCS-certified using the official MCS installer search.
- If you sign a contract away from a trader's business premises or at a distance, check the cancellation rights in your paperwork and don't let anyone rush you past them.
- This page covers online and advertised solar offers. If you've had an unsolicited phone call or doorstep visit instead, the cold-call/doorstep pattern needs separate checks.

### If you've already signed an agreement or paid

If you're still within your cancellation window, you may be able to withdraw from the agreement; check the paperwork for the exact deadline and process. If you paid by card, contact your bank or card provider about a chargeback or, for a qualifying credit-card payment, a Section 75 claim. If you entered a finance agreement you're unhappy with, contact the finance provider directly to raise it.

### How to report an online solar panel scam (UK)

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is there a genuine government scheme that pays for free solar panels?**

I found no current UK scheme that promises free solar panels to anyone who completes a simple online postcode form. ECO4 (which runs until 31 December 2026) can include solar PV in specific eligible projects and households; it is not a universal free-panel offer. The Boiler Upgrade Scheme supports eligible heat-pump or biomass-boiler installations, while the Smart Export Guarantee pays eligible generators for exported electricity rather than paying for every installation. Check the current rules on GOV.UK or Ofgem and verify the installer independently.

**How do I check a solar panel installer is genuinely certified?**

Use the official MCS installer search to confirm the installer holds genuine certification before agreeing to anything.

**How is this different from a solar panel cold call or doorstep visit?**

This page covers online adverts and lead-generation sites. An unsolicited phone call or doorstep visit has different warning signs and should be treated as its own scam pattern.

**I've already signed a solar finance agreement I regret — can I cancel?**

Check the paperwork for cancellation rights and deadlines. If the agreement included credit, contact the finance provider as well as the trader.

**How do I report an online solar panel scam?**

Report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

## Fake ASOS Website Scam UK: Spot a Copycat Store

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/asos-copycat-scam-uk/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-26

Found an ASOS-looking site with huge discounts from a social ad? How to spot a fake ASOS copycat website, buy safely, and report it in the UK.

### ASOS plus a sale word decides nothing

ASOS says ordinary ASOS shopping takes place at `asos.com`, but its UK help page also identifies `asossamplesale.com` as the official ASOS Sample Sale. A name containing ASOS, outlet, sale or clearance is therefore neither proof of legitimacy nor proof of fraud. Start from ASOS's UK Customer Care page and follow the official link it publishes.

The Sample Sale help pages put it plainly: ASOS Sample Sale is part of ASOS.com, and the Sample Sale terms say the contract is with ASOS.com Limited and that all products offered there are ASOS products. That is why a word test cannot work in either direction — reading the letters in an address will not separate an ASOS-run sale from somebody else's shop wearing ASOS branding. What replaces it is a habit: reach an address the way ASOS publishes it, not the way an advert offers it.

### The verification route, step by step

- Open a fresh tab and type `asos.com` by hand. Do not arrive from a search advert, a social post, an email or a message.
- Go to Customer Care from there, and look for the official links ASOS itself publishes for shopping and for its Sample Sale.
- Compare the address you were sent against the one ASOS publishes, character for character. A near miss is a miss.
- If it appears nowhere in ASOS's own help pages, treat it as unverified and keep your card details to yourself.
- Still unsure? Ask ASOS Customer Care through the official site before paying, not after.

This works because it takes your judgement out of the loop. Copied logos, lifted product photography and a working basket are cheap to assemble, so how convincing a page looks carries almost no information — where you got the address from carries all of it. NCSC guidance on shopping and paying safely online makes the same point about deceptive shopping sites: navigate to a retailer independently instead of trusting a link you were handed.

### Reading a web address, and what that can and cannot settle

Reading an address is worth learning, as long as you know what it proves. The owner is the part immediately to the left of the first single slash. In `asos.shop-deals.example/sale` the owner is `shop-deals.example`, and every character further left — brand names included — is decoration chosen by whoever holds it.

These are warning signs to resolve against ASOS's own help pages, never verdicts on their own:
- The brand pushed into a subdomain, so it reads as ASOS at a glance.
- The right name with a different ending welded on, such as `.shop`, `.online` or `.com.co`.
- A country or year tag that makes the address look like a regional ASOS site.
- A brand plus sale word combination — the one that genuinely cannot be read, because ASOS publishes its own Sample Sale address.
- A padlock in the address bar, which certifies encryption and nothing about honesty. Certificates are free.

### Checking an `asos.com` order, and the limit of that check

An order placed through `asos.com` should appear in the correct ASOS account under My Orders. ASOS Sample Sale orders use a separate account and do not appear there. If an expected `asos.com` order is missing, check that you used the right account and contact ASOS Customer Care through the official site before deciding what happened.

ASOS documents where an ordinary order lives: My Account, then My Orders, then Track parcel, with the estimated delivery date shown in the account and in the confirmation email. ASOS Sample Sale is explicit that its orders sit outside that view — you will not see Sample Sale orders on an ASOS.com account, and viewing them means creating a separate Sample Sale account. A blank My Orders page is therefore a prompt to check which account and which ASOS service you used, not evidence that nothing was bought from ASOS.

Treat the messages around an order the same way. ASOS's help pages warn that people impersonate it through social media, free webmail accounts, WhatsApp and fake sites, and say ASOS contacts customers through an ASOS-branded email address or a verified social account. A confirmation email proves little on its own, because whoever built a fake shop also wrote its emails.

### If you entered personal details on a site you now doubt

A fashion checkout collects more than a card number: a name, a delivery address, a contact number, often a password for a new account. Rather than guessing what will be done with any of it, treat what you typed as exposed and close the openings you control.

- Change the password anywhere you reused whatever you set on that site, starting with the email account attached to it.
- If card details went in, ring your card issuer on the number printed on the card or shown in its own app, and ask about stopping the card and watching the account.
- Keep the confirmation page and everything that arrives afterwards, and check any claim about the order by returning to the address you typed yourself.

Cifas Protective Registration is a narrower step, not a routine response to every suspicious checkout. It is a paid service running for two years that places a warning flag against your name and details so participating organisations carry out extra checks, and Cifas presents it as a measure for people at heightened risk of identity fraud. It is not insurance, and it does not guarantee every application in your name will be checked.

### Legal rights may be hard to enforce against an untraceable seller

Statutory rights do not vanish because a trader used a brand's name without permission. GOV.UK sets out the usual distance-sale sequence for an online purchase: tell the trader you are cancelling within 14 days of receiving the goods, send them back within a further 14 days, and receive the refund within 14 days of the trader receiving the goods or evidence that you returned them. The standard delivery charge you paid is refundable, and exceptions and possible deductions still apply.

The difficulty is the trader, not the right. A cancellation notice needs somebody to serve it on, and a seller hiding behind a lookalike address may not reply, may publish no returns address, and may not be identifiable at all. Where a reply does arrive and makes the refund conditional on confirming your card number, or on installing software so the money can be sent, that is a continuation of the same approach rather than a resolution — and your realistic route then runs through the payment instead of the seller.

### If you already paid

Screenshot the shop while it is still standing — the product page, the basket total, the address bar — and keep the advert or message that delivered you there. Sites like this are built to disappear.

Then look at how the money left. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may apply, never automatically, to a purchase funded by credit. It needs the required relationship between the credit and the supplier, plus a cash price — counted per item, or per qualifying set — of more than £100 and no more than £30,000. MoneyHelper explains that an intermediary in the payment chain can affect whether cover exists at all, and the Financial Ombudsman Service has reported that misunderstanding credit protection has cost consumers money. So a £45 clothing order sits under the price test whatever card paid for it, and a credit card alone does not make a claim valid.

Chargeback is a card-scheme process rather than a statutory entitlement, with rules and deadlines set by the scheme, so raise it with your issuer promptly instead of waiting to see whether a parcel turns up. Money sent by bank transfer for clothing is the hardest version of this: tell your bank the same day.

If poor-quality goods did arrive, keep them — they are evidence, and [what a counterfeit means for a refund](/guides/fake-ray-ban-website-scam-uk/) is covered separately. The [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) puts the payment, account and identity steps in order.

### Where to report a copycat ASOS shop

Tell ASOS through the Customer Care pages you reach by typing `asos.com`, so the brand knows the address is circulating. Then use the public routes:

- A suspicious website goes to the NCSC, through its reporting form for scam websites.
- A paid advert goes to the Advertising Standards Authority. Flagging it inside the platform that served it is a useful extra step rather than a substitute.
- A phishing email goes to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.
- A suspicious SMS text can be forwarded to 7726 free of charge, and your mobile network will look into the sender.
- Lost money belongs in a fraud report. Report Fraud takes them online at `reportfraud.police.uk` and on 0300 123 2040; readers in Scotland should call Police Scotland on 101 instead.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is `asossamplesale.com` a real ASOS website?**

Yes. ASOS's Sample Sale help pages say ASOS Sample Sale is part of ASOS.com, and its terms say the contract is with ASOS.com Limited and that all products offered there are ASOS products. That is exactly why the word test fails: an address pairing the ASOS name with a sale word can be genuine. Confirm any address from ASOS's UK Customer Care page rather than from the words in it.

**An advert sent me to an "ASOS outlet" address. Is it a copycat?**

Not automatically, and not automatically genuine either. Because ASOS publishes its own Sample Sale address, the words prove nothing in either direction. Open a fresh tab, type `asos.com`, go to Customer Care and see whether the address you were sent matches a link ASOS itself publishes. If it does not appear there, do not pay.

**I received an order confirmation email. Doesn't that make the shop real?**

Not on its own, because whoever built a fake shop also wrote its emails. ASOS says it contacts customers through an ASOS-branded email address or a verified social media account, so free webmail or a WhatsApp number announcing itself as ASOS customer care does not match that description. Check the order in the account it was placed with, and ask ASOS Customer Care through the official site.

**My order is not in My Orders. Does that prove no order was placed with ASOS?**

No. An order placed through `asos.com` should appear in the correct ASOS account under My Orders, but ASOS Sample Sale orders use a separate Sample Sale account and do not appear there. Check that you signed in to the right account, then contact ASOS Customer Care through the official site before deciding what happened.

**Is `asos.shop-deals.example` an ASOS address?**

No. The owner of a web address is the part immediately to the left of the first single slash, which here is `shop-deals.example`. Everything further left, brand names included, is decoration the site chose for itself. Reading the address this way rules an address out; confirming one in ASOS's own help pages is what rules it in.

**I paid £45 by debit card and nothing arrived. Where does that leave me?**

Below the Section 75 cash-price test, which needs more than £100, and on a debit card rather than a credit agreement. Ask your bank about chargeback instead, since card schemes set their own rules and deadlines for it, and raise it promptly. Report the loss as well so the site is on record.

**Is it worth reporting a copycat if I never bought anything?**

Yes, and it costs nothing. Send the address to the NCSC through its reporting form for scam websites, tell ASOS through its Customer Care pages, and take a paid advert to the Advertising Standards Authority as well as reporting it inside the platform that ran it.

## Fake Nike Website Scam UK: Spot a Counterfeit Shop

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-nike-website-uk/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Found a Nike site with huge discounts you reached from a social ad? How to spot a fake Nike website, buy safely, and report it in the UK.

### No single signal decides it — weigh several together

Trainer advice usually opens with the discount. The more useful opening is that no single fact about a sneaker listing settles the question, so the method has to be a risk screen rather than a test with one answer.

Availability that conflicts with how Nike released a shoe is genuinely useful evidence. It is not proof, because Nike does not sell only through its own app and site: it refers to Nike-authorised retailers, and stock also reaches resale sellers who acquired it lawfully. So collect several signals and read how they combine:
- Seller identity, established away from the seller's own website and advertising.
- Release history: does this exact shoe, in these sizes, square with how and when Nike released it?
- Price, read against both retail and the current resale market rather than retail alone.
- Payment method, and whether it leaves you any route back.
- Returns and complaints information, and whether it names a company you can look up.
- The domain, opened by typing it rather than by following a link.

One weak signal is a reason to look harder. Several at once — an unfamiliar seller, a scarce release, a full size run, a price far below the market and a payment method with no recourse — is the pattern to walk away from.

### How Nike releases coveted shoes, and where else they legitimately appear

Nike describes SNKRS as its destination for highly coveted releases, and its help pages document a launch calendar, SNKRS Drawings and SNKRS Pass reservations. In a Drawing you enter inside a window and learn afterwards whether you were selected. A SNKRS Pass reserves a pair, and Nike's own SNKRS material says selected pairs may be reserved for collection at a nearby retailer, not only at a Nike store. SNKRS Reserve works differently again: it can make sizes to order during a limited pre-order window.

That is why the release mechanism is a lead rather than a conclusion. A shop holding stock of a sold-out shoe is not describing something impossible, so check the specific release in Nike's launch calendar and then check the specific seller. Do not accept a seller's own claim to be authorised: Nike lists its own stores in a retail directory, and an established sports retailer is something you can confirm away from its advertising. Allocation, date and provenance all still need checking on the individual listing.

### Genuine resale is not the same thing as counterfeit

Paying more than retail for a sold-out pair is a normal, lawful transaction. Resale is an established market, scarcity genuinely pushes prices up, and a high asking price is not by itself a fraud signal.

The risk lives in the seller and the payment rather than in the figure. Above retail, from a seller whose authentication process you can examine, is a premium you are choosing to pay. Brand new, in every size, well under the market, from a site you had not heard of yesterday, is the combination worth refusing.

Scale and familiarity are not verification either. In 2024 Nike and Converse brought a US lawsuit against alleged counterfeiting networks; reporting on that case describes 52 alleged networks operating 98 websites and 267 social media handles. Separately, Nike has taken legal action against StockX. Neither of those is a judgement on any listing in front of you. They are only a reason not to treat a platform's size as a substitute for checking a seller.

### Factory, outlet and clearance are not the test

Nike operates genuine Factory and Clearance stores and lists its UK stores in its own retail directory, so the word in a domain is not the finding. What matters is whether the address is exactly the one Nike publishes, and whether the company behind an unfamiliar one can be identified at all.

- Type the address by hand. `nike.com` opened yourself is not the same thing as a lookalike reached from an advert.
- Check any address you were sent against Nike's own help pages and store directory, which you get to from the address you typed, rather than against a search result.
- Identify the company independently. A named, established sports retailer can be checked away from its own site; an anonymous shop cannot.
- Prefer a payment route with recourse, because bank transfer, cryptocurrency and gift-card codes remove yours.
- Read the returns and complaints information and ask whether a real business could operate on it.

### What happens if counterfeit goods reach the UK border

GOV.UK sets out the process. Border Force can detain goods it suspects infringe intellectual property rights. Under the standard procedure, where the rights holder confirms the goods infringe and the importer or owner agrees or does not respond, the goods can be destroyed. An objection can instead lead to court proceedings or to the goods being released, so a rights holder's confirmation does not automatically close every case. Small postal or courier consignments can follow a separate simplified procedure. The Government's customs intellectual property enforcement report covering 2021 to 2023 says destruction was the main outcome for articles confirmed as counterfeit.

For a shopper the practical reading is blunt: money paid overseas for counterfeit goods can end up buying nothing at all, with no seller left to argue with.

### The unexpected customs fee

Do not pay through an unexpected customs link. Check the parcel directly with the courier using contact details you obtained independently. Genuine import VAT or duty may be collected by the parcel company, while confirmed counterfeit goods are handled through the Border Force infringement process rather than released because a shopper pays a surprise fee.

GOV.UK explains when VAT, customs duty and handling charges apply to goods sent from abroad, so a charge existing at all is not the tell. What marks out the scam version is the route it arrives by: an unexpected message, a short deadline, and a payment page you did not reach by going to the parcel company yourself.

### If you already paid

Keep the shoes and the box if anything arrived, together with the order page, the advert and any tracking reference. Do not assume Nike will authenticate them for you — its public help material does not promise that its ordinary contact channels will inspect a suspected counterfeit. Report the seller through the contact route on `nike.com`, hold on to the physical evidence, and ask your nation's consumer service or your card issuer what to do next.

On the money: a Section 75 claim under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may be available on a credit-funded purchase. It depends on the required relationship between the credit and the supplier, and on a cash price — per item, or per qualifying set — of more than £100 and no more than £30,000. A £160 pair might therefore fall inside it where the identical pair bought on a debit card does not, but the figure and the card type do not settle a claim between them; MoneyHelper is the place to read what a covered arrangement looks like. Debit purchases lean on chargeback, governed by each card scheme's own rules and deadlines rather than by statute. A bank transfer to a shop that has stopped replying needs a call to your bank immediately.

Citizens Advice sets out the refund position for counterfeit goods. That guidance is published as advice for England, with its own Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland versions, so use the one for your nation. Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) puts these steps in order.

### Reporting a fake Nike shop

One limitation worth stating plainly: several third-party sites publish Nike brand-protection email addresses that we could not match against Nike's own published contacts, so we do not repeat them here. Use the contact route on `nike.com`, reached by typing the address in yourself.

- The web address itself goes to the NCSC, through its scam-website reporting form.
- Phishing emails go to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.
- A suspicious SMS text can be forwarded to 7726, free of charge.
- Paid adverts are the Advertising Standards Authority's remit; the platform that ran one should hear about it as well.
- Money lost goes into a Report Fraud report — `reportfraud.police.uk`, or 0300 123 2040. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101 instead.
- Counterfeit goods have a route of their own. The consumer service for your nation may refer or share relevant complaint information with Trading Standards or another appropriate enforcement body: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.

### Frequently asked questions

**A site has a sold-out release in every size at half price. Is that possible?**

It is a high-risk claim, especially after a scarce release has sold out, but it is not impossible by definition. Check the exact release in Nike's launch calendar, verify whether the seller is an established retailer, and do not rely on the seller's own claim that it is authorised.

**Is paying above retail on a resale platform a scam?**

Not in itself. Resale is a legitimate market and scarcity genuinely pushes prices up. The risk lives in the seller's authentication process and in your payment protection, not in the fact that the figure exceeds what Nike charged.

**What is SNKRS, and does buying elsewhere mean a shop is fake?**

SNKRS is Nike's destination for highly coveted releases, with a launch calendar, Drawings and Pass reservations, and SNKRS Reserve can make sizes to order in a limited pre-order window. It is not the only route. Nike refers to Nike-authorised retailers, and a SNKRS Pass can reserve selected pairs at a nearby retailer, so buying elsewhere proves nothing on its own.

**Could customs really destroy trainers I have paid for?**

Border Force can detain goods it suspects infringe intellectual property rights, and under the standard process they can be destroyed where the rights holder confirms infringement and the importer or owner agrees or does not respond. An objection can lead to proceedings or release instead. Government reporting covering 2021 to 2023 says destruction was the main outcome for articles confirmed as counterfeit.

**A message says my parcel is held and a fee is due. Is that always a scam?**

Not always, because genuine import VAT or duty may be collected by the parcel company. Do not pay through an unexpected link, though. Check the parcel with the courier on contact details you obtained independently. Confirmed counterfeit goods are handled through the Border Force infringement process rather than released because a shopper pays a surprise fee.

**How do I report the shop to Nike itself?**

Through the contact route on `nike.com`, opened by typing the address. We print no brand-protection email address, because the ones circulating on third-party sites could not be matched against Nike's own published contacts. Do not expect Nike's ordinary contact channels to authenticate your shoes; keep them as evidence instead.

## Fake Online Pharmacy UK: Spot an Illegal Medicine Site

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-online-pharmacy-uk-scam/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-23

Found a site selling prescription medicine cheaply with no prescription needed? How to spot a fake online pharmacy, check it, and report it.

### What a fake online pharmacy looks like

A fake online pharmacy sells prescription-only medicines without a proper prescription or clinical check, or supplies counterfeit, expired, wrongly dosed, or contaminated medicines. These sites often look professional and may be advertised by email, search, or social media. An example of the style is: `No prescription needed! Genuine medication delivered discreetly to your door - up to 80% cheaper than UK pharmacies.`

The medicines can be fake or dangerous, and your card and personal details may also be harvested. This guide shows the warning signs, how to check a pharmacy is genuine, and what to do if you have already ordered.

### Why these sites are convincing

Lower prices, no need for an appointment, and discreet delivery are all genuinely appealing, especially for medicines people feel embarrassed to ask a doctor or pharmacist about. Professional branding, customer reviews, and payment logos can make an illegal site look just as credible as a real pharmacy.

The rule that protects you: a genuine UK pharmacy will not supply a prescription-only medicine unless there is a valid prescription or another lawful clinical route. A site promising prescription-only medicine with no prescription and no meaningful clinical check is unsafe.

### Signs an online pharmacy is fake

- It sells prescription-only medicines with no prescription or clinical consultation required.
- Prices are far below normal UK pharmacy prices.
- There is no verifiable UK address, registered pharmacist, or contact number.
- It uses pressure tactics such as limited stock or time-limited discounts.
- The website has spelling errors, a generic template look, or an unusual web address.
- It arrived by unsolicited email or a social-media ad rather than a search for a known pharmacy.
- You cannot find the business on the pharmacy register for its part of the UK (the GPhC register for Great Britain, or the PSNI register for Northern Ireland).

### How the scam works

First, an ad, email, or search result offers cheap medicine with no prescription. Second, you order and pay, often by card. Third, you either receive nothing, receive counterfeit or wrongly dosed medicine, or your card and personal details are used for fraud. Fourth, there is no genuine pharmacist to contact if something goes wrong.

Checking the seller against official registers before you order is the safest protection.

### How to check an online pharmacy is genuine

Do not order from a site just because it looks professional or appears in an advert.

- Check the pharmacy is registered on the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC) register for England, Scotland, and Wales, or the Pharmaceutical Society of Northern Ireland (PSNI) register for Northern Ireland.
- For Northern Ireland-based sellers only, also check the MHRA's register of online medicine sellers — since 1 January 2021 that register no longer covers Great Britain, so a genuine GB pharmacy will not appear on it.
- In Great Britain, do not rely on an EU-style distance-selling logo as proof of legitimacy; MHRA says the GB logo scheme stopped from 1 January 2021. Northern Ireland has separate rules, so still verify the seller directly.
- Never buy a prescription-only medicine from a site that avoids a genuine prescription or lawful clinical assessment.
- Check the MHRA's official 'Not Recommended' list of suspicious online medicine sellers at gov.uk/check-suspicious-online-medicine-seller — being on it is a clear do-not-buy sign.
- Be suspicious of prices far below normal UK prices and of sites you cannot verify independently.
- If in doubt, use the NHS website or a pharmacy you already know.

If you are unsure whether a linked site is genuine, our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/ helps, and our /guides/fake-pandora-website-uk-scam/ guide covers the same pattern with counterfeit goods.

### If you have already ordered

Do not take any medicine from an unverified source if you have concerns about what it contains. Speak to a pharmacist, GP, or NHS 111 if you are unsure what you have taken or feel unwell; call 999 in an emergency.

### How to report a fake online pharmacy (UK)

Report a suspicious online seller of medicines to the MHRA through the GOV.UK suspicious online medicine seller reporting service. If you think a medicine or medical device is fake, falsified, defective, or has caused a side effect or adverse incident, report that through MHRA Yellow Card.

If the scam reached you by email, forward it to the NCSC at `report@phishing.gov.uk`; if by text, forward it to 7726. If you lost money or shared sensitive information, report it to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. Keep all the evidence, including any medicine received.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is buying from an online pharmacy ever safe in the UK?**

Yes, if it is a genuine registered pharmacy and the medicine is supplied through a lawful route. Check the pharmacy register for your part of the UK before ordering — the GPhC register for England, Scotland, and Wales, or the PSNI register in Northern Ireland (where the MHRA's online medicine seller register also applies).

**A site sells prescription medicine with no prescription needed - is that legal?**

Treat it as unsafe. Prescription-only medicine should not be supplied without a valid prescription or another lawful clinical route. A site advertising "no prescription" medicine is a major red flag.

**How do I check if an online pharmacy is genuinely registered?**

Search for the pharmacy on the GPhC register for England, Scotland, and Wales, or the PSNI register for Northern Ireland. The MHRA's online medicine seller register covers Northern Ireland-based sellers only, so do not treat a GB pharmacy's absence from it as a scam sign.

**I've taken medicine from a site I'm now unsure about - what should I do?**

Seek medical advice if you feel unwell or are unsure what you have taken. Keep the packaging and order details, contact your bank if you paid by card, and report the site.

**How do I report a fake online pharmacy?**

Report suspicious online medicine sellers to the MHRA through GOV.UK. Use Yellow Card for suspected fake, falsified, defective, or side-effect/adverse incident reports. Forward scam emails to `report@phishing.gov.uk` and scam texts to 7726. If you lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

## Fake Pandora Website UK: Spot a Counterfeit Jewellery Site

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-pandora-website-uk-scam/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

A 'Pandora' site selling charms at huge discounts? Check pandora.net and Pandora's authorised-retailer guidance before entering card details.

### What a fake Pandora website looks like

A fake Pandora website copies Pandora's branding, product photos, and layout, then advertises steep discounts — often 50% or more off — to draw in bargain hunters, usually via a social media ad or a link in a search result. An example of the style is: `HUGE CLEARANCE SALE — up to 70% off all Pandora charms and bracelets. Ends tonight!`

Orders are taken and paid for, but items either never arrive, arrive as cheap counterfeits, or the site vanishes shortly after taking payment.

### Why these sites are convincing

Fake shops copy genuine product photos and branding directly from Pandora's real site, so the goods look authentic in listings. A large discount and a countdown timer create urgency that discourages the pause needed to check the site properly.

Pandora's brand-protection guidance says its two official websites are `pandoragroup.com` and `pandora.net`, and that Pandora products are also sold through authorised retailers. It also says Pandora does not authorise retailers to sell its jewellery on internet auction sites and does not authenticate jewellery bought from unauthorised retailers or online retailers — so a bargain listing outside Pandora's own channels carries real risk even before you consider whether the site itself is fake.

### Signs a Pandora website is fake

- The web address is not `pandora.net` and is not a retailer you can verify through Pandora's authorised-retailer guidance.
- Discounts are unusually large across the entire range, not a specific, time-limited genuine promotion.
- There's no verifiable company registration, physical address, or working contact details.
- Payment is requested only by bank transfer, rather than by card or a recognised payment provider.
- Reviews are missing, all suspiciously positive, or copied from elsewhere.
- The site was found through a social media ad rather than a search for Pandora directly.

### How the scam works step by step

First, an ad or search result leads you to a site using Pandora's name and product images. Second, a large discount and urgency push you to order quickly, without checking the site itself. Third, you pay — usually by card, sometimes by bank transfer if asked. Fourth, the item never arrives, arrives as a counterfeit, or the site disappears entirely, and further contact attempts go unanswered.

Checking the web address against `pandora.net` and Pandora's authorised-retailer guidance before paying anything breaks the chain.

### How to check a Pandora website safely

Do not enter card or personal details until you've checked the site.

- Go to `pandora.net` directly, or use Pandora's official store locator to find an authorised retailer, rather than following a link from an ad.
- Look for a UK company registration, verifiable using the free Companies House register, and genuine contact details.
- Be suspicious of sitewide discounts far beyond anything Pandora's own site or known retailers are running.
- Pay by credit card where possible — for a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and no more than £30,000, Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act makes your card provider jointly responsible if goods don't arrive or aren't as described; for debit cards or lower amounts, ask your card provider about chargeback instead.

### If you've already paid or shared details

If you paid by a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and no more than £30,000, contact your card provider and ask about a Section 75 claim. For debit cards or lower amounts, ask about chargeback instead. Counterfeit goods are not as described, but enforcing consumer rights against a fake or disappearing seller can be difficult — keep the item, packaging, order confirmation, screenshots, and payment records as evidence.

If you shared personal or card details on a fake site, monitor your statements for unrecognised transactions and contact your bank if you spot any.

### How to report a fake Pandora website (UK)

Report the site to Pandora directly through its brand-protection reporting route at `pandoragroup.com`, including the web address, screenshots, and your receipt or order confirmation if you have one.

For consumer advice, contact the service GOV.UK lists for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262. GOV.UK’s consumer-rights guidance separately says the appropriate helpline can refer a complaint to local Trading Standards or share complaint information with another enforcement authority; whether anyone investigates or takes action depends on the case. If you lost money, report the fraud to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Pandora itself a scam, or just some sellers?**

Pandora is a genuine, established jewellery brand. The scam is fake websites copying its name and photos — Pandora's own guidance says it does not authorise sales through auction sites and does not authenticate items from unauthorised online sellers.

**How do I know if a Pandora website is genuine?**

Pandora's consumer site is `pandora.net`. Use Pandora's store locator or authorised-retailer guidance, and treat any other site — especially one found via a social media ad with steep discounts — with caution.

**I paid by credit card for fake Pandora jewellery — can I get my money back?**

For a qualifying credit-card purchase over £100 and no more than £30,000, ask your provider about a Section 75 claim. For debit cards or lower amounts, ask about chargeback. Keep evidence that the item is counterfeit, not as described, or never arrived.

**The item arrived but looks like a cheap counterfeit — what now?**

Keep the item, packaging, and any order confirmation as evidence, then contact your card provider about a refund and report the site to Pandora and to your nation's consumer service.

**How do I report a fake Pandora website?**

Report it to Pandora through its brand-protection pages at `pandoragroup.com`, to the consumer service for your nation (Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262), and to Report Fraud at `reportfraud.police.uk` or 0300 123 2040 if you lost money. Report Fraud covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland. If you live in Scotland or the crime happened there, contact Police Scotland on 101.

## Fake Ray-Ban Website Scam UK: Spot a Copycat Store

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-ray-ban-website-scam-uk/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Found a Ray-Ban site with huge discounts from a social ad? How to spot a fake Ray-Ban copycat website, buy safely, and report it in the UK.

### A very low price is a warning sign, not a verdict

Counterfeiters copy branding, photography and increasingly the packaging, and the low number is the whole pitch. What that number cannot do is settle the question by itself, because Ray-Ban discounts too: its current UK terms of sale advertise reductions of up to 50% on selected styles. A figure well under the usual one is a reason to stop and check rather than a finding you can act on.

Treat the price as the trigger for the checks instead of the answer to them. Note the exact model on offer — the model number, the frame colour, the lens — then reach Ray-Ban's own site by typing `ray-ban.com` and find that model there. A gap far wider than anything Ray-Ban itself is advertising, on a seller you cannot otherwise verify, is the combination that should end the purchase. On its own, though, no price authenticates or condemns a particular pair of sunglasses.

### What the UK store locator can and cannot confirm

Ray-Ban is an EssilorLuxottica brand and it publishes a UK store locator. That locator does one narrow job well: it confirms that a physical shop a seller names is actually a listed Ray-Ban location. It does not do the wider jobs a seller would like you to assume. It does not show that an unrelated web address belongs to a listed shop, and it is not a complete register of every authorised online seller.

So take a locator match as one piece of evidence, then finish the job separately:
- Look the shop up independently and obtain its contact details for yourself, rather than using the ones printed on the site you are assessing.
- Ring or email the shop on those independently obtained details and ask whether the website is theirs.
- Where a site claims an online affiliation with the brand, ask Ray-Ban Customer Care to confirm it.

A partner badge, a certificate graphic or a registration number dropped into a footer is a claim a site has made about itself. None of it is verification, and none of it substitutes for a check you carried out from the brand's side.

### A documented 2016 social-media campaign, and the current picture

Security researchers at ESET documented one version of this in detail in 2016. In the Facebook campaign they observed, posts spread through compromised accounts and tagged the account holder's friends so a link read as a personal recommendation; advertised discounts ran as high as 90%; and some of the checkout pages sent card details without encryption. That is a historical example of the mechanism, not a description of what any particular advert is doing today.

For the current picture Ray-Ban's own FAQ is the better source. It says counterfeiters operate through websites, marketplaces and social media, and it describes account compromise and misuse of personal data among the harms. Two habits follow from that. Ask a friend on a different channel whether they really posted a sale link before you trust it. And treat a warehouse sale, closing-down sale or clearance event that exists only inside a social feed, with nothing about it on Ray-Ban's own site, as unverified until you have checked it there.

### Physical tells are supporting evidence, never a conclusive test

There is no visual inspection on this page that will authenticate a pair of sunglasses, and it is worth being sceptical of any page that offers one.

Ray-Ban does say that an SKU is usually printed inside the left temple, and it uses that code in its own support process. Checking the code against the same model on the official site is worth doing, and a mismatch is a genuine warning. A matching code is not proof of provenance — a code can be reproduced like anything else printed on a frame.

The same limit applies to etching, hinge feel, frame weight and what is in the box. An inconsistency there is supporting evidence worth taking seriously; a clean pass is not a certificate. If you are genuinely unsure what you are holding, ask the seller for evidence of where the pair came from, and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care what it can tell you about the model. Provenance is the more answerable question, and it is answered by checking the seller rather than by squinting at a lens.

### Limit what a bad outcome costs you

NCSC guidance on shopping and paying safely online covers the part of an eyewear purchase you control most. Before a card number goes into a site you have not verified:
- Reach the site by typing its address, not by following an advert, an email or a social post.
- Use a payment route that leaves you somewhere to go. A shop insisting on bank transfer, cryptocurrency or gift-card codes has removed your recourse deliberately.
- Set a password you use nowhere else if the site makes you create an account.
- Look for named company details, a stated returns address and a complaints route. Be wary where a single web form is the only way to reach anybody.

None of that authenticates the sunglasses. It reduces what a wrong decision costs, which is a different objective and a far more achievable one.

### If a pair has already arrived

Keep the frames, the case, the packaging and any printed insert, and photograph the listing and the advert before both disappear. With counterfeits the goods themselves are the evidence.

Citizens Advice says a buyer has a legal right to a full refund for counterfeit goods within 30 days of paying, with different remedies after that window closes. Its guidance page is written as advice for England and offers separate versions for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so read the one for your own region rather than treating a single page as a UK-wide route. Citizens Advice also points debit-card users towards chargeback and eligible credit-card users towards Section 75. For consumer advice, contact the service GOV.UK lists for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262. GOV.UK’s consumer-rights guidance separately says the appropriate helpline can refer a complaint to local Trading Standards or share complaint information with another enforcement authority; whether anyone investigates or takes action depends on the case.

Eyewear prices sit right on the Section 75 boundary, so read that carefully. A Section 75 claim under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may be available, not guaranteed. It turns on three things: credit funded the purchase, the required credit-to-supplier relationship exists, and the cash price — per item, or per qualifying set — came to more than £100 and no more than £30,000. So a £140 pair charged directly to a qualifying credit arrangement may be covered, while a £96 pair falls under the price floor. A high enough figure plus a credit card is not a guarantee; MoneyHelper's guidance on card protection explains what the arrangement itself has to look like. Chargeback is worth raising either way, though card schemes rather than statute set its rules and deadlines.

Our [scam recovery checklist](/recovery/) covers the card, account and identity steps in sequence.

### Reporting a fake Ray-Ban shop

Ray-Ban runs its own route for reporting a suspicious listing, website, social profile or post: a report-fakes form linked from its FAQ. Reach it by typing `ray-ban.com` and following the brand's own links, never by clicking anything inside the advert. Ray-Ban's FAQ says Luxottica has requested takedowns and works with customs and law enforcement, so a brand report is worth making — alongside the public routes rather than instead of them.

- Submit the web address itself to the NCSC, using its scam-website reporting form.
- Complain to the Advertising Standards Authority about a paid advert, and flag the post inside whichever platform served it.
- Forward a phishing email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.
- Where money has gone: Report Fraud, at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040. Scottish readers report instead to Police Scotland, on 101.

### Frequently asked questions

**Could £29 Ray-Bans ever be a real clearance deal?**

It is a strong warning sign rather than a verdict. Ray-Ban's UK terms of sale currently advertise reductions of up to 50% on selected styles, so genuine discounts do exist, but a figure far below anything Ray-Ban itself offers, from a seller you cannot verify, is a reason to stop rather than to buy. Compare the exact model on `ray-ban.com` and verify the seller before paying.

**How much does the Ray-Ban store locator prove about a seller?**

That a physical shop it lists exists, and little more. The locator does not show that a web address belongs to a listed shop, and it is not a full register of authorised online sellers. Look the shop up independently, ask it on contact details you obtained yourself whether the site is theirs, and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care to confirm any claimed online affiliation.

**The sale link came from a friend's account, so is it safe?**

Not necessarily. ESET documented a 2016 Facebook campaign that spread through compromised accounts and tagged the holder's friends so posts read as personal recommendations, and Ray-Ban's current FAQ says counterfeiters still work through social media. Message your friend on a different channel and ask whether they actually shared it.

**Can I tell a fake from the etching, hinges and weight?**

Not conclusively. Ray-Ban says an SKU is usually inside the left temple and uses it in its own support process, so checking that code against the official site is worthwhile and a mismatch is a real warning. A matching code is still not proof of provenance, and marking or packaging inconsistencies are supporting evidence rather than a verdict. If you are unsure, ask the seller for evidence of origin and ask Ray-Ban Customer Care.

**The sunglasses are clearly counterfeit. What refund can I ask for?**

Citizens Advice says you have a legal right to a full refund for counterfeit goods within 30 days of paying, with different remedies later. That page is written as advice for England, so read the Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland version if that is where you live. Keep the frames and packaging, and report it to your nation's consumer service, which may share suitable complaint information with Trading Standards.

**How do I report a fake Ray-Ban site to the brand?**

Ray-Ban publishes a report-fakes form for a suspicious listing, website, social profile or post, linked from its FAQ. Reach it by typing `ray-ban.com` yourself. Send the address to the NCSC as well, and take a paid advert both to the Advertising Standards Authority and to the platform that ran it.

## Fake SHEIN Website UK: How to Check the Site and Protect Your Details

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/shein-fake-website-scam-uk/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake SHEIN websites can take payments or capture personal details. Check the real UK domain and learn what to do if you entered information.

### What a fake SHEIN website is

A fake retail or phishing site can copy SHEIN's branding, product images and checkout design to persuade visitors to enter account, contact or payment details. Depending on the operation, criminals may use the information for unauthorised transactions or account takeover, take payment without supplying the advertised goods, or redirect the visitor through another deceptive page.

The current official UK storefront is https://www.shein.co.uk/. SHEIN's UK terms identify `shein.co.uk` as the site for the territory and say customers can be redirected to a local site when ordering for another country. A different domain is not the UK storefront, but do not accuse a site of fraud from its name alone: stop, verify independently and report it if it appears deceptive.

### How to check the website

1. Read the full address in the browser. On the UK store, the registrable domain should be `shein.co.uk`; words before or after that boundary can change the destination completely.
2. If a link arrived unexpectedly, do not use it. Open a new tab and type `shein.co.uk` yourself or use the official app obtained from an official app store.
3. Treat the padlock as an encryption indicator only. It does not prove who operates the site.
4. Check the seller's legal and contact information against SHEIN's own pages. SHEIN currently states that UK e-commerce services are provided by Infinite Towers Services Ltd and publishes UK contact details on its company-information page.
5. Compare the promotion in the official site or app. Do not rely on an email, advert or social post as confirmation of its own claim.

Modern public TLS certificates commonly validate control of a domain rather than the honesty or brand identity of the operator. Clicking the padlock and looking for wording such as “issued to SHEIN” is therefore not a reliable authenticity test.

### Warning signs

- A lookalike or misspelled domain rather than `shein.co.uk`.
- An unexpected message or advert using urgency, a prize or an implausible discount to push you to a link.
- A login, payment or verification request that cannot be reproduced after you navigate independently to the official site or app.
- Missing, contradictory or copied contact, returns, privacy or company information.
- A request for passwords, one-time codes or card details outside the checkout or account flow you opened independently.
- Payment by bank transfer, cryptocurrency or gift cards being demanded instead of normal checkout options.
- Broken pages, poor language or inconsistent design. These are clues, not proof; sophisticated phishing pages can look polished.

Do not rely on being logged in already as a test. Sessions expire and genuine services may ask users to sign in or complete additional security checks. SHEIN's terms expressly allow it to require additional account identification or a password reset.

### If you entered payment or login details

Act from a trusted device if possible:

1. Contact your bank or card issuer immediately through its official app, website or the number on the card. Tell it exactly what you entered and follow its advice about freezing or replacing the card.
2. Check transactions and report anything you do not recognise. Ask what card dispute or chargeback route applies; recovery is not guaranteed.
3. Change the SHEIN password through `shein.co.uk` or the official app. If that password was reused, change it on every affected account, starting with your email. Enable two-step verification where available.
4. If you supplied a one-time security code, tell the relevant provider. A replacement card alone may not secure a compromised account.
5. Keep the URL, screenshots, message, order record and payment details for your bank and any report.

For a qualifying direct credit-card purchase with a cash price over £100 and up to £30,000, section 75 may apply. Chargeback may be available for card payments in other situations. If you deliberately sent a UK bank transfer to a fraudster, ask the bank about the APP-scam reimbursement rules; eligibility and exceptions apply.

If you downloaded a file or app from the suspect site, stop using it, run the security checks recommended by your device provider or the NCSC, and change important passwords from a device you trust.

### How to report it

- Submit the URL through the NCSC scam website reporting service at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website.
- Forward the original suspicious email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.
- You can forward a suspicious SMS text to `7726` free of charge. For RCS, iMessage and app messages, use the relevant built-in reporting tool.
- Report suspected loss or theft to Report Fraud at https://www.reportfraud.police.uk/ or `0300 123 2040` in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, contact Police Scotland on `101`.
- Notify SHEIN through the customer-service route reached from `shein.co.uk`, not through the suspect message.
- For consumer guidance, use the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.

### Frequently asked questions

**What is SHEIN's official UK website?**

The current UK storefront is `https://www.shein.co.uk/`. Type it directly rather than trusting a link in an unexpected message.

**Does HTTPS prove the page is genuine?**

No. HTTPS encrypts the connection; it does not establish that the operator is SHEIN or is trustworthy.

**Should I call 159?**

You can use `159` to reach participating banks, but it does not cover every institution or every situation. The most direct option is usually the official number on your card or in your banking app. If calling after a suspicious call, use another phone where possible or make sure the previous call has disconnected.

**Can my bank refund a payment?**

It depends on how you paid and what happened. Contact the provider promptly and ask about unauthorised-payment protection, chargeback, section 75 or APP-scam reimbursement as appropriate.

**Why can fake sites appear in ads or search results?**

Placement is not proof of legitimacy. Criminals can use advertising and search-manipulation techniques, so check the destination domain every time.

## Fake UGG Website UK: How to Spot Counterfeit Boots and Protect Your Money

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/fake-ugg-website-uk/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-30

Fake UGG websites may sell counterfeits or take your money without delivering. Learn how to check a seller and what to do if you paid.

### What fake UGG websites do

Counterfeiters use websites and marketplace listings to make fake products look genuine. UGG says counterfeit sellers may copy its product photographs and website layouts, use unusually low prices and either send an inferior imitation or take payment and personal information without sending a product. UGG also says it actively works to remove counterfeit websites and marketplace listings.

Not every unfamiliar seller is necessarily fraudulent, and a low price alone does not prove that an item is fake. Treat several warning signs together as a reason to stop and verify the seller.

### Red flags to check

- The web address is not what you expected. UGG's official UK shop is at `ugg.com/uk/`. Look for misspellings, added words, unexpected characters or a different registrable domain.
- The domain itself uses UGG or a product name. UGG warns that a seller outside its own sites or authorised retailers whose domain includes “UGG”, a variation of it or a style name is likely to be selling counterfeits.
- The price is implausibly low. UGG identifies deep discounts as a common lure, but it does not publish a percentage at which an offer becomes fraudulent. Compare the exact style with UGG and established retailers.
- The seller information is weak. Missing or inconsistent contact details, policies, warranties or legal terms are warning signs.
- The site is badly assembled. Spelling errors, broken pages and inconsistent formatting can be clues, although a polished site can still be fake.
- The payment request is risky. Be especially cautious if a seller insists on bank transfer, cryptocurrency or another payment method with fewer purchase protections.
- Reviews exist only on the seller's site. Look at more than one independent source. Reviews and trust badges can be copied or manipulated.

An HTTPS connection or padlock only means that data is encrypted between your browser and that site. It does not establish that the seller is honest.

### How to verify a seller before buying

Go to UGG's official UK website at https://www.ugg.com/uk/ by typing the address yourself or using a saved bookmark. UGG says the safest options are UGG.com, an UGG shop, or a reputable and trusted retailer; its official site includes a store locator for authorised shops.

If buying elsewhere:

1. Check the complete domain, not just the page logo or search-result title.
2. Search for the retailer independently and compare its address, contact details and returns policy across reliable sources.
3. Compare the exact product and price with UGG's listing.
4. Use a card or a recognised payment service that offers a dispute process. Do not pay by bank transfer merely because the seller claims it is required.
5. Keep the product page, seller details, order confirmation and payment record.

Product photographs and packaging are not conclusive because counterfeiters copy genuine material and UGG changes labels, boxes and product details over time. UGG specifically notes that some genuine newer products may not carry the registered-trade-mark symbol.

### What to do if you have already paid

Contact your bank, card issuer or payment provider immediately using contact details from its official app, website or the back of your card. Explain whether the payment was authorised by you, whether goods arrived and whether they appear counterfeit.

- Debit or credit card: ask what dispute or chargeback process applies. Chargeback is a card-scheme process, not a guaranteed refund. A qualifying direct credit-card purchase with a cash price over £100 and up to £30,000 may also be covered by section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act; the rules can differ where an intermediary was used.
- UK bank transfer: ask the bank to treat it as a possible authorised push payment scam. Mandatory reimbursement protections cover many eligible Faster Payments and CHAPS scam payments made on or after 7 October 2024, subject to scope, limits and exceptions. A simple consumer dispute with a genuine trader is treated differently.
- Marketplace or payment service: open a case through its official buyer-protection or dispute channel immediately.

Save screenshots, the URL, order details, messages and transaction records. If an item arrives, photograph the product and packaging and follow your bank's, marketplace's or Trading Standards adviser’s instructions. Do not return it to an unverified address or pay an extra “release”, “customs” or refund fee without independently checking the request.

If you reused a password on the site, change it everywhere it was used and enable two-step verification. If you entered card details, follow your bank's advice about replacing the card and checking transactions.

### How to report it in the UK

- Report a suspicious website through the NCSC scam website reporting service at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website.
- Forward a suspicious email to `report@phishing.gov.uk`.
- You can forward a suspicious SMS text to `7726` free of charge. For RCS, iMessage and app messages, use the relevant built-in reporting tool.
- If money or information was stolen, report it to Report Fraud at https://www.reportfraud.police.uk/ or call `0300 123 2040` in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. In Scotland, report fraud to Police Scotland on `101`.
- For consumer advice, use the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.
- Notify UGG through the contact options on `ugg.com`; do not use contact details supplied by the suspect seller.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is `ugg.com/uk/` the official UK UGG website?**

Yes. The current official UK storefront is `https://www.ugg.com/uk/`. Check the registrable domain is exactly `ugg.com`.

**Does a padlock mean an UGG seller is genuine?**

No. It means the connection is encrypted. Scam sites can use HTTPS too.

**Does a very large discount prove the boots are fake?**

No single percentage proves fraud. UGG says unusually low prices are a warning sign, so verify the seller and compare the exact product before paying.

**Can I get my money back?**

Possibly, depending on the payment method and facts. Contact the provider promptly and ask about chargeback, section 75, APP-scam reimbursement or the marketplace's buyer protection. None should be described as an automatic refund.

**Where should I report a fake shop?**

Report the URL to the NCSC. If you lost money, use Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. You can also notify UGG.

## Is AliExpress a Scam? UK Guide to Marketplace Risk

URL: https://beatthescam.com/guides/aliexpress-scam-or-legit-uk-guide/
Category: Website Scams · Updated: 2026-07-13

AliExpress is an Alibaba marketplace, but listings and sellers vary. Keep payment on-platform and use the dispute or return deadline shown on the order.

### What is verified about the platform

Alibaba Group says AliExpress launched in 2010 as a global retail e-commerce platform that connects consumers with manufacturers and merchants. It is therefore inaccurate to describe the whole platform as a fabricated site.

Buyers can still encounter goods that do not arrive, do not match the listing, are unsafe or infringe intellectual-property rights. Assess the individual seller, listing and protection terms.

### Warning signs

- A price that is implausibly low for the claimed brand or specification.
- A seller with little history or reviews that do not discuss the actual product.
- Stock images with no useful buyer evidence.
- A request to pay, communicate or accept a refund outside AliExpress.
- Pressure to confirm receipt before inspection.

### Buyer Protection and Free Return are not one universal promise

AliExpress's 15-calendar-day Free Return window applies only to products carrying the `Free Return` label. It is a particular programme with its own eligibility and return-condition rules — not a universal 15-day guarantee for every order. Check the specific deadline shown on your own order rather than assuming the same window applies to non-delivery, damage or misdescription claims generally.

For a problem, open the order in the AliExpress account and use the dispute or return control before the deadline displayed there. Save screenshots of the listing, seller messages, tracking and the condition of the item.

Refund processing times vary by payment method and dispute type, so check the timeframe given for your specific case rather than assuming a fixed number of working days.

### UK card protection

Chargeback may apply under card-scheme rules, commonly with a time limit around 120 days. Section 75 may apply to a qualifying credit-card purchase where the cash price is over £100 and not more than £30,000, but a marketplace or payment intermediary can affect the required debtor-creditor-supplier relationship. Ask the issuer to assess the claim.

### Reporting

Use the order’s dispute process and AliExpress Help Centre. If the issue is fraud and money was lost, report at `reportfraud.police.uk` or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; in Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101. Unsafe products can also be reported to Citizens Advice for referral to Trading Standards.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is AliExpress owned by Alibaba Group?**

Yes. Alibaba Group identifies AliExpress as one of its e-commerce businesses.

**Does every AliExpress order have the same 15-day protection window?**

No. Fifteen days applies specifically to eligible `Free Return` products; other dispute rights and deadlines depend on the specific order.

**Is section 75 automatic on AliExpress?**

No. The cash-price and credit requirements matter, and the marketplace/payment structure may affect the claim.
